statement: In healthy volunteers given single analgesic amounts in crossover laboratory studies, how much of a ketamine dose reaches the bloodstream depends on the route. Measured against an intravenous dose in the same people, an intramuscular injection gave 93% (0.930, SE 0.026) and a swallowed solution 16.6% (0.166, SE 0.028), each the mean of four people, with a second calculation on all six people giving 19.5% (0.195, SE 0.028) for the swallowed solution (Clements et al., 1982). A later study of three men found 18.3% (SD 4.7) and 17.6% (SD 3.8), for the two mirror-image forms, after a swallowed tablet (Yanagihara et al., 2003), so a figure close to the 1982 one has been found by a second group, though not under the same condition: the earlier study used a solution drunk in orange juice and the later one two swallowed tablets, each measured against its own study's intravenous reference. The intramuscular figure has not been measured again in the sources read here, and the 2016 review repeats it beside a much larger intramuscular amount than the one at which it was measured. Blood levels rose fast after the intramuscular injection (peak 243 ng/mL, SE 49, at 22 minutes, SE 4; ketamine present in under 4 minutes; peaks between 100 and 425 ng/mL across people) and stayed low after the swallowed solution (peak 44 ng/mL, SE 10, range 15 to 80, at 30 minutes, SE 5). The 1982 abstract and results call the oral loss a failure to absorb, while the discussion of the same paper argues that absorption from the gut was complete and the drug was broken down in the liver before reaching the circulation; the metabolite figures in that paper support the discussion. Both headline figures rest on four people, the intravenous reference is described in a separate five-person study without saying who provided it, and no confidence interval appears anywhere in either paper. The time to peak the later study prints for the swallowed tablet cannot be reproduced from the sampling times that paper lists (study card sc_yanagihara_2003). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Almost all of a dose injected into a muscle reaches the blood: about 93 in every 100 parts, in one small study. When the same amount is swallowed, only about 17 in 100 gets there, because the liver breaks most of it down first. Both figures come from four people each. After a muscle injection the blood level peaks in about 20 minutes; after swallowing it peaks later and stays much lower. A later study of three men found about the same figure for swallowing.
population: Healthy fasting adult volunteers in two crossover laboratory studies reported together (5 people in the intravenous study, 6 in the intramuscular and oral study, with each bioavailability figure printed for 4 of them), and 3 healthy Japanese men aged 27 to 40 in the later study
exposure: A single amount of ketamine by one named route (study conditions: 0.25 and 0.125 mg of base per kg of body weight intravenously; 0.5 mg/kg as an intramuscular injection; 0.5 mg/kg as an oral solution in orange juice; and in the later study a 20 mg intravenous injection and a swallowed tablet containing 50 mg)
comparator: An intravenous dose in the same person as the reference for absolute availability, with saline on a separate occasion in the 1982 study
outcome: Share of the dose reaching the bloodstream (bioavailability), peak blood level and time to that peak
magnitude: Clements et al. (1982): intramuscular Farea 0.930 (SE 0.026, n=4 printed values 0.965, 0.923, 0.972, 0.859); oral Farea 0.166 (SE 0.028, n=4: 0.145, 0.163, 0.112, 0.245) and 0.195 (SE 0.028) from Eq. 2 across 6 people; intramuscular Cmax 243 ng/mL (SE 49) at tmax 22 min (SE 4); oral Cmax 44 ng/mL (SE 10) at 30 min (SE 5). Yanagihara et al. (2003), swallowed tablet in 3 men: bioavailability 18.3% (SD 4.7) for the (R)- and 17.6% (SD 3.8) for the (S)-enantiomer; Cmax 42.6 (SD 13.3) and 40.4 (SD 14.2) ng/mL at 33.3 (SD 15.3) and 30.0 (SD 30.0) min.

risk_of_bias.note: Order was randomized in the 1982 crossover and the two extravascular routes were masked against each other, but the method of randomization is not described, the assay is unvalidated in the report, both headline figures are printed for four of six people with no explanation, and the intravenous reference they are ratios to is described in a separate five-person study (card sc_clements_1982, overall high). The later tablet figure comes from an open, unrandomized study (card sc_yanagihara_2003, overall high).

inconsistency.note: The two independent oral estimates agree closely (16.6% and 19.5% against 18.3% and 17.6%), although they were made on different preparations; the intramuscular figure has no second measurement to disagree with.

indirectness.note: Bioavailability by route is measured directly in healthy volunteers, which is what the claim states.

imprecision.note: Four to six people in 1982 and three in 2003, with no confidence interval anywhere; the individual oral estimates run from 0.112 to 0.309 and intramuscular peak concentrations from 100 to 425 ng/mL.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two small primary studies.

grade.reasoning: Within-person controlled-administration studies with an intravenous reference start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for the missing individual data behind both headline figures, the untraceable intravenous reference and the unvalidated assay; imprecision −1 for four to six people per figure, three in the replication, and no intervals. Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the only route measured twice gave the same answer, or for indirectness. The status is replicated for the oral figure only, and for the number rather than the condition, because the two estimates come from different preparations (a solution and a tablet): the intramuscular figure of 93% rests on four people in one 1982 report and is still the figure reviews carry.

statement: In three healthy Japanese men who received five racemic ketamine preparations at least a week apart, measured against the same men's intravenous curves, about 32% of a sublingual tablet reached the bloodstream (32.2%, SD 8.2, and 32.1%, SD 7.2 for the two mirror-image forms), about 29 to 31% of a suppository (28.9%, SD 18.9, and 30.8%, SD 30.6) and about 44 to 46% of a nasal spray (43.8%, SD 11.4, and 46.4%, SD 12.9), the highest figure of the preparations tested (Yanagihara et al., 2003). Peak levels were between 29.3 and 61.6 ng/mL at about 17 to 40 minutes, and the metabolite norketamine was formed least after the nasal spray (area 115.9 and 100.7 ng·h/mL against 533.8 and 494.9 after the swallowed tablet, although the nasal pair is headed as the area to 8 hours in the table and called the area to 6 hours in the abstract and the discussion, because norketamine was below the detection limit 8 hours after the spray, so the two are not measured over the same window). Each figure is the mean of three men. Two of the conditions did not deliver what their names say: the men swallowed the sublingual tablets with saliva, so that condition was partly gastrointestinal, and not all of them had a bowel preparation before the suppository, which the authors give as the reason the rectal values varied so much that the spread is about the size of the figure itself. The study was open, the order of the five sessions is not described, no test statistic is printed, no elimination half-life is given for any of these preparations, and the two times to peak printed for the nasal spray cannot be means of three measurements taken at the sampling times the paper lists. A 2016 review nonetheless carries the rectal (about 30%) and nasal (about 45%) figures forward in its text, second-hand and without the sample size of three, which it prints only in its table. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: A small study gave three men ketamine in different forms, one at a time. Compared with an injection into a vein, about 45 in every 100 parts of a nasal spray reached the blood, about 30 in 100 of a tablet under the tongue and about 30 in 100 of a suppository. Only three men took part, the men swallowed the tablets that were meant to stay under the tongue, and the suppository figures varied enormously between them. The study says nothing about how long the drug lasted after these forms.
population: Three healthy Japanese men aged 27 to 40 and weighing 60 to 72 kg, each receiving all five preparations
exposure: A single racemic ketamine preparation (study conditions: two sublingual tablets containing 25 mg each, one suppository containing 50 mg, and an aqueous solution containing 25 mg given by nasal atomizer, each at least a week apart)
comparator: A 20 mg intravenous injection in the same men as the reference for absolute availability
outcome: Share of the dose reaching the bloodstream, peak level and time to peak, and norketamine exposure
magnitude: Bioavailability, (R)- then (S)-enantiomer: sublingual tablet 32.2% (SD 8.2) and 32.1% (SD 7.2); suppository 28.9% (SD 18.9) and 30.8% (SD 30.6); nasal spray 43.8% (SD 11.4) and 46.4% (SD 12.9); swallowed tablet 18.3% (SD 4.7) and 17.6% (SD 3.8) in the same men. Peaks 61.6 (SD 21.3) and 56.9 (SD 22.8) ng/mL at 40.0 and 36.7 min sublingual, 42.8 (SD 31.1) and 38.8 (SD 30.2) at 23.3 min rectal, 29.4 (SD 16.5) and 29.3 (SD 13.8) at 22.5 and 17.5 min nasal. Norketamine area 115.9 and 100.7 ng·h/mL nasal (headed as the area to 8 hours in Table 2, called the area to 6 hours in the abstract and the Discussion) against 533.8 and 494.9 to 8 hours after the swallowed tablet. n = 3 for every figure.

risk_of_bias.note: Open administration with no randomization, counterbalancing or order described; two conditions did not deliver what their labels say (sublingual tablets swallowed with saliva, suppositories without a standard bowel preparation); no test statistic, interval or individual value for any of seventy tabulated numbers; the assay's detection limit is never stated although conclusions rest on it (card sc_yanagihara_2003, overall high).

inconsistency.note: One study; no second measurement of any of these preparations in the sources read here.

indirectness.note: The preparations were measured directly; but the tablet and suppository were made by the authors' own group, so the figures describe those preparations, not every sublingual, rectal or nasal product.

grade.reasoning: A within-person crossover with an intravenous reference starts high (METHODS §6.3), but this one is open and unrandomized, two conditions were not delivered as labelled, and nothing is reported with a test statistic or an interval: risk of bias −2. Imprecision −1 for three men with standard deviations approaching the means. Very low, which is the floor. These are nevertheless the figures the 2016 review carries as the rectal and nasal bioavailability of ketamine, which is why the claim names their sample size.

statement: After a single intravenous amount in healthy volunteers, blood ketamine falls in two phases, fast at first and then over a few hours. In 1982 the terminal half-life was 186 minutes (standard error 10 in the text and 8 in the table) and total clearance 19.1 mL/min/kg; the half-life after an intramuscular injection was 155 minutes (SE 12), which the authors report as not significantly different from the intravenous value, and after a swallowed solution 174 minutes (SE 50), for which that paper prints no comparison at all (Clements et al., 1982). In three men in 2003 the terminal half-life after an intravenous injection was 126.8 minutes (SD 47.4) for the (R)- and 117.3 minutes (SD 47.9) for the (S)-form, with clearance 1.1 and 1.2 L/h/kg, and no half-life is printed for any of that study's other preparations (Yanagihara et al., 2003). A 2016 review gives, second-hand, a distribution half-life of 2 to 4 minutes and an elimination half-life of 2 to 4 hours, with 4 to 7 hours for S-ketamine. The body turns ketamine into norketamine: the review reports that about 80% is converted, that norketamine appears in plasma 2 to 3 minutes after an intravenous injection and peaks at 30 to 60 minutes, and that recent work indicates norketamine is itself broken down quickly and may not be the main substance circulating. Norketamine was measurable after every route in 1982, with peaks of 40 ng/mL (SE 6) after the intravenous, 92 (SE 10) after the intramuscular and 200 (SE 44) after the oral condition, while the dose-corrected areas (35.4, 31.3 and 36.7) were similar, which the authors read as showing that a swallowed dose is absorbed and then broken down in the liver before reaching the circulation. How long ketamine lasts after being taken under the tongue, given rectally or sprayed into the nose is not reported in either study; for a swallowed dose the only figure is the 1982 oral half-life of 174 minutes, whose standard error of 50 minutes is about a third of the mean. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: After a dose into a vein, the level in the blood drops quickly at first, then falls by half every two to three hours. Two small studies found about three hours and about two hours. The body turns most of the ketamine into another substance, norketamine, which shows up in the blood within minutes. After a swallowed dose there is much more norketamine than ketamine, because the liver changes most of it before it reaches the rest of the body. Only one rough figure is given for how long it lasts after a swallowed dose, and neither study gives one for a nose spray or the other ways of taking it.
population: Healthy volunteers in two small crossover laboratory studies (5 and 6 people in 1982; 3 men in 2003), with the ranges of a 2016 narrative review added second-hand
exposure: A single amount of ketamine by a named route (study conditions: 0.25 and 0.125 mg/kg intravenously, 0.5 mg/kg intramuscularly and 0.5 mg/kg as an oral solution in 1982; a 20 mg intravenous injection and four other preparations in 2003)
comparator: Within-person comparison between routes and between each person's own measurements over time; the review's summary of other studies
outcome: Terminal half-life and clearance of ketamine, and the formation and blood levels of its metabolite norketamine
magnitude: Clements et al. (1982): intravenous terminal half-life 186 min (SE 10 in the Results, SE 8 in Table II), clearance 19.1 mL/min/kg (SE 1.1); intramuscular 155 min (SE 12) and 23.2 mL/min/kg (SE 2.7); oral 174 min (SE 50). Norketamine peaks 40 (SE 6), 92 (SE 10) and 200 ng/mL (SE 44) at 63, 78 and 60 min, dose-corrected areas 35.4 (3.8), 31.3 (3.8) and 36.7 (3.9), described as not significantly different. Yanagihara et al. (2003), intravenous, n=3: 126.8 min (SD 47.4) for (R)- and 117.3 (SD 47.9) for (S)-ketamine; area 138.0 (15.6) and 126.3 (15.1) ng·h/mL; clearance 1.1 (0.2) and 1.2 (0.1) L/h/kg; steady-state volume of distribution 2.5 L/kg. Peltoniemi et al. (2016), second-hand: distribution half-life 2–4 min, elimination 2–4 h (S-ketamine 4–7 h), about 80% converted to norketamine.

risk_of_bias.note: Both primary studies are rated high overall by their cards: unvalidated assays with no stated detection limit, no protocol, missing values, and in the 2003 study an open, unrandomized order. The 1982 paper prints two different standard errors for its own half-life and a wrong unit for the areas.

inconsistency.note: The two intravenous half-lives (186 minutes and about 120 minutes) differ by about an hour, which the papers do not reconcile; the amounts, assays, samples and sampling periods differ, and the review's range of 2 to 4 hours brackets both. The 1982 paper itself shows that a shorter sampling period gives a much shorter apparent half-life from its own data (card sc_clements_1982), so the two figures are not measured in the same way. A strict reading that treats them as unexplained would downgrade one level and give very low.

indirectness.note: Half-life, clearance and metabolite formation were measured directly in healthy volunteers. The review's ranges are second-hand and are used only to frame the primary figures.

imprecision.note: Five or six people in 1982 and three in 2003, with no confidence intervals; the oral half-life has a standard error of 50 minutes on a mean of 174, and the 2003 half-lives have standard deviations of about 47 minutes.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two small primary studies.

grade.reasoning: Controlled-administration studies in volunteers start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for unvalidated assays, missing values and the 1982 paper's internal inconsistencies; imprecision −1 for three to six people and intervals that are never printed. Not downgraded for inconsistency: the two independent estimates are in the same range and the difference is explained by amount, assay and sample, though a strict reading would give very low. Replicated, because two independent groups measured the intravenous half-life and the first-pass formation of norketamine; the figures for how long ketamine lasts after the non-injected routes are missing from both.

statement: In healthy volunteers scanned while racemic or (S)-ketamine was being infused, brain activity measured as glucose use or the fMRI signal goes up rather than down, and most at the front. In 10 volunteers given racemic ketamine, whole-brain glucose metabolism rose 24.5% (SD 14.3) from each person's own drug-free scan and rose in every participant (p<0.01); the rise was largest in the anterior cingulate (34%) and frontal cortex (30 to 34%) and smallest in the occipitomedial cortex (16 to 17%), with no decrease in absolute glucose metabolism in any region examined, although relative metabolism (each region divided by the whole brain) fell in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex, and front-to-back ratios shifted accordingly (Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al., 1997). In a second group of 10 given the (S)-form, regional increases ran from 19.6% in the frontomedial to 27.35% in the parietal cortex, with cortical regions about 2 to 3 times more affected than deeper structures and the whole-brain change (12%) not reaching significance (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997). A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled the published peak coordinates of 33 functional-imaging studies in 628 healthy volunteers, and whose confidence the editors rate critically low, found only two clusters that survived correction for multiple testing, each resting on part of the 395 people in the two analyses that produced results rather than on all 628: more activity at rest in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (658 voxels, 495 after correction) and, during executive-function tasks, in the right Heschl's gyrus (160 voxels, 142 after correction); across all 23 task studies together nothing was significant in either direction, and no decrease is reported in any of the three analyses, which the review states outright for the pooled task analysis and which is what its table shows for the other two (Ait Bentaleb et al., 2024). Two things sit beside this. In the same Zurich laboratory the equimolar (R)-form moved the other way, lowering glucose metabolism significantly in two regions (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997; the figures are on card sc_vollenweider_1997a), so the direction given here is that of racemic and (S)-ketamine. And the 2016 review reports, second-hand, that at an anaesthetic amount of (S)-ketamine whole-brain blood flow rose while the metabolic rate of oxygen and of glucose stayed virtually unchanged, so blood flow and energy use need not move together. What these scans cannot show is which change produces which experience: both 1997 studies report every symptom-to-brain correlation as a significance level with a direction and print no correlation coefficient anywhere, they made about 150 to 180 comparisons without correcting for their number, which the enantiomer paper states and calls exploratory while the companion paper calls its correlational results only preliminary and nowhere says whether any correction was made; one of them had no dummy condition and in the other every participant recognised the drug. All of this describes a single session with ketamine in the body, not any lasting change. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people are given ketamine in a scanner, their brain uses more energy, not less, especially at the front. In one study of 10 healthy people, whole-brain energy use rose by about a quarter, and it rose in every single person. A 2024 summary of 33 imaging studies found the clearest agreement in one spot near the front of the brain at rest. One mirror-image form of ketamine, called R, moved the other way and lowered energy use in two areas. These scans cannot show which brain change causes which feeling, and they only describe what happens while the drug is in the body.
population: Healthy volunteers screened to be free of psychiatric history and of non-medical drug use: 10 in each of the two Zurich PET studies (6 men and 4 women in each), and 628 people in the 33 studies pooled by the 2024 meta-analysis, of whom 395 are in the two analyses that produced results
exposure: Subanaesthetic intravenous ketamine during the scan (study conditions in Zurich: a 20 mg or 15 mg induction amount in saline over 5 minutes, 5 minutes with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.02–0.03 or 0.014–0.02 mg/kg/min for 60 or 53 minutes; in the pooled studies, intravenous amounts the review describes as within the range used in depression trials)
comparator: The same people's drug-free baseline scan (Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al., 1997) or placebo scan (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997); placebo or a baseline condition in the pooled studies, 7 of 10 resting-state studies being within-person
outcome: Whole-brain and regional glucose metabolism, cerebral blood flow or activation during the drug
magnitude: Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al. (1997), racemic, n=10: whole-brain glucose metabolism +24.5% (SD 14.3, Wilcoxon p<0.01, higher in every participant); cingulate anterior +34%, frontal +30 to 34%, insula +19 to 23%, parietal +18 to 25%, somatosensory +19 to 25%, motor +15 to 18%, temporal +16 to 19%, occipitomedial +16 to 17%; no decreases. Frontomedial/temporomedial ratio 1.31→1.44 (left) and 1.41→1.53 (right), frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04→1.14 and 1.06→1.16 (all p<0.05). Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al. (1997), (S)-ketamine, n=10: frontomedial +19.6%, frontolateral +20.1%, cingulate anterior +23.5%, cingulate posterior +24.0%, parietal +27.35%; thalamus +17% (p<0.07); whole brain +12% (p<0.09, not significant). Ait Bentaleb et al. (2024): resting state, left anterior cingulate/paracingulate BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z=4.265, p<0.001, 658 voxels, 495 after correction; uncorrected only, right insula BA 47 (36; 24; −6), Z=3.432, 30 voxels, and right fusiform gyrus BA 30 (22; −34; −16), Z=2.933, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks (9 studies): right Heschl's gyrus BA 48 (44; −16; 6), Z=3.306, 160 voxels, 142 after correction; uncorrected right rostral anterior cingulate BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z=2.889, 26 voxels. No effect size or interval is recoverable from a coordinate-based meta-analysis.

risk_of_bias.note: The racemic study was open with a drug-free baseline instead of a dummy infusion, and in the enantiomer study every participant recognised the drug, so expectancy is uncontrolled for both the scans and the ratings; regions of interest were placed by hand with no stated blinding; about 150 to 180 comparisons were made without correction and regions, ratios and correlations are reported selectively (cards sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b, both high). The 2024 meta-analysis appraised none of its primary studies, has no protocol and is rated critically low confidence (card sc_ait_bentaleb_2024).

inconsistency.note: The direction is the same everywhere: increases, largest frontally, and no decrease in any analysis. The meta-analysis's null result across all task domains is explained by pooling studies of different cognitive tasks.

indirectness.note: Healthy volunteers scanned during the drug, which is what the claim states. Nothing here speaks to repeated use, to people who use ketamine outside a laboratory or to people with a psychiatric diagnosis.

imprecision.note: Ten people in each Zurich study and 5 to 34 per pooled study; a coordinate-based meta-analysis recovers no effect size or interval, and the two corrected clusters are the only results that survive a stringent threshold.

publication_bias.note: Egger's tests were run and were null, but with 9 or 10 studies they have almost no power, and only studies that published whole-brain peaks can enter such a meta-analysis.

dose_response.note: Blood level did not predict the metabolic change in the racemic study, and every dose moderator in the meta-analysis was null in 9 or 10 studies.

grade.reasoning: Within-person challenge studies start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −2: one study had no dummy condition at all, the other's blind did not hold, and both report many uncorrected comparisons selectively, while the meta-analysis pooling the wider literature appraised no primary study. Imprecision −1: ten people per Zurich study, small primary studies, and no recoverable effect size from the pooled maps. Not downgraded for inconsistency or indirectness. Very low, the floor. Replicated in direction, but counted carefully: the two FDG studies come from one laboratory in Zurich and share their method, so the independent support is the 2024 meta-analysis, whose resting-state cluster sits in the same anterior cingulate region and which does not include either Zurich study.

statement: In 10 healthy volunteers who received, a month apart and in counterbalanced order, a placebo scan, (S)-ketamine and an equimolar amount of (R)-ketamine, the two mirror-image forms did different things. (S)-ketamine produced a short-lived psychosis-like state: depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances from pseudohallucinations to complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy, with heightened feelings or euphoria reported by 30%, indifference by 30% and heightened anxiety by 40%, alongside higher scores for deactivation, introversion, emotional irritability and anxiety on a mood scale. The same people on (R)-ketamine reported no psychotic symptoms but a state of relaxation, with only trend-level changes on the scales. Every one of the 10 scored higher under (S)- than under (R)-ketamine on both global scales (altered-states score 37.0, SD 12.6, against 15.6, SD 8.6; ego-pathology score 24.6, SD 11.8, against 1.3, SD 1.6). The printed altered-states mean and standard deviation for the (S) condition do not follow from the ten per-person values printed above them, which give 38.2 (SD 10.3); the printed pair is the one printed for racemic ketamine in the companion study, a different ten people (cards sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b). The brain scans went in opposite directions: (S)-ketamine raised glucose metabolism across most regions, while (R)-ketamine tended to lower it, significantly in the temporomedial cortex on both sides (−13.4%) and the left insula (−14%). Blood levels were similar in the two conditions (mean 379 ng/mL, SD 71, against 389, SD 74) (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997). Three things limit this. The blind did not hold: every participant recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect, and all had had an (S)-ketamine session beforehand. The two forms were not compared with the racemic mixture in these same people, so the conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic part of racemic ketamine rests on a comparison with the different sample of the companion study, not on anything measured here; the amounts over a session do work out at about the 60% of the racemic amount the paper states, once the shorter infusion is counted (editors' recomputation on card sc_vollenweider_1997a), but the potency ratio behind that choice comes from a pilot study reported in one sentence without a sample size, a method or a reference. And a separate three-person study found no significant difference between the forms in how the body handles them, which with three people and no test statistic says very little (Yanagihara et al., 2003). A 2016 review reports, second-hand, that S-ketamine has about four times the affinity of R-ketamine for the NMDA receptor and has been postulated to be about four times as potent as R-ketamine and twice as potent as the racemate, that R-ketamine slows the elimination of S-ketamine (clearance 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine alone against 18.5 for the S-form inside the racemate in ten healthy men), and that it contradicts itself on which form produces more of the psychosis-like effects: its pharmacodynamics section reports more auditory and visual disturbances with the S-form, while its abstract and summary report fewer such effects with S-ketamine than with the racemate or the R-form. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Ketamine comes in two mirror-image forms, S and R. In one study, 10 healthy people were given each form on different days, a month apart. The S form produced a short psychosis-like state with hallucinations and a changed sense of self; every single person scored higher on it than on the R form. The R form produced no such symptoms, just a relaxed state. Brain scans moved in opposite directions too. But everyone could tell when they had been given a drug, only 10 people took part, and the study did not compare the forms with the ordinary mixture in the same people.
population: 10 healthy volunteers (6 men, 4 women, mean age 30.4 years) screened for absence of personal and family psychiatric history and of non-medical drug use, each acting as their own control; separately, 3 healthy men in the pharmacokinetic study
exposure: Intravenous (S)- or (R)-ketamine (study conditions: a 15 mg induction amount in 20 mL saline over 5 minutes, 5 minutes with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014–0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 minutes, the (R) condition equimolar to the (S) condition)
comparator: The same people's placebo scan and their other enantiomer condition
outcome: Psychopathology and mood ratings for the scan period, and regional brain glucose metabolism during the infusion; in the second study, pharmacokinetic parameters of the two enantiomers
magnitude: Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al. (1997), n=10, within-person: altered-states global score 37.0 (SD 12.6) under (S)-ketamine against 15.6 (SD 8.6) under (R)-ketamine; ego-pathology global score 24.6 (SD 11.8) against 1.3 (SD 1.6); higher under (S) in all 10 participants (editors' calculation of the within-person difference: 22.6 points, SD 6.3, and 23.3 points, SD 10.9; exact two-sided sign test p = 0.002). Emotional reactions under (S): euphoria or heightened feelings 30%, indifference 30%, heightened anxiety 40%. (R)-ketamine: no psychotic symptoms; oceanic boundlessness p<0.06, well-being p<0.09, emotional irritation p<0.08. Glucose metabolism under (R): whole brain −9.8% (p<0.07, not significant), temporomedial cortex −13.4% bilaterally and left insula −14% (p<0.05). Blood levels 269 to 523 ng/mL (mean 379, SD 71) under (S) and 280 to 508 (mean 389, SD 74) under (R).

evidence.locator: Results › Psychopathology (3.2.1) and (3.2.2)
evidence.extracted: (S)-ketamine produced depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances ranging from pseudohallucinations to elementary and complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy, with auditory changes described as illusions rather than true hallucinations, and emotional reactions of heightened feelings or euphoria in 30%, indifference in 30% and heightened anxiety in 40%; mood-scale scores rose for deactivation (p<0.01), introversion (p<0.05), emotional irritability (p<0.05) and anxiety (p<0.01). Equimolar (R)-ketamine produced no psychotic symptoms in the same people but a state of relaxation, with oceanic boundlessness rising only at trend level (p<0.06), well-being at p<0.09 and emotional irritation falling at p<0.08.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 201 (claim writer)

The printed means are 37.0 (SD 12.6) and 24.6 (SD 11.8) against 15.6 (SD 8.6) and 1.3 (SD 1.6). Editors' calculation from those ten pairs: every participant scored higher under (S)-ketamine, the within-person difference being 22.6 points (SD 6.3) for the altered-states score and 23.3 (SD 10.9) for ego pathology (exact two-sided sign test p = 0.002); the printed (S) altered-states mean and SD do not reproduce from the ten values above them, which give 38.2 and 10.3.

risk_of_bias.note: Within-person, placebo-controlled and counterbalanced, but the blind did not hold (every participant recognised the (R)-ketamine condition and all had had a prior (S)-ketamine session), the ratings are partly self-reported and partly made by an unblinded psychiatrist, the method of counterbalancing is not described, and about 180 comparisons were made without correction (card sc_vollenweider_1997a, overall high).

inconsistency.note: One study for the psychopathological contrast; the direction was the same in all 10 participants. The three-person pharmacokinetic null result concerns a different outcome and is reported as a qualifier.

indirectness.note: The claim is about the two pure forms given in a laboratory, which is what was tested. The comparison with the racemic mixture is indirect, resting on a different sample in the companion paper, and the statement says so.

imprecision.note: Ten people in one laboratory; most outcomes are reported as percentage changes with significance levels and no intervals, and the smallest attainable two-sided p in these paired tests is 0.002.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from a single laboratory study; the study was supported in part by a pharmaceutical company, which the card records as a flag.

large_effect.note: Not applied: upgrades apply only to evidence that starts low (METHODS §6.3), although the difference was large and in the same direction in every participant.

grade.reasoning: A within-person, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced study starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: the blind did not hold for self-rated and observer-rated outcomes, and the reporting is selective and uncorrected. Imprecision −1: ten people in one laboratory, with no intervals or effect sizes printed. Low. The size of the contrast is nevertheless unusually clear for such a small study, because every participant scored higher under (S)-ketamine on both global scales. What the study cannot support is the further step to racemic ketamine as people encounter it, or the review's second-hand potency ratios, which the review itself calls a postulate.

statement: In people who use several drugs, tested by one research group at University College London at parties, nightclubs or squat parties within 30 minutes of saying they had taken ketamine, ketamine use that night compared with no ketamine that night is associated with much lower scores on most memory and thinking tests and with strong self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like experiences and bodily and perceptual changes; three days later most of these differences had gone, but some memory differences remained and, in one of the two studies, dissociation and psychosis-like scores were still higher; these studies cannot attribute what remained to the night of use. On the night (Curran & Morgan, 2000), 20 people who had taken ketamine, against 19 peers from the same settings who had not (all 20 in the ketamine group and 17 of the 19 peers had also smoked cannabis that night), recalled 3.83 against 8.61 ideas of a short story (maximum 21), correctly judged 42.35 against 76.05 sentences in 2 minutes, made 10.8 against 22.37 correct serial-seven subtractions and named 11.20 against 17.74 category members; an implicit (word-stem) memory task did not differ. They rated dissociation at 44.00 against 5.47, and impaired memory at 72.40 against 16.63, bodily numbness at 60.30 against 6.16 and altered time perception at 59.60 against 9.79 on ratings from no symptom to severe symptom. In a second sample with no group free of ketamine (Curran & Monaghan, 2001; 18 people who used ketamine more than twice a month and 19 who used it less), both groups scored similarly low on story recall and category naming on the night (although letter fluency was already lower in the more frequent group, 10.39 against 17.42), rated very high dissociation (34.83 and 39.26) and rated themselves more sedated and more anxious than three days later. Three days later, at home (by their own account no one had taken ketamine on days 1 to 3, although 36% of the 2000 ketamine group had taken more after the first test that night and everyone in that study had used alcohol or cannabis on days 1 and 2), the 2000 groups no longer differed in serial-seven subtractions (21.30 against 23.37) or digit-cancellation times, and their symptom ratings (11 of 14 with group × day interactions) were similar apart from a trend to more self-rated memory problems in the ketamine group (26.45 against 11.95); in the second sample dissociation had fallen to 4.56 and 3.47, while the more frequent group still rated more impaired memory (35.94 against 15.42) and concentration (33.11 against 12.74) than the less frequent group, rated more sedation on both days and more often reported alcohol on the day of the retest (8 of 18 against 4 of 19, timing not stated). Story recall was still lower in the 2000 ketamine group (7.75 against 10.18) but did not differ from the comparison group's first-night score, which the authors attribute to missed practice after poor memory of the first session; category naming and sentence judging were lower on both days, which fits differences that predate the night, after-effects or missed practice: the paper's practice check found no difference for category naming, and its check for sentence judging, printed as p<0.009, gives p ≈ 0.04 on the editors' recalculation from its own table, about the same as for category naming. In the second sample, by day 3 the group that used ketamine less often recalled about twice as much of the story as the group that used it more often (9.16 against 4.56), whose immediate recall was no better than on the night (its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39); the more frequent group had less schooling. The studies disagree on whether dissociation and psychosis-like scores stay raised: three days after use they were still higher in the 2000 ketamine group than in its comparison group (17.75 against 5.37; 62.35 against 26.42), but low in both groups of the second sample; the same team describes a laboratory study in which healthy volunteers given ketamine did not differ from volunteers given placebo three days later (second-hand, as described by Morgan et al., 2009). In the 2000 study a single depression rating did not differ between groups on either day, and depression scores on an anxiety and depression questionnaire were somewhat higher in the ketamine group on both days (the first rating covered the two days up to the test on the night) and below the range the authors call clinically significant, while anxiety did not differ. Neither study asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it. Use was self-reported and not tested, amounts and content are unknown, and the testers were not reported to be blind to group. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: At parties and clubs, people tested within half an hour of taking ketamine did far worse on memory and thinking tests than people there who had not taken it: they remembered less than half as much of a short story, for example. They felt strongly cut off from their body and surroundings, numb, and as if time had changed. Three days later, at home, their attention scores matched the other group's and most of these feelings had gone. Some memory scores were still lower; this may be because people remembered little of the first test and so had less practice, because of after-effects, or because the groups were different to begin with. One study found that feeling detached was still higher after three days; the other did not. In that other study, three days later, people who used ketamine more often rated their memory and concentration as worse than people who used it less often. What people took was never tested, and both studies come from one research team.
population: Young adults who use several drugs, recruited at private parties, nightclubs and squat parties by one research group at University College London and tested where they were using drugs: 20 who had taken ketamine that night and 19 who had not (Curran & Morgan, 2000); 18 who used ketamine more than twice a month and 19 who used it less, all of whom had taken it that night (Curran & Monaghan, 2001)
exposure: Ketamine taken that evening, by self-report, within 30 minutes before the first test; amount and content not verified
comparator: Peers from the same parties or club with little or no ketamine use who had not taken it that night (2000); in the 2001 sample no group without ketamine: people who used it twice a month or less against people who used it more often, and each group against itself three days later
outcome: Memory, thinking and attention test scores, and self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like (schizotypal) experiences, bodily and perceptual symptoms and mood, on the night of use and three days later
magnitude: Curran & Morgan (2000), 20 against 19, within 30 minutes of reported use (day 0) and 3 days later (day 3), means (SD): day 0 immediate story recall 3.83 (2.17) against 8.61 (2.57), delayed 2.48 (1.50) against 6.87 (3.32); sentences correctly judged 42.35 (13.33) against 76.05 (21.45); serial sevens 10.8 (6.56) against 22.37 (8.19); category fluency 11.20 (4.38) against 17.74 (5.39); letter fluency 16.00 (4.59) against 21.32 (5.42); cancellation time 69.90 (18.46) against 54.92 (11.66) s; word-stem targets 3.00 against 3.58 (no difference); standardized differences about 0.9 to 2.0 (editors' calculation). Dissociation 44.00 against 5.47 (day 0), 17.75 (SD 17.41) against 5.37 (day 3, p<0.008); schizotypal 87.40 against 33.37, 62.35 against 26.42 (p<0.001). Symptom ratings day 0: impaired memory 72.40 against 16.63, numbness 60.30 against 6.16, altered time 59.60 against 9.79; 11 of 14 ratings with group × day interactions; day 3 impaired memory 26.45 against 11.95 (trend, p<0.04). Day 3: serial sevens 21.30 against 23.37; cancellation 58.45 against 57.96 s; immediate recall 7.75 against 10.18; category fluency 14.85 against 19.68; sentences 63.30 against 79.11 (practice check printed p<0.009, editors' recalculation p ≈ 0.04). HADS depression 4.45 against 1.89 (day 0, covering the two days before) and 4.30 against 1.68 (day 3), below the 8–11 range. Curran & Monaghan (2001), 18 (13.53 days a month) against 19 (0.45 days a month): day 0 immediate recall 4.67 and 5.00, letter fluency 10.39 against 17.42, dissociation 34.83 and 39.26; day 3 dissociation 4.56 and 3.47, schizotypal 25.28 and 28.95 (no group differences); day 3 immediate recall 4.56 against 9.16 and delayed 4.39 against 8.05 (interaction F(1,35) = 13.5 and 6.7; the more frequent group's delayed recall was 3.11 on day 0), category fluency 14.06 against 18.95; day-3 ratings of impaired memory 35.94 against 15.42 and impaired concentration 33.11 against 12.74; alcohol on day 3 in 8 of 18 against 4 of 19.

evidence.extracted: Two groups of people who all used several drugs, recruited at private parties or a nightclub and aged 18 to 29: 20 who had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing, and 19 who had little or no previous ketamine use and had not taken it that evening. Both groups were tested on the night (day 0) in a small quiet room away from the music and again 3 days later (day 3) in their homes, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order; 7 more people tested once were not retested and 2 were discarded for taking drugs on the day of the second session. Story (prose) recall was scored in idea units, maximum 21, and the speed of comprehension test asked people to judge as many of 100 sentences as they could in 2 minutes. The self-ratings were an adapted dissociative states scale, a state schizotypal symptom questionnaire built for the study, a mood scale, 14 symptom ratings anchored at no symptom and severe symptom, and an anxiety and depression questionnaire rated for the last two days; no measure asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it.

risk_of_bias.note: Groups were formed by what people chose to take that night; use was self-reported and never tested (hair collected but not analysed); the testers were not reported to be blind to group; alcohol and cannabis use between the sessions was neither controlled nor verified; the schizotypy questionnaire was built for the study and the dissociation scale used only its self-rated items; the ketamine group of the first study differed in education and past antidepressant use; several printed statistics do not match their tables (cards sc_curran_2000 and sc_curran_2001: ROBINS-E very high overall, high for the night-of-use contrast).

inconsistency.note: The two studies agree on the night of use and on the fading of attention deficits and dissociation by day 3, but disagree on whether dissociation and psychosis-like scores stay raised after three days, which the authors cannot explain.

indirectness.note: People who use ketamine tested where they use it, which is the population asked about; because amounts and content are unknown, the results cannot be tied to any amount.

imprecision.note: 20 and 19, and 18 and 19 people; the night-of-use differences are large and clear, but the day-3 differences sit near the limit of what samples this size can detect (card sc_curran_2000, power).

large_effect.note: Standardized differences on the night are about 1 to 2 (editors' calculation), but a large difference between small self-selected groups does not qualify for an upgrade (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Within the ketamine group of the first study the reported amount taken did not correlate with any cognitive or symptom score (card sc_curran_2000); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational field studies outside a laboratory start low (round brief; METHODS §6.3) and are rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (the day-3 findings) and imprecision, below the floor: very low. Strict reading: the direction of the night-of-use differences is not in doubt, given their size, their reappearance in a second sample and the authors' report that they match laboratory studies of single doses, but their size and what remains on day 3 are very uncertain. Overlapping evidence: both studies come from one laboratory with the same test battery; the samples are distinct (20 and 19; 18 and 19), so the status is replicated by the same team, not replicated. statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with lower scores on some memory and planning tests, but not on others, when people are tested within days of their last use; in the largest study people who used ketamine less often did not score lower, but in a smaller field study a group who used it from once a month to twice a week did, three days after a night of use. Whether ketamine causes the differences is unknown. In the largest comparison (Morgan et al., 2009; five groups of 30, one session after a required 24 hours without psychotropic drugs), people who used ketamine more than four times a week (19 of 30 said daily), tested a mean of 1.6 days after last use (range 1 to 7; the follow-up paper gives a mean of 2 days, SD 2.60 rather than 1.27, for the same session), solved fewer planning problems in the fewest moves (7.66 against 8.89 to 9.53) and recognised fewer patterns (about 83% against 90% to 95%, editors' reading of a figure) than each of the other four groups, which included 30 people who used other drugs but not ketamine and 30 who used no illicit drugs, and made more errors on a spatial working-memory task (about 32 against 11 to 19, editors' reading of a figure; the paper does not say against which groups this difference was tested); their word recognition was lower too, although the editors could reproduce only one of the reported pairwise differences from the printed table. Story recall, letter and category fluency, a response-inhibition test and memory for which voice spoke a word did not differ, and people who used ketamine less often (a mean of 3.25 days a month, last use a mean of 11.3 days before) and people who had stopped did not differ from the controls on any test. The frequent group had fewer years of education (12.27 against 14.23 to 15.33), a lower vocabulary-test estimate of earlier ability (45.67 against 47.13 to 51.53) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3), none adjusted for, and it was tested so soon after use that withdrawal or other after-effects of recent use cannot be excluded (the authors raise withdrawal). A year later (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010; the same people, 25 of the 30 retested), averaged over both sessions the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than every other group and recognised fewer patterns than the groups who used ketamine less often or had stopped, with no difference from the two control groups reported; but its mean errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' 88.41% and 89.58% (changes the paper did not test), and its planning score improved into the other groups' range, although 22 of the 25 were still using ketamine at least monthly. Two smaller field studies by the same team, which tested people three days after a night of use, found lower story recall and category fluency: in a group who used ketamine from once a month to twice a week, against peers with little or no ketamine use (Curran & Morgan, 2000), and in people who used it more than twice a month (a reported 13.53 days a month) against people who used it less (Curran & Monaghan, 2001), a comparison in which the more frequent group had less schooling and already had lower letter fluency on the night of use. The larger study did not find these differences. The 2000 paper itself attributes its day-3 story-recall difference to missed practice in a design that tested people while intoxicated first; its practice checks do not separate the category-naming and sentence-judging differences from missed practice either (sentence judging by the editors' recalculation); and the larger study's authors extend the explanation to the earlier story-recall differences. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In one London team's studies, people who used ketamine more than four times a week, tested a day or a few days after they last used it, did worse than people who used other drugs or none on some memory and planning tasks, such as remembering which boxes they had already searched and recognising patterns. They did as well at remembering a story and at naming words. In this study, people who used ketamine a few times a month did as well as everyone else. The frequent group also had less schooling and lower scores on a vocabulary test, and more of them had family members with mental illness, so the tests cannot show that ketamine caused the difference. A year later, the same people's scores had moved closer to the others', even though most were still using. Earlier, smaller studies that tested people three days after a night out found lower story and word scores, even in a group who used ketamine a few times a month, compared with people who hardly used it; part of this may be because they remembered little of the first test and so had less practice.
population: People who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London: five groups of 30 recruited from the unit's database and by word of mouth (25 of the 30 frequent participants retested a year later), and two smaller samples recruited at parties, nightclubs and squat parties
exposure: Frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week in the main study; more than twice a month in one field study), by self-report checked with hair analysis in the main study; less frequent use (at least once a month and less than four times a week)
comparator: 30 people who used other drugs but not ketamine and 30 who used no illicit drugs, tested the same way; in the field studies, peers with little or no ketamine use, or people who used ketamine twice a month or less
outcome: Memory, planning and attention test scores in sessions without intoxication: at least 24 hours (a mean of 1.6 days, range 1 to 7, for the frequent group) after last use in the main study, 3 days after a night of use in the field studies
magnitude: Morgan et al. (2009), 30 per group, frequent group tested 1.6 days (range 1–7; 2 days, SD 2.60, by the follow-up paper) after last use: spatial working-memory errors about 32 against about 11–19 (editors' reading of Figure 1; F(4, 145) = 8.05); strategy 32.73 against 26.53–28.93; Stockings problems in minimum moves 7.66 against 8.89–9.53 (F(4, 145) = 6.58); pattern recognition about 83% against about 90–95% (editors' reading of Figure 2; F(4, 145) = 6.37); word recognition d′ 2.36 against 2.67–2.97 (F(4, 145) = 2.74; only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces, editors' recalculation). No differences: story recall (immediate 8.11–8.32), letter fluency (15.14–17.53), category fluency (14.73–17.27), Hayling test. Infrequent (3.25 days a month) and ex-ketamine groups: no differences from controls. Confounders: education 12.27 against 14.23–15.33 years; spot-the-word 45.67 against 47.13–51.53; family history of mental illness 8 of 30 against 1–3. Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al. (2010), 25 of 30 frequent retested (mean interval 366.6 days for all retested participants): errors 29.58 to 19.92 (other groups 11.48–18.32, then 12.48–15.89); pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (controls 88.41% and 89.58% at follow-up; averaged over both sessions lower than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups only; mean changes not tested); Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (others 9.33–9.87 at follow-up). Field studies, 3 days after use: category fluency 14.85 against 19.68 (2000) and 14.06 against 18.95 (2001); story recall 7.75 against 10.18 (2000) and 4.56 against 9.16 (2001); sentences correctly judged 63.30 against 79.11 (2000; practice check printed p<0.009, p ≈ 0.04 on the editors' recalculation); the 2000 ketamine group used ketamine from once a month to twice a week.

risk_of_bias.note: Education, premorbid ability and family history of mental illness differ and are not adjusted for; testers knew the groups; recruitment partly from the unit's own database; exposure self-reported, checked by hair for ketamine only; the 24 hours without psychotropic drugs before testing could not be verified, and the frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days after use by one report of the session (a mean of 2 days with a wider spread by the other); several post hoc results in the 2009 tables cannot be reproduced; 5 of the 30 frequent participants were not retested at one year (cards sc_morgan_2009 and sc_morgan_2010b: ROBINS-E high; sc_curran_2000 and sc_curran_2001: very high).

inconsistency.note: The studies agree in direction, but not on which tests differ: story recall and category fluency were lower three days after a night of use in both field studies and did not differ in the larger study; the larger study's spatial working-memory and pattern-recognition differences narrowed over a year in people still using. The 2000 field study's ketamine group used ketamine at the frequency the larger study calls infrequent (once a month to twice a week), yet scored lower three days after a night of use, while the larger study's infrequent group did not.

indirectness.note: The comparison is the one asked about; how soon after use people were tested (1 to 7 days, 3 days) is stated for each result.

imprecision.note: 30 per group (25 retested), 18 to 20 per group in the field studies; the null results (story recall, fluency) do not exclude moderate differences, and several of the reported pairwise differences depend on the analysis.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: Differences appear in the most frequent group only and not in people using a few times a month, but the groups also differ in education and family history, and the one-year correlations between change in amount and change in scores are weaker in the plotted data than in the text (card sc_morgan_2010b); no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Less education and lower premorbid estimates in the frequent group would more plausibly enlarge than hide the differences; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low. Overlapping evidence: Morgan et al. (2009) and Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al. (2010) report the same participants and count once; the two field studies are separate samples from the same laboratory; the 2009 sample came partly from the unit's database, so overlap with the earlier samples cannot be excluded. Status mixed rather than replicated by the same team: every comparison points the same way (lower scores with frequent use on some tests), but which tests differ is inconsistent between the field studies and the larger study, and the proposed explanation (missed practice in the two-session design) fits the 2000 paper's own practice checks but cannot be separated from other explanations in these designs. Rated as worded, an association; whether it lasts or reverses after stopping is the separate, contested claim on what happens after people cut down or stop (section 9). The narrative review (Morgan et al., 2012) is used only to qualify, and its causal wording is not adopted.

statement: In people who used ketamine frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether lower memory and thinking scores fade after they cut down or stop, and the question is contested. People who had stopped scored no lower than people who did not use ketamine: 30 people abstinent for at least a month by their own account (a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980, although their hair, covering about the previous 3 months, held some ketamine on average) did not differ on any test from 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs (Morgan et al., 2009), and the 23 or 24 of them retested a year later (the paper's tables and text differ), 3 of whom had resumed at least monthly use, again showed no deficits (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010); but they were different people from the frequent group and had used less before stopping (2.55 days a month just before stopping and a group peak of 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13), although 12 had once used frequently and 8 daily and the group had used ketamine for more years (7.63 against 6.07), so these comparisons cannot show recovery, as the authors themselves state. In the only study that retested a group of people who had cut down (Morgan et al., 2004), 18 of the 57 ketamine participants of two earlier field studies (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down how often they used (from a mean of 6.45 to 1.61 days a month, although the amount they reported taking per occasion rose; 8 had not used for more than 6 months), were retested 3 to 4 years after a session held 3 days after a night of use, beside 10 polydrug controls: their lower category fluency no longer differed (group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032), a gain the authors report as correlated with the reduction in use (r = 0.712) and, as strongly, with time since last use (r = 0.723); but immediate story recall and digit-cancellation speed (66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 seconds) were lower at both sessions with no reported change, delayed recall was lower overall while the controls' fell at follow-up, and sentence judging was lower across both sessions although it appeared to improve, which fits differences that were there before as well as lasting effects, as the authors concede for story recall; the authors also note that the participants from the second field study were already slower on the attention task at the first session. People who were still using a year later (22 of 25 at least monthly; 20.08 days a month for all 30 at the first session, 16.0 for the 25 at follow-up) had better mean scores on spatial working memory (errors 29.58 to 19.92) and pattern recognition (83.68% to 89.04%), changes the paper did not test, and significantly better strategy and planning scores (P = 0.003 each), which the authors attribute partly to practice on tasks with only one version and to a poor start; their reported correlations between change in amount and change in errors and pattern recognition (r = 0.623 and −0.732) are weaker in the plotted points (about 0.55 and −0.55, editors' calculation). Letter fluency fell over the year in the abstinent and frequent groups, and also in both control groups. All the evidence comes from one research group, with self-reported use. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Nobody knows yet whether the memory differences seen in people who use ketamine most days go away after they cut down or stop. In one London team's studies, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month, most of them for many months, did as well on memory and thinking tests as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But they were different people, most of whom had used less before stopping, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything. The only study that followed a group who had cut down retested 18 people: after 3 to 4 years, one word test had caught up with the comparison group, while story memory and speed stayed lower, as they had been at the first test. That could mean lasting effects, or differences that were there before they started. People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, partly perhaps from practice.
population: People who used ketamine frequently and then stopped or cut down, studied by one research group at University College London: an ex-ketamine group of 30 (23 or 24 retested a year later, by the paper's tables and text) and 18 people from two earlier field studies who had cut down, retested after 3 to 4 years
exposure: Stopping ketamine (abstinent for at least a month, a mean of 344 days) or cutting down (from a mean of 6.45 to 1.61 days a month)
comparator: People who used other drugs but not ketamine and people who used no illicit drugs, tested at the same times; people who still used ketamine frequently
outcome: Memory and thinking test scores after stopping or cutting down, and their change over time
magnitude: Ex-ketamine group (Morgan et al., 2009; 30 people, abstinent a mean of 344.43 days, range 120–2980, hair ketamine 3.55 (13.63) ng/mm; 2.55 days a month before stopping, peak 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13): no differences from 30 polydrug and 30 non-drug controls on any test; 23 or 24 retested a year later, 3 again using at least monthly: no deficits at either session (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). Morgan et al. (2004), 18 who had cut down (6.45 to 1.61 days a month, the self-reported amount per occasion rising) against 10 polydrug controls, 3–4 years apart: category fluency group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032 (first session t = 2.42, P = 0.023; no difference at follow-up); change in category fluency with change in use r = 0.712 and with time since last use r = 0.723; story recall group F(1,26) = 4.36 (immediate) and 4.43 (delayed); digit cancellation 66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 s; sentences judged group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007. Frequent group over a year (22 of 25 still using at least monthly; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010): errors 29.58 to 19.92 and pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (mean changes, not tested); strategy 31.63 to 27.33 and Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (P = 0.003 each); correlations with change in amount r = 0.623 and −0.732 as printed, about 0.55 and −0.55 from the plotted points (editors' calculation).

risk_of_bias.note: Selection: the 3-year follow-up kept 18 of 57 original ketamine participants, all of whom had cut down, and excluded the one who had developed schizophrenia; testers knew the groups; use and abstinence were self-reported (hair results only for the one-year cohort, in which the abstinent group's hair held some ketamine on average and its days since last use are contradictory); the abstinent group was not reclassified when 3 of 23 resumed monthly use (cards sc_morgan_2004a: ROBINS-E very high; sc_morgan_2009 and sc_morgan_2010b: high).

inconsistency.note: Category fluency caught up after cutting down while story recall and speed did not; people who had stopped showed no deficits, while people who cut down kept some; reported correlations are weaker in the plotted data.

indirectness.note: The question is whether the same people recover; most of the evidence compares different people (those who had stopped, who had used less, against those still using), and the only within-person data come from people who cut down rather than stopped.

imprecision.note: 18 against 10 people in the only within-person study, 24 to 30 per group in the others; the absence of deficits in people who had stopped cannot exclude moderate differences.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: The correlation between the fall in use and the gain in category fluency (r = 0.712, 18 people) is within one small selected sample, and the people who used most had most room to improve (regression to the mean is not excluded; card sc_morgan_2004a); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence: neither recovery nor persistence after stopping can be shown with these designs. Status contested, with a debate box: the same research group has published both conclusions (impairments that appear long-lasting, Morgan et al., 2004; impairments that may be reversible, Morgan et al., 2009 and the 2012 review), each with credible support and a credible critique. Overlapping evidence: the 2009 and 2010 papers are one cohort; the 2004 follow-up is a subset of the two field studies. The narrative review is second-hand and is used only to qualify; its group of 30 people abstinent for at least a year cannot be matched to a primary report.

debate.question: Do the lower memory and thinking scores of people who use ketamine often fade after they cut down or stop?
debate.evidence_yes: People who had stopped scored no lower than either comparison group on any test: 30 people abstinent for at least a month (a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980) in one session (Morgan et al., 2009), and the 23 or 24 of them retested a year later at both sessions, 3 of whom were again using monthly (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010), although 8 had once used daily and the group had used ketamine for longer than the other ketamine groups. In the only study that retested a group of people who had cut down (Morgan et al., 2004; 18 people whose use fell from 6.45 to 1.61 days a month, beside 10 polydrug controls), category fluency, lower 3 days after a night of use, no longer differed 3 to 4 years later (F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032), errors in sentence judging fell to the controls' level, and the gain in category fluency correlated, by the authors' account, with the reduction in use (r = 0.712) and with time since last use (r = 0.723). Even people who were still using did not get worse on average over a year: their mean spatial working-memory errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and their pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' 88.41% and 89.58% (changes the paper did not test), and their planning improved into the other groups' range (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). The same authors' narrative review reads these results as showing that memory impairments may be reversible (Morgan et al., 2012, second-hand).
debate.evidence_no: In the 18 people who had cut down, immediate story recall and digit-cancellation speed were lower than in the controls at both sessions with no reported improvement, and sentence judging was lower across both sessions although the authors describe it as improving (immediate recall F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047; cancellation 66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 seconds; sentences F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007), which the authors read as long-lasting impairment of episodic memory and possibly of attention (Morgan et al., 2004); 10 of the 18 had used ketamine within the previous 6 months (editors' arithmetic from the 8 who had not). Over a year, letter fluency fell in the abstinent (17.36 to 15.12) and frequent groups (16.38 to 13.48), which the authors describe as a possible progressive decline (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). Averaged over both sessions, the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than all other groups and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and abstinent groups, and within that group, by the authors' account, larger increases in the reported amount went with worse changes on both tasks (r = 0.623 and −0.732 as printed), which would fit effects that depend on how much people use.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether ketamine caused the lower scores in the first place: no study tested anyone before they started using, and the frequent groups had less schooling and lower vocabulary-test scores. Whether the same people recover after stopping: the people who had stopped were different people, who had used less before stopping (2.55 days a month, a peak of 11.21, against 20.13 in the frequent group), and only the 3-year follow-up retested a group defined by having cut down; it kept 18 of 57 original ketamine participants (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down, had no group that kept using, and took its first measurement 3 days after a night of use, when after-effects and missed practice may still have lowered scores. The differences that remained were present at the first session and did not change, which fits differences that predate use as well as lasting harm; the improvements in people still using fit practice on tasks with one version and recovery from a poor start as well as anything else. Letter fluency also fell in both control groups, by amounts similar to the abstinent group's. All the studies come from one research group, with self-reported use, testers who knew the groups and 10 to 30 people per group.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). No study read shows whether ketamine's effects on memory and thinking reverse, because none shows what those effects were. What the sources do show is that people who had stopped, after at least a month and usually many months, scored like people who did not use ketamine in two sessions a year apart (Morgan et al., 2009; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010); that people who were still using improved significantly on two tasks over a year and, on average but without a test, on two others, while their letter fluency fell, as it also did in the group that had stopped and in both comparison groups (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010); and that in a small, selected follow-up one test caught up after people cut down while story recall and speed did not change (Morgan et al., 2004). A reading consistent with all of this is that the lower scores of people using ketamine most days include a part that does not outlast heavy use (recent use, after-effects or withdrawal, missed practice) and a part that may have been there before use began, but the studies cannot separate the two. The claims of recovery and the claims of lasting impairment come from the same research group (Morgan et al., 2004; Morgan et al., 2009; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2012), and both go further than its data.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before regular ketamine use and repeatedly afterwards, with ketamine use and abstinence verified by hair and urine analysis, enough people who continue, cut down and stop to compare them, comparison groups retested on the same schedule with alternate test versions, testers blind to group, and losses reported by baseline scores. None of the sources read reports such a study.

statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with more delusion-like (unusual) beliefs, more dissociation in everyday life and somewhat more depressive symptoms, which the authors call mild to moderate in one study and below clinical levels in two others; whether ketamine causes these differences is unknown. In one session (Morgan et al., 2009; groups of 30), people who used ketamine more than four times a week scored higher than 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs on a delusions inventory (22.72 against 13.03 and 9.43), on unusual experiences in daily life when not under the influence of drugs, on a dissociative experiences scale (784 against 488 and 321) and on a depression inventory (11.48 against 7.17 and 7.23, which the authors call mild to moderate depression); the editors could reproduce the differences from both control groups for delusions and dissociation, but for depression only the difference from the group who had stopped. People who used ketamine less often (at least monthly but less than four times a week) or had stopped scored between the frequent and non-drug groups on several of these scales, but their reported excess of delusional ideation over the non-drug group could not be reproduced from the printed table. A year later (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010; the same people), delusional ideation (8.39 and 8.04 items endorsed in the frequent group, against 5.63 and 4.50 in the polydrug and 3.90 and 3.95 in the non-drug group) and dissociation were still highest in the frequent group, while the groups who used ketamine less often or had stopped were also reported above the non-drug group on delusional ideation (P = 0.009 and 0.016); depression scores had risen in the frequent (7.08 to 10.67) and abstinent groups (4.96 to 9.00), the frequent group reported more negative life events over the year, and the first report gives the frequent group's depression score at the same first session as 11.48, so either the two reports disagree or the 5 people not retested averaged about 33. Three days after a night of use, a ketamine group that used ketamine from twice a week to once a month rated more dissociation (17.75 against 5.37) and psychosis-like experiences (62.35 against 26.42), on scales of how they felt at that moment, one of them built for the study, than peers with little or no ketamine use, and slightly higher depression scores on both test days, the first rating covering the two days up to the test on the night (Curran & Morgan, 2000); in a second sample, people who used ketamine more than twice a month and people who used it less did not differ in dissociation or psychosis-like scores three days after use (Curran & Monaghan, 2001). In 18 people who had cut down, retested after 3 to 4 years, psychosis-like (schizotypal) scores stayed higher than in 10 controls (18.67 against 4.0) and depression scores, measured only at follow-up, were higher (5.27 against 2.00, although the printed test, U = 55.5, gives p ≈ 0.10 on the editors' recalculation), while dissociation did not differ (Morgan et al., 2004). The frequent group of the main study had more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3) and less education; nobody was assessed before using ketamine, the measures are self-ratings, and no study read gives a rate of diagnosed psychotic illness (one person in the 3-year follow-up had developed schizophrenia and was excluded, a single case that gives no rate). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In one London team's studies, people who used ketamine more than four times a week reported more unusual beliefs, more moments of feeling detached from themselves or their surroundings in everyday life, and a little more low mood than people who used other drugs or none. On average, their low-mood scores were at most mild to moderate. A year later the same differences were there, and low mood had risen in the frequent group and in people who had stopped. People who used ketamine less often were in between on some of these scales. In two smaller studies that asked how people felt at that moment, three days after a night out, feeling detached was higher in one study but not in the other. The frequent group had more family members with mental illness and less schooling, and nobody was asked these questions before they started, so the studies cannot show that ketamine caused the differences.
