risk_of_bias.note: Family history of mental illness and education differ and are not adjusted for; all outcomes are self-ratings, some on scales built or adapted for the studies; testers knew the groups; samples are self-selected volunteers; several reported post hoc differences, and the 3-year follow-up's depression test, cannot be reproduced from the printed figures, and the frequent group's depression at the first session differs between the 2009 and 2010 papers (cards sc_morgan_2009, sc_morgan_2010b: ROBINS-E high; sc_curran_2000, sc_curran_2001, sc_morgan_2004a: very high).

inconsistency.note: Delusion-like beliefs and depressive symptoms point the same way in every comparison with people who did not use ketamine, but dissociation was raised in some comparisons and not in others (no difference after cutting down; none between frequent and less frequent use three days after a night out), and the depression differences are fragile.

indirectness.note: The outcomes are the self-rated experiences asked about; none of the scales is a diagnosis, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: 10 to 30 people per group; differences at the limit of significance for depression, with intervals that would include small differences.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: The ordering of delusional ideation across groups (frequent above infrequent and abstinent, above the controls) and its correlation with amount per session in the frequent group (r = 0.433, one of an unstated number of correlations) are suggestive, but frequent against infrequent use was not tested in the one-year data and the groups differ in family history; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low. Overlapping evidence: Morgan et al. (2009) and Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, et al. (2010) are the same participants and count once; the 3-year follow-up (Morgan et al., 2004) is a subset of the two field studies' participants, so the field studies and the follow-up are not independent of each other; the narrative review (Morgan et al., 2012) is second-hand and only qualifies. Status replicated by the same team: in every sample of this one group that included people who did not use ketamine, people who used it scored higher on delusion-like or psychosis-like scales and on depressive symptoms than those who did not (the depression differences are fragile), while the dissociation findings are less consistent. Rated as worded, an association; the editors draw no causal conclusion.

statement: In healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory, with salt water given to the same people as the comparison, scores on tests of learning and remembering words fall during the session and, in the two studies that tested again after the infusion had stopped, were no longer detectably lower within about an hour of its end; what happens to attention and to other thinking tests differs between laboratories and with the infusion used. In 15 volunteers given a 1-hour infusion, free recall of a 12-word list was lower on the ketamine day (drug F1,14 = 9.63, p = .008; drug x time F4,52 = 4.35, p = .004), most at 55 minutes (F1,13 = 18.79, p = .001) and still at 90 minutes (F1,13 = 6.25, p = .026), as was recognition of the same words (F1,13 = 17.48, p = .001; lower at 10 and 55 minutes) and, less markedly, a score for noticing repeated words as the list was read (drug x time F4,56 = 2.71, p = .05; lower at 55 minutes only); 13 of 15 people recalled less, 9 of 14 recognised less and 9 of 15 scored lower on the attention measure than their own pre-infusion level on the ketamine day, which is not a comparison with the salt-water day (Malhotra et al., 1996). In 15 men given three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels over 2 hours, measured and stable at 60 and 120 minutes in the two larger conditions while the smallest stayed below the assay threshold, recall of two spoken narratives fell with the condition (F3,41 = 5.11, p = 0.004), by 21.2 of the units the authors score, which they report as an 18.6% fall from the salt-water day to the largest condition, with immediate and delayed recall affected alike; no effect was detected on a colour-word task, a letter-watching task, word generation or a spatial memory task, which the authors themselves say may reflect how sensitive those tasks were (Newcomer et al., 1999). In a study of 18 volunteers given 40-minute infusions, with 14 to 16 of them behind each cognitive result, recall of a three-word set after a 10-minute delay fell at the larger amount (dose x time F8,120 = 3.4, P = .002) while immediate recall did not change (F8,120 = 0.0) on a task at which people recalled close to all three words on every day, so that comparison cannot show that immediate recall is spared; word generation fell (16.1 words after salt water, 15.1 and 12.9 at the two amounts; high against salt water F1 = 8.4, P = .007), vigilance changed by about one target of 30 (29.7, 29.6 and 28.5 correct; F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001), and a bedside test of global cognition did not change (F8,136 = 1.4, P = .2) (Krystal et al., 1994). The same study's card-sorting result (perseverative errors 6.5, 16.8 and 31.9) is a comparison of 6, 5 and 8 different people on their first test day with no baseline, not a within-person drug effect. Three things limit all of this: none of the studies reports a blinding check; the samples are 14 to 18 people, no study prints a confidence interval for a cognitive measure, and one of the three never tested anyone after the infusion had stopped; and the claim that the memory effect is separate from the attentional and psychosis-like effects rests on one adjustment at one time point and on six correlations in 14 to 15 people (from .02 to -.41), which are far too few to show that two things are unrelated. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In lab studies, healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein remembered fewer words, and recognised fewer of them, than on a day when the same people were given salt water. The difference was largest while the drug was being infused. In the two studies that tested again after it stopped, scores matched the salt-water day within about an hour. Attention and other thinking tests were affected in one study but not in another, which the researchers put down to the different infusions and to how hard each task was. Everyone was tested once, in a laboratory, and the studies had 14 to 18 people each. Counts like 13 of 15 compare each person with their own score before the drug, not with their salt-water day.
population: Healthy adults screened to exclude psychiatric illness and, in one study, any previous use of ketamine or phencyclidine: 18, 15 and 15 people in three laboratory studies, with 14 to 16 contributing to several of the cognitive analyses
exposure: A single subanaesthetic amount of ketamine into a vein during the session (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes; a 0.12 mg/kg bolus then 0.65 mg/kg over 1 hour; three fixed infusions over 2 hours aimed at steady blood levels, of which only the two larger were above the assay threshold)
comparator: Salt water (saline) given to the same people on another day, with each day's own pre-infusion test as the reference
outcome: Scores on tests of learning, recall, recognition, attention, word generation, vigilance and global cognition during and shortly after the session
magnitude: Malhotra et al. (1996), n = 15 (14 for recognition): free recall drug F1,14 = 9.63 (p = .008), drug x time F4,52 = 4.35 (p = .004), lower at 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.79 (p = .001) and 90 minutes F1,13 = 6.25 (p = .026); recognition drug F1,13 = 17.48 (p = .001), drug x time F4,52 = 7.95, lower at 10 minutes F1,13 = 8.92 (p = .01) and 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.78; attention drug x time F4,56 = 2.71 (p = .05), lower at 55 minutes F1,14 = 8.79 (p = .01); 13 of 15, 9 of 14 and 9 of 15 people scored lower than their own pre-infusion level on the ketamine day. Newcomer et al. (1999), n = 15 men: total paragraph recall F3,41 = 5.11 (p = 0.004), immediate F3,41 = 3.92 (p = 0.02), delayed F3,41 = 5.03 (p = 0.005); fall of 21.2 units from placebo to the largest condition, reported as 18.6%; non-verbal recognition F3,40 = 2.93 (p = 0.045), described by the authors as preliminary; no effect detected on the Stroop, continuous performance, word generation or spatial delayed response tasks. Krystal et al. (1994), n = 14 to 18: 10-minute delayed three-word recall dose x time F8,120 = 3.4 (P = .002), immediate recall F8,120 = 0.0 at ceiling; word generation 16.1 (SEM 1.3), 15.1 (1.2) and 12.9 (1.3) words, dose F2,28 = 4.4 (P = .02); vigilance 29.7 (0.1), 29.6 (0.2) and 28.5 (0.4) of 30 targets, F2,26 = 8.6 (P = .001); MMSE dose x time F8,136 = 1.4 (P = .2).

grade.reasoning: Within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized order start high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -1: none of the three studies reports a blinding check and the condition is likely to have been recognizable; in one study the attention measure used as a covariate comes from the same word list as the memory scores, its degrees of freedom do not match the sample for several analyses and one printed p value contradicts its own statistic; in another the easiest tasks sat at ceiling and the card-sorting comparison is between unmatched groups; in the third the printed dose-to-dose p values are one-tailed and data missing at the largest condition are missing because of a drug effect. Not downgraded for inconsistency: the fall in verbal learning and memory is found in all three laboratories, and the disagreement about attention, word generation and vigilance is explained by the different infusions and blood levels and by task sensitivity, which the authors of the steady-state study state themselves; a reading that treated that disagreement as unexplained would give very low. Not downgraded for indirectness, because the claim stays with healthy volunteers in a laboratory during the session. Independent replication: three laboratories (Yale and West Haven; the National Institute of Mental Health; Washington University) agree on the verbal memory finding, and the two later studies were designed partly to extend the first, so they are not blind to it.

statement: In the one study read here of ketamine given to people with schizophrenia, 9 inpatients who were actively psychotic but stable, all on a fixed amount of haloperidol for four weeks, received on four separate days over two weeks a blinded placebo injection and three amounts of ketamine (study conditions: 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, each given over 60 seconds); two of the nine never received the largest amount, which the non-blind staff withheld on safety grounds and replaced with a blinded placebo injection, so seven people contributed to it. Twenty minutes later the BPRS total was 33.4 (6.0) after placebo and 38.3 (7.1), 39.3 (5.0) and 45.3 (7.7) after the three amounts, significant at the two larger ones (p = .005 and p = .01), with the psychosis items carrying the change (8.0 to 9.8, 9.3 and 12.3); the paper does not say whether the figures in brackets are standard deviations or standard errors, and the editors read them as standard deviations. By 90 and 180 minutes the total score was at or below its own baseline in every condition, while the psychosis score was back near baseline but a little above it at the two smaller amounts (7.0 against baselines of 6.8 and 6.6). Seven of the nine people had at least a 50% rise in the psychosis score, one changed by less than 25% and one did not change. What people described often repeated their own illness: at the smallest amount, perceptual distortions, illusions and depersonalisation; at the two larger ones, suspiciousness, delusions, hallucinations and disorganised thinking, with two people whose extensive paranoid delusions returned in part. Four of the nine spontaneously reported symptoms coming back later, at interviews 8 and 24 hours afterwards: two had delusions return about 6 to 8 hours after the injection, needing no treatment (lasting 12 hours in one and over 12 hours in the other, by the paper's table), one reported nightmares on two nights, and one reported the same visual hallucinations recurring occasionally over the next several days and declined the second series. These later reports were not rated with any instrument, because they had not been expected, and the paper gives their timing differently in three places: 8 to 24 hours in the abstract, about 6 to 8 hours in the results, and 4 to 24 hours in the heading of the table that lists them, whose own entries run from 12 hours to several days. The study cannot answer two questions it is often cited for. Whether antipsychotic medication blocks the effect: in the six people retested without haloperidol the BPRS total rose from 37.3 (7.5) to 46.6 (5.9) at the largest amount, reported only as a trend (p = 0.07), no psychosis-score rise was significant, and the comparison between the two conditions rests on at most four paired observations at that amount, with different starting scores. And whether negative symptoms change: the negative-symptom scale named in the methods is never reported, and the sentence stating no change cites a table that holds no negative-symptom measure, while the two people with mainly negative symptoms went in opposite directions (one 50% worse, one 60% better). The order of the four conditions was chosen by non-blind staff for safety rather than randomized, the largest amount was routinely not given first, no blinding check is reported, and there was no comparison group of people without schizophrenia. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study, nine people with schizophrenia, all taking an antipsychotic medicine, were given ketamine into a vein on three days and a dummy injection (placebo) on a fourth. Twenty minutes after the two larger amounts their symptom scores were higher than after the dummy injection, and what they described often repeated their own illness: suspicion, delusions, hallucinations and muddled thinking. Their overall scores were back to their usual level by an hour and a half. Four of the nine said symptoms came back hours later, which nobody had expected or measured. Nine people, with the order of days chosen by staff rather than at random, is very little to go on.
population: 9 inpatient volunteers with schizophrenia (DSM-III-R; 5 men and 4 women, mean age 30, mean length of illness 9.3 years), actively psychotic but stable, on a fixed daily amount of haloperidol for four weeks; 6 of them were retested after at least four weeks without it
exposure: A single amount of ketamine into a vein over 60 seconds (study conditions: 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, one condition per day over two weeks, the largest routinely not given first), on top of haloperidol 0.3 mg/kg per day in the first series and after four to eight weeks without it in the second
comparator: A blinded placebo injection in the same people within the same series, and, for 6 of the 9, the same four conditions repeated without haloperidol
outcome: Clinician-rated symptom scores (BPRS total and its psychosis, withdrawal and anxiety subscales) at 20, 90 and 180 minutes, the described content of the symptoms, and what people reported at interviews 8 and 24 hours later
magnitude: Lahti et al. (1995), on haloperidol, 20 minutes after the injection (n = 9, 9, 9 and 7; the paper does not label the figures in brackets, which the editors read as standard deviations): BPRS total 33.4 (6.0) after placebo, 38.3 (7.1) at 0.1 mg/kg, 39.3 (5.0) at 0.3 mg/kg (p = .005) and 45.3 (7.7) at 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01), against baselines of 34.6, 33.2, 35.2 and 36.9; psychosis subscale 8.0 (3.1), 9.8 (3.3) (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) and 12.3 (2.5) (p = .02), against baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9; at 90 and 180 minutes the total is at or below its own baseline in every condition (0.5 mg/kg 32.3 and 32.3), while the psychosis score is 7.0 at both times at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg against baselines of 6.8 and 6.6. Seven of nine people had at least a 50% rise in psychosis score. Off haloperidol (n = 6, 5 at the largest amount): total 37.3 (7.5) after placebo and 46.6 (5.9) at 0.5 mg/kg, p = 0.07; no psychosis-subscale rise significant. Four of nine reported symptoms returning 6 to 8 hours later or over the following days, by spontaneous report. No test statistic, confidence interval or effect size is printed anywhere in the paper.

grade.reasoning: A within-person comparison with a blinded placebo condition starts high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -2: the order of the four conditions was chosen by unblinded staff on safety grounds rather than randomized and the largest amount was routinely not given first, so what was given is partly confounded with the session number and with what people had come to expect; no blinding check is reported for a drug whose effects are unmistakable, and the outcomes are one clinician's ratings; and the reporting is selective, with about ten p values printed for roughly 96 implied comparisons, no test statistics or intervals anywhere, a negative-symptom conclusion drawn from data that are never shown, and a transcription error in one table cell. Imprecision -1: nine people, seven at the largest amount, and five to six in the comparison without haloperidol. Not downgraded for indirectness: the claim stays with what happened to these patients in this study. Not downgraded for inconsistency, because there is only one study. Very low, which is the floor. What the study supports is the short-lived rise in symptom scores at the two larger amounts in people with schizophrenia on haloperidol, and the clinical description of what was induced; it does not support any statement about negative symptoms, about whether antipsychotic medication blocks the effect, about the shape of the relation to the amount given, or about how often later recurrences happen.

statement: In healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory, with salt water given to the same people on another day as the comparison in every study read here in full but one open study, where the comparison was the same people's drug-free baseline, perception, thinking and the sense of self change during the session; where symptoms were rated again after the infusion stopped, they had gone or nearly gone within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour of its end (Krystal et al., 1994; Malhotra et al., 1996), and nothing read here rated them later. A 2020 meta-analysis of 36 within-person placebo-controlled studies in 725 healthy volunteers, whose confidence the editors rate low, found higher clinician-rated symptom scores under ketamine than under salt water on every pooled measure: total 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.77; 25 studies), psychosis-like ('positive') 1.55 (1.29 to 1.81; 21 studies) and withdrawn or blunted ('negative') 1.16 (0.96 to 1.35; 22 studies) standard deviations of the within-person difference, the psychosis-like effect being the larger of the two (difference 0.36, 0.12 to 0.61), a comparison its authors qualify because the two analyses did not rest on exactly the same studies and because they call the withdrawn or blunted effect large as well (Beck et al., 2020). In that pooled set the comparison was not always made on another day: the dummy condition was salt water in 35 of its 36 studies and not reported in one, and in its total-symptom analysis 2 of the 19 studies classed by day gave both conditions on the same day, where the pooled effect was larger (2.29, 1.69 to 2.89, against 1.39, 1.12 to 1.66 in the 17 that used separate days; P = .007), which the authors suggest could reflect unblinding or better control of day-to-day variation. The review gives no recovery time, states that the time course of these effects has still to be characterised, and took its ratings 1 to 120 minutes after the infusion began in the 17 studies that report the timing, so nothing in it was measured after the session. Those pooled figures are peak values, taken at each study's largest amount and at the rating time with the highest score, so they are the largest effects the studies saw; the studies also disagreed widely about size (I2 65% to 76%, the three values printed in the review's Results, whose abstract instead prints a range of 77% to 83% that matches none of them) and showed small-study asymmetry (Egger z 4.27 to 5.12), with trim-and-fill estimates of 1.37, 1.49 and 1.09. In the single studies read here the picture is the same. In 18 volunteers (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, test days in randomized order), scores for conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour, suspiciousness and unusual thought content rose at the larger amount but not at the smaller or after salt water, as did withdrawal and blunting, dissociation (CADSS) and self-rated perceptual change; the authors state scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion, and describe what was rated as hallucinatory behaviour as distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations, while also describing ideas of reference with paranoid content and loosening of associations at the larger amount (Krystal et al., 1994). In 15 volunteers given a 1-hour infusion the 18-item BPRS total rose from 19.3 (SEM 0.4) to 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and was 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes, against 19.1, 18.7 and 18.7 after salt water, carried by thought disorder (3.0 to 6.3) and withdrawal-retardation (3.3 to 6.6), each a three-item score whose floor is 3, while the hallucinations item did not differ (1.2 against 1.0, p = 0.190) and the hostility-suspiciousness score did not change at all (F = 0.1, p = .90); the 90-minute value, 30 minutes after the end of the infusion, is not marked as differing from the salt-water day, and nothing was rated later (Malhotra et al., 1996). In 15 men given three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels, psychosis-like scores and a negative-symptom scale rose with the condition (F3,42 = 21.84 and 10.55), the authors called the syndrome mild, and no abnormal symptoms were found at an abbreviated, unblinded check about 48 hours later; in that study the item scored for hallucinatory behaviour was deliberately widened so that distortions of perception counted on it, and the authors detected no formal thought disorder or language disorganisation during the conditions tested apart from modest changes on one negative-symptom subscale, so its psychosis-like rise is not evidence of hallucinations; that study is also one of the 36 pooled above, so it is not separate support for the pooled figures (Newcomer et al., 1999). In an open study without a dummy condition, symptoms began on average 4.5 minutes after the start of the infusion (Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al., 1997). What these studies cannot settle is how far the state resembles a psychiatric illness: ego-pathology scores were about two thirds of published values for people with first-episode schizophrenia and two of the five dimensions were clearly less affected, with no patients studied in that paper (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997), and the authors of the open study limit their model to the start of acute psychotic episodes. Blinding is the weak point of the whole literature: the visible signs (blurred vision in 8 of 18 people at the larger amount in one study, with nystagmus in about half of them and vomiting in 2) make it unlikely that raters or participants stayed unaware of the condition, and no study read reports a blinding check. All of this describes one session with ketamine in the body in screened volunteers, not repeated or non-medical use.
plain: In lab studies, healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein felt and showed changes in perception, thinking and their sense of self that people rating them scored much higher than after a dummy infusion of salt water in the same people. In one open study there was no dummy day at all: the comparison was the same people before the drug. Pooling 36 such studies in 725 volunteers, the ketamine scores were well above the salt-water scores on every measure, and most so for psychosis-like experiences. Some of them gave the salt water on the same day, not another day (2 of the 19 that one analysis could sort by day). The effects were strong during the infusion. Where people were rated again after it stopped, the scores were back to about their usual level within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour. That comes from two single studies: the 36 pooled studies measured nothing after the session. What was scored as hallucinations was mostly distortions of real sights and sounds, not seeing things that were not there. People also became suspicious and their thinking became muddled. The pooled numbers are peak values from each study's largest amount, and the studies disagree a lot about how big the effects are.

risk_of_bias.note: Blinding is unverifiable or broken in every study read in full (cards sc_krystal_1994, sc_malhotra_1996, sc_newcomer_1999, sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b, all rated high overall); the review selected each study's peak value by design, and 9 of its 36 studies were not double-blind, 3 of them unblinded. Against the downgrade: blinding status did not change the review's pooled effect significantly in any of the three outcomes, and the review's own across-study summary rates performance and detection bias low. The downgrade is kept, because that is a contrast between studies, no primary study checked whether blinding held, and the peak-value selection is untouched by it.

inconsistency.note: I2 75.7%, 74.9% and 64.6% in the review's Results (its abstract prints a range of 77% to 83%, which matches none of them); prediction intervals about 0.28 to 2.72, 0.44 to 2.65 and 0.39 to 1.93 (editors' calculation on the card, reproduced independently by the second reader); the direction is consistent.

imprecision.note: 725 people across 36 studies; the pooled intervals are narrow.

publication_bias.note: Egger z = 4.27, 5.06 and 5.12, all P < .001; trim-and-fill estimates 1.37, 1.49 and 1.09 remain large and are stated in the claim.

grade.reasoning: Within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order start high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -1: no study read in full reports a blinding check, the condition produced visible signs in nearly half the people at the larger amount in one study, the main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings, one of the two imaging studies had no dummy condition at all, and the pooled estimates are peak values chosen at each study's largest amount and highest-scoring rating time (the review's confidence is rated low with AMSTAR 2, provisionally, because one item can be judged only from a supplement neither reader opened). The review's own finding that blinding status did not change the pooled effect in any outcome counts against that downgrade; it is kept because the comparison is between studies rather than within them, because no primary study checked whether blinding held, and because the peak-value selection is unaffected by it. Inconsistency -1: heterogeneity across the pooled studies is high (I2 65% to 76% in the Results), subgroup analyses did not explain most of it, and the editors' prediction intervals run from about 0.3 to 2.7, so the size of the effect is uncertain even though its direction is not. Not downgraded for indirectness, because the claim is restricted to healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory. Not downgraded for imprecision: 725 people and narrow intervals around each pooled estimate. Not downgraded for publication bias, although the Egger tests were significant for all three outcomes, because the trim-and-fill estimates stay large and the claim carries both; a reading that counted that asymmetry as a further downgrade would give very low. Rated as worded, including the size. A claim worded only to the direction and the short duration would sit a level higher, because every one of the 36 pooled studies found an increase and the laboratories read in full agree. Overlapping evidence (METHODS 6.3): Newcomer et al. (1999) is one of the 36 pooled studies, in the total and the positive analyses, so it is not independent of the pooled estimates; Malhotra et al. (1997), a separate report, is pooled as well (the review does not say whether it shares participants with Malhotra et al., 1996), while Krystal et al. (1994) is not among the 36; at least 8 of the 36 list a review author among their authors; and the two 1997 studies come from the same Zurich laboratory. How long the effects last is carried by the two studies that rated people again after the infusion stopped, and by nothing else: the review gives no recovery time, states that the time course has still to be characterised, and took its ratings during the session.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (it says that its secondary outcomes, which it does not name, will be published elsewhere), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (citing an expert review, the authors say that up to 20% of patients given intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression need such treatment); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial of 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression who had ketamine through a drip in hospital, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less in those picked at random to hear music than in those who heard none. The report we read gives no results on how the sessions felt or whether depression improved. An earlier review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests, where music often went with less worry or pain; it found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression. So it is not known whether music changes how a ketamine session feels.
population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)
magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.

risk_of_bias.note: The trial (card sc_greenway_2024), RoB 2 some concerns: open label by necessity; sequence generation and allocation concealment not described; one usual-care patient excluded from analysis without a stated reason; more infusions missing without music (8 against 3), handled by inverse-probability weighting; who measured blood pressure, and whether they knew the group, not described. The review's studies were not appraised by the review and cannot be appraised here, and its highlights state benefits that its limitations disclaim (card sc_kheirkhah_2024).

inconsistency.note: Directions vary between the review's procedural trials (one null, one with more dreams or emergence reactions), as the statement says; the trial measured a different outcome.

indirectness.note: For the question asked (how a session feels, or how well treatment works), the trial reports only blood pressure, and its comparison was no music without a sound or attention control; the review's evidence is second-hand (METHODS §6.3) and mostly from ketamine given with other sedatives during procedures, often in children, and the only controlled ketamine-alone study used mothers' voices, partly spoken.

imprecision.note: One trial of 32 patients (interval for the smaller systolic rise 2.9 to 12.0 mm Hg); for how sessions feel, only small studies, mostly without a comparison group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the trial was registered (NCT04701866), but its registry record and protocol supplement were not read, so the reported outcome was not compared with the registered one.

grade.reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3), and every anchor has been checked by a second reader. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.

statement: As described second-hand in a 2018 narrative review of ketamine pharmacology, whose figures are taken from the primary studies it names and have not been appraised here, ketamine's best-characterised action is to block the NMDA receptor, one of the receptors for the brain's main excitatory messenger: it sits inside the open channel at the phencyclidine site, with a trapping capability of about 86% against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801. Reported affinities for the racemic drug span Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar across about twenty studies, almost all in animal tissue, in cell lines or in frog eggs (rat and mouse tissue, with guinea pig and dog brain as well, and receptors grown in cells or in frog eggs), beside two human cortex values of 0.42 and 0.67 micromolar that the review does not describe as post-mortem, a word it uses only of the separate brain samples that gave the two mirror-image forms their values; which receptor subunits are blocked most depends on how much magnesium is present, and one study found no subunit difference at all. A 40-minute infusion of the kind used to treat depression was estimated to occupy at most 31% of the receptors, give or take 18 percentage points, a spread the review prints without saying whether it is a standard deviation or a standard error. The review tabulates about fifteen other targets, among them nicotinic, muscarinic, opioid and sigma receptors, the monoamine transporters and sodium, calcium and HCN1 channels; most of the values it prints for them are about 10 to 1000 micromolar, above the blood levels reached in people (about 0.8 micromolar after that infusion, about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia), but several fall inside that range by the review's own account: it treats concentrations up to about 10 micromolar as clinically relevant and says some nicotinic subtypes may therefore act in people (one blocked at 0.24 micromolar in frog eggs, another at 3.1), it reports a muscarinic M1 value of 5.7 micromolar in frog eggs as a clinically relevant concentration against 45 micromolar in cells, and it links block of the HCN1 channel (8.2 to 15.6 micromolar for the mixture, 4.1 to 7.4 for the S form) to anaesthesia, while its own table also lists a dopamine transporter value of 4.6 micromolar and an L-type calcium value of 9.2 micromolar. The body turns ketamine into norketamine, mainly through the liver enzymes CYP2B6 and CYP3A4, and then into dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines; norketamine also blocks the NMDA receptor (S-norketamine Ki 1.70 to 2.25 micromolar, the R form about eight times weaker in the values the text prints, though the review's own table also carries a pair of values that would remove that difference) while dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines are weak or inactive there. In patients with treatment-resistant major depression given that infusion, peak blood levels were 204.13 ng/mL (SD 101.46) for ketamine at 40 minutes, 73.54 (31.86) for norketamine at 80 minutes, 13.27 (6.92) for dehydronorketamine at 110 minutes and 23.19 (11.88) for one hydroxynorketamine pair at 230 minutes, and total exposure to that metabolite pair exceeded exposure to ketamine itself. How much of this is human evidence is the main point: the receptor numbers are overwhelmingly from animal tissue and from receptors grown in cells, the review states that the brain levels of ketamine and its metabolites in people are not known, the proposal that the hydroxynorketamines carry part of ketamine's antidepressant action rests on rodent experiments almost all from the review's own authors, six of whose eleven are named as co-inventors on a patent application covering those metabolites and two of them on a granted patent, with one independent supporting study named beside them and two independent studies cited after 'but see' in a parenthesis without saying what they found, and the review states that no clinical study of R-ketamine in people with depression had been published and that none had compared the two mirror-image forms with each other or with the mixture. A second narrative review, written for a UK scientific committee, adds that ketamine also blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, may strengthen GABA inhibition, releases dopamine and is a weak opioid agonist, but gives no study for several of these statements, and the first review sets against the dopamine account two human imaging studies that found no change in striatal binding, a human study in which a dopamine blocker did not stop ketamine's psychosis-like effects, and a study finding no activity at any dopamine receptor up to 10 micromolar, measured on human receptors grown in cells, whose mouse part found no change in evoked dopamine release.
plain: Ketamine's best-understood action is to block the NMDA receptor, a docking point for the brain's main 'go' signal, by sitting inside its channel. The body breaks ketamine down into norketamine, which blocks the same receptor more weakly, and then into other substances that barely block it at all. Nearly all the numbers come from animal tissue or from receptors grown in dishes, not from people: the review says nobody knows how much ketamine reaches the human brain. The idea that the breakdown products do some of the work in depression comes from mice, in studies mostly done by the review's own authors. Six of the review's eleven authors are named on a patent application for these substances. All of this is reported second-hand from reviews, not from the original studies.
population: Pharmacology as assembled in two narrative reviews: binding and electrophysiology mostly in rodent tissue, cell lines and frog eggs with a few human post-mortem brain samples, and blood measurements in healthy volunteers and in patients treated for depression or pain
exposure: Ketamine and its metabolites norketamine, dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines (the human blood figures come from a single 0.5 mg/kg infusion over 40 minutes given to patients with treatment-resistant depression)
comparator: The concentrations at which each target is affected, set against the blood levels reached in people; and, for the metabolites, ketamine itself
outcome: Which receptors and channels ketamine and its metabolites act on and at what concentrations, how the body breaks ketamine down, and how much of this rests on human rather than animal or laboratory evidence
magnitude: Zanos et al. (2018), second-hand: NMDA receptor Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar for racemic ketamine across about twenty studies (human cortex 0.42, SE 0.03, and 0.67, SE 0.15); trapping capability about 86% against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801; estimated maximum receptor occupancy after a 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion 31% plus or minus 18%, against 32% plus or minus 6% estimated in rats, neither spread labelled in the review; S-norketamine Ki 1.70 to 2.25 micromolar and R-norketamine 13.0 to 26.46; (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine about 10.4 to 21.0 micromolar and (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine above 100, neither inhibiting NMDA currents up to 10 micromolar; most other targets 10 to 1000 micromolar, with several inside the concentrations reached in people by the review's own account (nicotinic IC50 0.24 and 3.1 micromolar, muscarinic M1 IC50 5.7 micromolar against Ki 45 micromolar in cells, HCN1 EC50 8.2 to 15.6 and 4.1 to 7.4 micromolar, dopamine transporter IC50 4.6 micromolar, L-type calcium IC50 9.2 micromolar); peak blood levels in treatment-resistant major depression after that infusion 204.13 ng/mL (SD 101.46) ketamine, 73.54 (31.86) norketamine, 13.27 (6.92) dehydronorketamine and 23.19 (11.88) for the (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine pair, whose total exposure (1038 and 1366 h.ng/mL in the two patient groups) exceeded that of ketamine (873.5 and 975.4).

evidence.locator: III. Pharmacodynamics, introductory paragraph; sections B to I; Table 3
evidence.extracted: The review's working test is whether a target is affected within the concentrations reached in people, which by its own Table 1 are about 0.8 micromolar after the antidepressant infusion and about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia. Most other targets fall outside that range, at about 10 to 1000 micromolar: opioid receptors in the tens to hundreds, sigma receptors 19 to 139 in the text (Table 3 also lists a racemic Ki of 0.15), the serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine transporters from about 4.6 to 290, most above 60, sodium and calcium channels mostly in the hundreds to thousands but with a sodium Ki of 11.5 and an L-type calcium IC50 of 9.2 in frog myocytes, and GABA-A effects only at hundreds, with no binding seen at subanaesthetic doses in a human imaging study. The review itself places several targets within the clinically relevant range: nicotinic receptors (alpha4beta4 blocked at IC50 0.24 micromolar in oocytes, alpha3beta4 at 3.1, alpha7 at about 17 to 20, with the review calling concentrations up to about 10 micromolar clinically relevant), HCN1 channels (8.2 to 15.6 micromolar for the racemate, 4.1 to 7.4 for the S form, which it links to anaesthesia) and the muscarinic M1 value reported at 45 micromolar in cells and at 5.7 micromolar in oocytes, which it calls a clinically relevant concentration. The review states that many of these findings have not been confirmed by independent laboratories.

grade.reasoning: Every supporting anchor is a narrative review's account of primary studies that have not been read here, so the claim stays at draft, says in its statement that its figures are second-hand, and is not shown in the at-a-glance box (METHODS 6.3). The primary studies behind the receptor values are laboratory binding and electrophysiology experiments, mostly in animal tissue and in receptors grown in cells, which start low. Risk of bias -1: neither review has a search strategy, selection criteria or any appraisal of what it cites; the pharmacology review's metabolite sections rest on its own authors' work on compounds six of its eleven authors are named on a patent application for, its text ranges mix Ki with IC50 values and omit tabulated values that would weaken the contrast drawn, and it carries a unit conversion error. Indirectness -1: second-hand throughout, and preclinical evidence is always indirect (METHODS 6.3); the review itself states that the brain levels of ketamine and its metabolites in people are not known. Not downgraded for imprecision or inconsistency, because no pooled estimate is offered and the ranges are reported as ranges. Very low, which is the floor. Counted as one source: the second review is used only as context and for the targets beyond the NMDA receptor that it names without a study, so the two are not independent replication. A second reader's blind reading of the pharmacology review (AI reader 229, 31 October 2026) confirmed every number used here and corrected five statements about them, chiefly that the review places several non-NMDA targets inside the concentrations reached in people rather than above them, so the claim no longer reads as evidence that ketamine acts at the NMDA receptor alone at those levels.

The review's erratum (10.1124/pr.116.015198err) corrects only the copyright line and affects no number. statement: In three groups of people who had used ketamine non-medically, none drawn from a sampling frame, so that each share describes that sample only and none shows how common a reason is among people who use ketamine, people most often said they took it for its effects and for fun or partying, and many first took it through friends; the effects most often valued were changes in perception and feeling detached from the body or the surroundings, and the downsides most often named were memory problems, feeling less sociable and nausea (London) and fear of the K-hole, health risks and coming down (Sydney). In Sydney, Australia, 100 adults with at least one non-medical use (70 men; aged 19 to 42; 46 with a university degree; 99 had used ecstasy; 58 had used ketamine more than 10 times and 26 called their use regular) were recruited between January 1998 and October 1999, after being approached by the researcher who did every interview (39), told by a friend (38) or reached through radio (15) or a print advertisement (8) (Dillon et al., 2003). Asked their main reason for first taking it, 62 said its effect, 25 that friends were using it and 11 curiosity; asked why they went on (several answers allowed), 74 said the effect, 61 'to party', 42 that friends were using it, 35 that they were using other drugs and 32 that it felt good. The best things they named were altered senses (78), an out-of-body experience (52), a euphoric rush (50), the group experience (49), bringing on other drugs (42) and escaping reality (38), down to stress release (4); the worst were fear of the K-hole, a state of intense detachment (45), health risks (35), coming down (32), limited availability (22) and impurities (15), while 10 named nothing. The two main things they did on ketamine were most often dancing (78) and staying at home (27). 56 had experienced the K-hole, more often those with 20 or more lifetime uses than those with 10 or fewer (odds ratio 4.3, 95% CI 1.58 to 11.71; printed p < 0.001, but χ² 8.64 gives p ≈ 0.003, editors' calculation), a comparison in which more occasions also mean more chances. 69 intended to use it again. Their ratings of effects as positive or negative have no stated denominator and in many rows exceed the share who had ever had the effect (feeling separated from the body: had it 57, rated it positive 68), so they are not the views of the people who had each effect. In London, 90 people who used ketamine recreationally and mainly snorted it, found through dance-scene website advertisements and by referral (about half had taken part in the research team's earlier studies or knew someone taking part), were interviewed, mostly at University College London, in three groups of 30: frequent use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (twice a month to under four times a week) and former use (none for at least 84 days); interview dates are not reported, and the paper was received in October 2007 (Muetzelfeldt et al., 2008). Most had been introduced by a friend or acquaintance and already used several drugs; 79 called their first experience positive, and 8 did not enjoy it but went on. Of the 89 who answered statements about starting, 72 agreed that they were offered a line and enjoyed it, 69 that they enjoyed psychedelic drugs and it sounded interesting, 67 that friends were doing it, 56 that they wanted to explore their consciousness further, 51 that they saw people doing it at a party, 33 that it helped them get into music, 32 that they were bored of other drugs, 15 that they wanted to forget their troubles and 9 that they did not know what it was (editors' counts: the former-use shares are of 29, and the printed totals average the three groups' percentages). The printed test saying that the former-use group more often wanted to explore their consciousness (χ²(2) = 10.36, p = .035) does not fit the shares shown: 17 of 30, 17 of 30 and 22 of 29 give χ²(2) ≈ 3.1, p ≈ 0.21, and p = .035 fits 10.36 only on 4 degrees of freedom (editors' calculation). On a five-point scale, 65 of the 90 rated 'melting into the surroundings' quite or very appealing, 64 visual hallucinations, 58 an out-of-body experience and 58 'giggliness'; the effects most often rated as disliked were impaired memory (45), decreased sociability (45), nausea (38) and impaired concentration (29); the full list is not printed. In their own words, people most often liked the detachment at first (34) and the general high later (20); 13 called it unlike anything else they had tried and 9 liked its short duration; 8, 7 of them in the frequent-use group, now liked it for relieving boredom, filling a gap, satisfying cravings or escape, reasons the authors link to dependence. At first they most often disliked the intensity (22), nausea or vomiting (19) or losing control (15); about recent use, 13 disliked a weaker effect through tolerance or poorer quality, and there were 30 mentions of unwanted psychological effects, most often feeling less sociable (9). The places most named as ever used in were a friend's house (76 of 90) and home (64), ahead of squat parties (53), outdoor parties (51) and clubs (47) (editors' counts). The authors read the starting accounts as suggesting, besides friends' influence, mainly a wish to experiment and openness to new experience and, to a lesser extent, pleasure seeking. In north-west England, 12 people aged 18 to 32 (8 men, 4 women, all employed or students) who called their use current and regular, found through the authors' own club-scene contacts and then by asking each participant to recommend another, were interviewed in 10 in-depth interviews in a study begun in summer 2005 (Moore & Measham, 2008); no counts are given except where all 12 shared a view. Fun and the pleasure of intoxication were the main reasons in their accounts, with 'playful' effects valued and, for two, a short effect that they felt they could control, unlike psychedelic drugs. What people wanted differed: some wanted mild, sociable effects, some intense ones (one described sometimes taking it intending to have an out-of-body experience), and some moved between the two, stronger states being described as less sociable; ketamine was tied to the gathering after a club night, to extend the night, as one drug among several. All 12 described trying to control the effects, including making the amount they took more predictable; bad experiences were often explained as their own misjudgement of amount or setting, and taking too much was described mainly as the way into a K-hole they had not wanted, or a stronger one than they wanted, which some described as frightening (stuck in a loop, or sinking into blackness), while some who called themselves experienced sought the K-hole out as a 'journey'. They described injecting and habitual use outside club nights as problem use and presented themselves as sensible against mostly negative portrayals of ketamine; the authors note that the intensity and sociability described were produced in conversation, not measured. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show tolerance and a weaker or poorer product: in London 13 of 90 disliked a weaker effect through tolerance or poorer quality, and in Sydney 22 of 100 said they needed more to get the same effect, 15 named impurities and 8 tolerance among the worst things. What happens when people then take more is described only in the north-west England accounts of unwanted K-holes above. None of these samples can show how common any reason is: none had a sampling frame, all three were reached partly through the researchers themselves (their own approach or contacts), the questions were unvalidated and differed between studies (so the shares are given side by side, not pooled), most people used many other drugs and were not asked about occasions without them, people who inject, are in treatment or use outside these networks are few or absent, and the data date from 1998 to about 2007. The three teams, in two countries and with three methods, agree on the kinds of reasons people give, not on how often each is given. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Three groups of people who used ketamine were asked why they took it and what they liked about it. None was chosen at random, so the numbers describe these groups only, and the studies are from 1998 to about 2007. In Sydney, 100 people who had used ketamine at least once took part in 1998 and 1999: 62 said they first took it for its effect, 25 because friends were using it and 11 out of curiosity. The best things they named were changed senses (78), feeling outside their body (52) and a rush of joy (50); the worst was fear of the K-hole, a state of feeling deeply cut off from the body and the world (45), and 56 had been in one. In London, 90 people rated effects: 65 liked feeling they melted into their surroundings, 64 seeing things, and 58 each feeling outside their body or giggling, while 45 disliked memory problems and 45 feeling less sociable. Of 89 asked how they started, 72 said they were offered some and enjoyed it, 67 that friends were doing it, 56 that they wanted to explore their mind and 15 that they wanted to forget their troubles; 8 of the 90 said they now liked it for easing boredom or cravings, filling a gap or escape. The places they most often named were a friend's house and home, more than clubs. In long interviews with 12 people in north-west England, fun came first: some wanted a mild, chatty effect and others a strong one; some sought the K-hole, others found an unwanted one frightening, and they said unwanted K-holes came mainly from taking too much. Some people feel little from an amount; tolerance and a weaker product were among the reasons these people gave. Most also used many other drugs.
population: People who had used ketamine non-medically, in three samples without a sampling frame: 100 adults in Sydney, Australia, with at least one lifetime use, recruited January 1998 to October 1999 (70 men; aged 19 to 42, mean 29.7; 41 gay or bisexual; 46 university graduates; 72 in full-time work; extensive other drug use), recruited by the interviewer's own approach, friends, radio and a print advertisement; 90 people who used ketamine recreationally, interviewed mostly at University College London, in three groups of 30 (frequent, infrequent and former use; 63 men, 27 women; mean ages 25.9 to 27.4), recruited through dance-scene websites and the research team's earlier participants and their contacts (interview dates not reported; paper received October 2007); and 12 people aged 18 to 32 (8 men, 4 women; all employed or students) in north-west England's club scene who described their use as current and regular, recruited by peer referral from the authors' contacts (study begun summer 2005)
exposure: Ketamine taken by people's own choice, mostly snorted (82 of 100 in Sydney, where 11 usually injected it into a vein and 4 into a muscle; all in London and north-west England), usually among several other drugs; self-reported, with content unknown
comparator: None for the shares (descriptive); in London, groups by frequency of use are compared descriptively; no group without ketamine use
outcome: Self-reported reasons for first and continued use; effects named or rated as liked, best, disliked or worst; settings and activities; reasons the authors link to dependence; accounts of wanted and unwanted states, including the K-hole; needing more for the same effect
magnitude: Dillon et al. (2003), Sydney, n = 100 (each share is also a count): main reason for first use the effect 62, friends using 25, curiosity 11; reasons for continuing (several allowed) the effect 74, to party 61, friends using 42, using other drugs 35, it feels good 32; best things altered senses 78, out-of-body experience 52, euphoric rush 50, group experience 49, to bring on other drugs 42, escaping reality 38, well-being 26, dancing all night 23, creativity 20, stress release 4; worst things fear of the K-hole 45, health risks 35, coming down 32, limited availability 22, impurities 15, psychological problems 11, nothing 10, tolerance 8, physical responses 1; two main activities on ketamine (two choices) dancing 78, staying at home 27, chilling out 25, listening to music 19; ever had a K-hole 56; 20 or more uses against 10 or fewer, OR 4.3 (95% CI 1.58 to 11.71), χ² 8.64, printed P < 0.001 (p ≈ 0.003 on 1 degree of freedom, editors' calculation); needed more for the same effect 22 (subgroup shares not used: they cannot be reconciled with the total); intend to use again 69; ratings, for example separated from body ever 57, positive 68, negative 16 (denominator not stated). Muetzelfeldt et al. (2008), London, n = 90 (30 per group; coded narratives and ratings): prior knowledge 80 (88%); peer-pressure theme 21 (23%); first experience positive 79, not enjoyed but continued 8; liked at first: dissociation 34 (37.8%), contentedness 16, intense merriment 10, intensity 9; compared with other drugs: different 13, short duration 9, less comedown 5; liked now: general high 20 (22.2%), same as at first 15, relaxing 14, relief from cravings or filling a gap 6; dependence-type reasons 8 (7 frequent, 1 infrequent); rated quite or very appealing: melting into the surroundings 65 (72.2%), visual hallucinations 64 (71.1%), out-of-body experience 58 (64.4%), giggliness 58 (64.4%); most often rated disliked: impaired memory 45 (50%), decreased sociability 45 (50%), nausea 38 (42.2%), impaired concentration 29 (32.2%); disliked at first: intensity 22, nausea or vomiting 19, loss of control 15, dissociation 9; disliked about current use: weaker effect (tolerance or poorer quality) 13, cognitive disorganization 9, negative psychological effects 30 mentions; concern about compulsive use 25 (28%). Starting statements (frequent / infrequent / former %, printed total; count of 89, editors'): offered a line and enjoyed it 80.0/86.7/75.9, 80.9 (72); enjoy psychedelic drugs and it sounded interesting 80.0/63.3/89.7, 77.7 (69, 77.5%); friends were doing it 73.3/76.7/75.9, 75.3 (67); explore my consciousness further 56.7/56.7/75.9, 63.1 (56, 62.9%); saw people doing it at a party 56.7/53.3/62.1, 57.4 (51, 57.3%); helped me get into music 33.3/36.7/41.4, 37.1 (33); bored of other drugs 33.3/43.3/31.0, 35.9 (32, 36.0%); forget my troubles 16.7/16.7/17.2, 16.9 (15); did not know what it was 3.3/16.7/10.3, 10.1 (9). Consciousness by group: printed χ²(2) = 10.36, p = .035; from the printed shares χ²(2) ≈ 3.1, p ≈ 0.21 (editors' calculation). Settings ever used (of 90; printed total, editors' count): friend's house 84.5 (76), home 71.1 (64), squat parties 58.9 (53), outdoor parties 56.7 (51), clubs 52.2 (47), pubs 34.4 (31; the infrequent group's 29.0% is not a possible share of 30), dinner parties 22.2 (20). Moore and Measham (2008), north-west England, n = 12 in 10 interviews: no counts except views held by all 12 (trying to control the effects; making the amount taken more predictable; awareness of mostly negative portrayals). Precision (editors' calculation, Wilson 95% intervals, chance only, not the unknown selection): 62 of 100, 52% to 71%; 45 of 100, 36% to 55%; 65 of 90, 62% to 80%; 45 of 90, 40% to 60%; 72 of 89, 72% to 88%; 15 of 89, 10% to 26%.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement and selection within each sample: unpublished, unvalidated questionnaires; in Sydney, one interviewer who also recruited 39 of the 100, and positive/negative ratings whose denominator cannot be the people who had each effect; in London, answers typed during the interview, one researcher coded every narrative, a second checked 4 interviews chosen at random, and the two then discussed the coding of each narrative together, only the top four rated effects printed (the Appendix with the full list is missing) and a printed test that does not fit its shares; in north-west England, no analytic method described and accounts that were also self-presentations against negative portrayals (cards sc_dillon_2003 and sc_muetzelfeldt_2008: JBI prevalence checklist, editors' summary high; sc_moore_2008: editors' qualitative checklist, high).

inconsistency.note: Three teams in two countries, with a survey, a structured interview and in-depth interviews, agree on the kinds of reasons (the drug's effects, fun or partying, friends, interest in new drugs) and on the valued effects (changed perception, detachment, laughter). The questions differ, so the shares are given side by side and not compared or pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: none of the samples has a sampling frame; all three were reached through the researchers' contacts, friends, the media or dance-scene and club networks in Sydney (1998 to 1999), London (before late 2007) and north-west England (from 2005); most used many other drugs; people who inject (in Sydney 11 of 100 usually injected into a vein and 4 into a muscle; one person in London occasionally; none in north-west England), people in treatment and people outside these networks are few or absent; reasons may differ in other places and in later years.

imprecision.note: Shares of 89 to 100 people carry 95% intervals of about ±10 points (editors' calculation); figures for groups of 30 and the 12-person interviews are worded as such and carry no comparison the claim rests on.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the people sampled (METHODS 6.3): starts low; risk of bias -1 (measurement, see the domain note) and indirectness -1 (coverage): very low, the floor; never upgraded. Status replicated: Dillon et al. (Sydney) and Muetzelfeldt et al. (London) are independent samples by different teams that agree in direction, and Moore and Measham's interviews are consistent with them; the agreement is about which kinds of reasons people give, not about how often each is given, which none of the three can show. About half of the London sample had taken part in the same team's earlier studies, so it is not independent of other ketamine findings from that team. Printed figures checked at the source: the Sydney K-hole test (χ² 8.64 printed with P < 0.001; p ≈ 0.003 on 1 degree of freedom) and the London consciousness test (χ²(2) = 10.36, p = .035, which the printed shares do not reproduce: χ²(2) ≈ 3.1, p ≈ 0.21) are corrected in the statement; the London total column is the average of the group percentages, so counts of 89 are given instead; the London pubs share (29.0% of 30) and the Sydney tolerance subgroups (24.3% and 52.2%) cannot be reconciled with their totals and are not used. The London group differences are not used as effects of frequency of use: the groups were self-selected and differed in education, premorbid-IQ estimate, employment and mental-health histories (card sc_muetzelfeldt_2008). Effects are what people reported, and most also used other drugs. The claim gives no advice on amounts, routes, timing, combinations or reaching a particular state; describing the effects people valued is a finding, not encouragement, and the north-west England account of how unwanted K-holes happened is reported as those 12 people's explanation.
