statement: In people who use ketamine outside medicine, ketamine use is associated with inflammation and damage of the bladder, urinary symptoms and, in some patients, involvement of the kidneys, but no study compared how often these problems occur in people who use ketamine and in people who do not. A systematic review with meta-analysis of published clinical series (Chan et al., 2022; Embase, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials searched to 26 June 2020, English only) included 45 articles on patients with urinary-tract problems attributed to ketamine (ketamine-associated uropathy), mostly from Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong and all retrospective by the authors' account: 4890 patients by the Results (4921 by the abstract), 72% men (editors' arithmetic), mean age 25.46 years, mean duration of ketamine use 54.99 months. Among 4314 patients in 37 studies, the pooled shares (random effects, 95% confidence intervals) were: needing to pass urine frequently 77.1% (56.9% to 92.2%), urgency 69.9% (48.8% to 87.3%), pain above the pubic bone 60.4% (35.3% to 82.9%), passing urine at night 58.0% (38.5% to 76.2%), painful urination 49.8% (28.5% to 71.1%), blood in the urine 46.3% (22.6% to 71.0%) and leakage 43.9% (21.0% to 68.2%); an overactive bladder muscle on testing 63.9% (45.6% to 80.3%); and, less often, swelling of a kidney from urine backing up (hydronephrosis) 30.2% (22.0% to 39.2%), urine flowing back towards the kidneys (vesicoureteral reflux) 22.0% (12.4% to 33.5%), narrowing of a ureter 19.4% (7.3% to 35.5%) and impaired kidney function 8.3% (4.8% to 12.6%). Pooled bladder measures (15 studies, 1221 patients) included a functional bladder capacity of 95.23 mL (63.57 to 126.88; 717 patients) and a maximum urine flow of 8.69 mL/s (5.54 to 11.83; 451 patients), which the review calls reduced without giving reference values; cystoscopy and biopsy findings from 14 studies (an inflamed and ulcerated bladder lining, loss of its surface layer, infiltrating eosinophils and mast cells, and fibrosis in some patients) are described in words only. These shares describe patients identified because they had urinary problems, largely in urology services, and they vary widely between series; they do not show how often people who use ketamine develop such problems. The review does not list or appraise its studies, reports no heterogeneity statistics and does not say how ketamine use or other drug use was established. The case series that its authors call the first report of the condition (Shahani et al., 2007; one hospital in Toronto) described 9 patients with chronic non-medical ketamine use, daily by the abstract, and urinary symptoms: urine cultures were sterile in all 9, cystoscopy showed ulcerative cystitis in all 9 by the abstract, and biopsies in 4 showed a lining that had lost much of its surface layer, with inflammation and eosinophils; after stopping ketamine, by the patients' own accounts, some improved and others did not fully recover, with no measurements or follow-up period. The only figures from people who use ketamine outside clinics come from an online survey promoted through a dance-music magazine's website between November 2009 and January 2010 (Winstock et al., 2012): 340 of the 1,285 respondents who had used ketamine in the past 12 months (printed as 26.6%; 80.3% in the UK; mean age 23.5) said they had had at least one of five urinary symptoms that they associated with ketamine in that year, most often needing to pass urine frequently (224, 17.4%) and least often blood in the urine (19, 1.5%); respondents who reported larger typical amounts per session reported all five symptoms more often, and those with more days of use three of them, in univariate tests whose group rates are not printed; of 251 who described how their symptoms changed, 128 said they improved when they stopped, 108 that they stayed the same while they kept using and 8 that they got worse after stopping; and 35 of the 340 had seen a general practitioner. Almost all survey respondents also drank alcohol (98%) and used other drugs, and the symptoms were reported, and linked to ketamine, by the respondents themselves, with no examination. The review's authors call stopping ketamine essential (it was regarded as key in 11 of 19 articles on treatment, and surgery is reported as effective only when patients avoided further use), but none of the studies they describe compared people who stopped with people who continued. These studies show that urinary-tract damage was found in, and urinary symptoms were reported by, people who use ketamine, many of them young; they do not show that ketamine caused these problems, how common the problems are among people who use ketamine, or that stopping helps. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Doctors have described urinary problems linked to ketamine in more than 4,000 patients, mostly young people in places in Asia such as Taiwan and Hong Kong. A review that pooled their reports found that about 77 in 100 of these patients needed to pee often, about 70 in 100 felt a sudden need to go and about 60 in 100 had bladder pain; in about 3 in 10, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney, and about 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function. Camera checks inside the bladder and tissue samples showed sore, ulcerated linings, scarred in some. The first report, from one hospital in Toronto, described 9 people who used ketamine daily. In an online survey of people in the dance-music scene, mostly in the UK, about 1 in 4 of the 1,285 who had used ketamine in the past year said they had urine problems they linked to ketamine, most often needing to pee often (17 in 100); people who reported using more reported symptoms more often. Of 251 who described their symptoms over time, about half said they got better when they stopped, and 8 said they got worse. The patients' numbers come from people who went to doctors because of urine problems, so they do not show how often people who use ketamine get these problems. No study compared how often these problems occur in people who use ketamine and in people who do not, the survey relied on what people said, and most also drank alcohol and used other drugs, so these studies cannot show that ketamine caused the problems, how common they are, or that stopping helps.
population: People who use ketamine outside medicine: patients with urinary-tract problems attributed to ketamine in published clinical series pooled by a systematic review (45 articles, 4890 patients, mostly from Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong, published up to June 2020; mean age 25.46 years, 72% men); 9 patients with chronic non-medical use (daily by the abstract) seen with urinary symptoms at one hospital in Toronto, reported in 2007 (ages given for 3 of them: 17, 25 and 28); and 1,285 respondents to an online survey of people in the dance-music scene (November 2009 to January 2010) who had used ketamine in the past 12 months, 80.3% in the UK, mean age 23.5, 70.3% men
exposure: Non-medical ketamine use, not tested in any source as far as reported: in the review, how use was established is not reported and only a mean duration of use is given (54.99 months); chronic use, daily by the abstract, with no amounts, duration or route, in the case series; any use in the past 12 months in the survey, with self-reported typical amount per session and days of use in the past month
comparator: None: no study included people who do not use ketamine; the review pools single-group shares and means only; within the survey only, respondents who reported smaller typical amounts per session or fewer days of use in the past month
outcome: Urinary symptoms, upper-tract findings (hydronephrosis, reflux, narrowing of a ureter, kidney function), bladder capacity and flow, and cystoscopy and biopsy findings in patients in clinical series (review); bladder appearance at cystoscopy and biopsy (and, in one patient, computed tomography) and the course described after stopping (case series); at least one of five urinary symptoms that respondents associated with ketamine in the past 12 months, their recalled course and help-seeking (survey)
magnitude: Chan et al. (2022), meta-analysis of published clinical series of patients with ketamine-associated uropathy, no comparison group: 45 articles (37 in the quantitative synthesis; search to 26 June 2020); 4890 patients (abstract 4921), 3518 men and 1372 women (72% men, editors' arithmetic), mean age 25.46 ± 6.03 years, mean duration of ketamine use 54.99 ± 43.54 months (± not labelled). Pooled prevalence among 4314 patients in 37 studies (random effects, 95% CI): frequency 77.1% (56.9 to 92.2), urgency 69.9% (48.8 to 87.3), detrusor overactivity 63.9% (45.6 to 80.3), suprapubic pain 60.4% (35.3 to 82.9), nocturia 58.0% (38.5 to 76.2), dysuria 49.8% (28.5 to 71.1), haematuria 46.3% (22.6 to 71.0), incontinence 43.9% (21.0 to 68.2), hydronephrosis 30.2% (22.0 to 39.2), vesicoureteral reflux 22.0% (12.4 to 33.5), ureteral stricture 19.4% (7.3 to 35.5), impaired renal function 8.3% (4.8 to 12.6); no heterogeneity statistics, and no study counts for most estimates, in the article. Pooled means (15 studies, 1221 patients with capacity data): functional bladder capacity 95.23 mL (63.57 to 126.88; n = 717), cystometric capacity 97.37 mL (58.23 to 136.51; n = 491), maximum cystometric capacity 202.09 mL (169.06 to 235.13; n = 140), voided volume 113.31 mL (59.44 to 167.19; n = 630), maximum flow 8.69 mL/s (5.54 to 11.83; n = 451); Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency score 21.66 (20.12 to 23.20; n = 750). Treatment (19 articles): stopping ketamine regarded as key in 11; uncontrolled series; no comparison of stopping with continuing. Shahani et al. (2007), 9 patients, no comparison group: urine cultures sterile 9 of 9; ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy 9 of 9 by the abstract (mild squamous metaplasia in the second patient); biopsies in 4, eosinophils in all 4 to a variable degree; course after stopping described in words only (first patient's urgency and frequency persisted, second improved, third incomplete, the other 6 said to benefit with pentosan polysulfate added). Winstock et al. (2012), 1,285 respondents with past-year use (of 3,806 surveys): at least one symptom 340 (printed 26.6%; 26.5% by the editors' arithmetic, Wilson 95% interval about 24.1% to 28.9%, editors' calculation); frequency 224 (17.4%), lower abdominal pain 145 (11.3%), burning or stinging 104 (8.1%), leakage 43 (3.3%), blood in the urine 19 (1.5%). Three groups by typical amount per session: chi-squared 37.95 burning, 78.29 frequency, 39.0 pain (each P < 0.001), 6.52 blood (P = 0.038), 7.44 leakage (P = 0.024); three groups by days of use in the past month (asked of the 792 with last-month use): pain 52.0 and frequency 39.56 (P < 0.001), burning 9.8 (P = 0.007), blood 0.62 (P = 0.74), leakage 5.66 (P = 0.06); group rates not printed. Recalled course (n = 251): improved on stopping 128 (51%), unchanged while still using 108 (43%), worse after stopping 8 (printed 3.8%; 3.2% of 251 and 7 of the 251 unaccounted for, editors' arithmetic). Help-seeking among the 340: general practitioner 35 (10%), specialist referral 10 (2.9%), emergency department 6 (1.8%). No comparison with people who do not use ketamine, so no relative or absolute difference can be given.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results); Material and Methods, 1st paragraph (right column)
evidence.extracted: A series of 9 patients with chronic recreational (non-medical) ketamine use, all described in the abstract as using it daily, who presented with severe painful urination, frequency, urgency and visible blood in the urine. All 9 had a history and physical examination, cystoscopy, urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology; 4 had bladder biopsies, all read by one pathologist; computed tomography and other tests were done as indicated. Abstract results: urine cultures were sterile in all cases; at cystoscopy all patients had severe ulcerative cystitis; biopsies in 4 showed loss of the surface lining (epithelial denudation) and inflammation with a mild eosinophilic infiltrate; stopping ketamine, with pentosan polysulfate added, appeared to give some relief of symptoms. No amounts, duration of use or route are given.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 810, right column, continuing on p. 811, left and right columns), 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 811, right column); Figures 1 and 2 (p. 811)
evidence.extracted: First (index) patient: a 28-year-old man with a 6-month history of painful blood in the urine, painful urination, urgency and pain after passing urine, which began only after he started daily ketamine use; he smoked a pack of cigarettes a day and had a history of juvenile diabetes, hyperthyroidism and peptic ulcer disease. Urine culture, urinalysis and cytology were negative; computed tomography showed marked inflammatory change and a very small bladder capacity; cystoscopy showed multiple red patches consistent with active cystitis; the biopsies showed a largely denuded lining with a thin layer of regenerating cells, a swollen superficial layer beneath it with the overall appearance of granulation tissue, a dense fibrotic deeper layer, and lymphocytes and mast cells with eosinophils predominating; tests for vasculitis were negative. Second patient: a 25-year-old woman with a 2-year history of frequency, urgency and discomfort above the pubic bone that, by her own account, began soon after she started experimenting with ketamine; cystoscopy showed mild squamous metaplasia and reddened, flat ulcerated patches. Third: a 17-year-old boy with recurrent painful urination and irritative voiding symptoms over several months, with cystoscopic findings similar to the first patient's. The remaining 6 had similar patterns of ketamine use, symptoms and cystoscopic findings; 3 of them had biopsies similar to the first patient's, with variable eosinophilic infiltrate. Ages and sexes of these 6 are not given.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs (right column)
evidence.extracted: Course after stopping ketamine: antibiotics and steroids had not controlled the first patient's symptoms; after he stopped ketamine he noticed that his blood in the urine had settled, but disabling urgency and frequency of urination continued. The second patient herself observed a significant improvement in her symptoms after she stopped. The third patient's symptoms did not resolve completely after he stopped; other treatments had limited success, and pentosan polysulfate, a medicine meant to supplement the bladder's protective (glycosaminoglycan) lining, helped relieve his irritative symptoms. All of the remaining 6 are said to have benefited from stopping ketamine with pentosan polysulfate added. No symptom scores, bladder measurements, repeat cystoscopy or follow-up period are reported for any patient.

evidence.locator: Comment, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 811, right column, continuing on p. 812, left column); Conclusions (p. 812, left and right columns)
evidence.extracted: The authors call this the first report of the condition they name ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis, and read the timing of onset and of stopping in all 9 as pointing to ketamine as a cause; they state that none of the 9 was using other illicit drugs, without saying how this was established. The only drug analysis is of a small amount of illicit ketamine obtained with the help of the Toronto police narcotics division (not said to come from the patients' own supply), found to be pure ketamine hydrochloride with a trace of dimethyl sulfoxide. Eosinophils were seen in all four biopsies, to a variable degree; the authors judge that the features appear distinct from classic eosinophilic cystitis, which has been described in association with bladder cancer, asthma and rhinitis, bladder outlet obstruction and some medicines. They state that the long-term course, including the possible development of scarred, small-capacity bladders, remains to be defined. Editors' note: the causal reading rests partly on the timing of stopping in all 9, but in the Results 2 of the 3 patients described one by one did not fully recover after stopping.
evidence.quote: implicates ketamine as a causal factor

Of the 1285, 80.3% (1032) were from the UK, 11.8% (151) from the USA and 7.9% (102) from elsewhere; mean age 23.5 years (SD 5.8); 70.3% (869) were male. The first page labels the study type as symptom prevalence in a prospective cohort with level of evidence 1b, but the Methods describe a single cross-sectional survey and nobody was followed up. Ethical approval came from an NHS research ethics committee.

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: a self-nominating, relatively poorly characterized population; reliance on self-reported experiences with a substance of uncertain composition; high levels of polydrug use and confounding effects of other substances; uncertain amounts and purity; what they call the most significant, no information on route of use for most respondents, so that higher risks with injecting cannot be excluded; and that symptom misattribution, other substance use, acute polydrug or alcohol use, or pre-existing conditions cannot be excluded. evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 466); Methods › Literature search, Screening process and selection criteria, and Data extraction (p. 467), and Data analysis and statistical analysis (p. 467, continuing on p. 468); Results, 1st paragraph, and Figure (PRISMA flow diagram) (p. 468)
evidence.extracted: A systematic review with meta-analysis of published literature on ketamine-associated uropathy, said to follow PRISMA. Embase, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched to 26 June 2020 (human studies in English; conference abstracts excluded; reference lists searched, adding no articles). Case series, case-cohort studies, non-randomised studies and randomised trials on ketamine use and uropathy were eligible; editorials, commentaries, reviews, case reports, non-human studies, articles without an English full text and studies of anaesthetic use were excluded; records were screened by at least two reviewers, with a third for disagreements. Of 1365 records, 913 remained after duplicates were removed, 183 full texts were assessed and 138 excluded (110 wrong study type, 23 unrelated to urology, 4 animal studies, 1 non-English), leaving 45 articles in the qualitative and 37 in the quantitative synthesis. Results were pooled (OpenMeta[Analyst], random effects, double arcsine transformation) when more than two studies with more than 100 patients reported them; the studies in each pool were checked for patient overlap; heterogeneity was to be assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Editors' note from reading the whole article: no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies is described, the included studies are not listed, no Q or I² value is reported for any pooled estimate, and how ketamine use or other drug use was established is not reported (card sc_chan_2022: AMSTAR 2 critically low).

evidence.extracted: Upper urinary tract findings and bladder function, pooled among patients with ketamine-associated uropathy (95% CI): hydronephrosis 30.2% (22.0% to 39.2%), vesicoureteral reflux 22.0% (12.4% to 33.5%), ureteral stricture 19.4% (7.3% to 35.5%), impaired renal function 8.3% (4.8% to 12.6%) and detrusor overactivity 63.9% (45.6% to 80.3%) (Table 1; the text rounds ureteral stricture to about 20% and impaired renal function to about 10%). Fifteen studies (1221 patients) reported bladder capacity: pooled functional bladder capacity 95.23 mL (63.57 to 126.88; n = 717), cystometric capacity 97.37 mL (58.23 to 136.51; n = 491) and maximum cystometric capacity 202.09 mL (169.06 to 235.13; n = 140). Urodynamic studies gave a pooled voided volume of 113.31 mL (59.44 to 167.19; n = 630) and maximum flow rate of 8.69 mL/s (5.54 to 11.83; n = 451), with no number of studies given (Table 2). Symptom scores (13 studies, 2135 patients) included a pooled Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency score of 21.66 (20.12 to 23.20; n = 750). In the 14 studies that included cystoscopy results and bladder biopsy findings, the findings are described in words only: inflammation of the bladder lining, red patches, new vessel growth and ulceration, with small haemorrhages in severe disease; loss of the lining (urothelial denudation), with granulation tissue, congestion, swelling and infiltrating lymphocytes, eosinophils and mast cells in the tissue beneath it; and fibrosis around the bladder in some patients. No reference values for capacity or flow are given.

evidence.extracted: Treatment was described in 19 articles, with no pattern consistent across studies; stopping ketamine was regarded as a key part of management in 11 of the 19. Results of oral, bladder-instillation and surgical treatments come from uncontrolled series, each with its own definition of improvement (Table 3), and surgery is reported as effective only when patients avoided further ketamine use (four articles cited). The abstract says that stopping ketamine was necessary for improvement, and the Discussion that it is consistently effective whatever the severity, citing a study of 66 people in which maximal voided volume was 387 mL after at least a year without ketamine against 243 mL after less than 3 months, and one in which hydronephrosis resolved in patients who stopped. Editors' note: no analysis in the review compares patients who stopped with patients who continued; the 66-person comparison, as described, is between different people with different lengths of abstinence, is second-hand, and is neither pooled nor appraised.

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: all included studies were retrospective; there was heterogeneity among the included studies, primarily because workup and treatment varied; treatment efficacy could not be fully assessed because baseline characteristics were described inconsistently; and most studies came from Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong, as the condition's incidence depends on where ketamine is popular. The Discussion summarizes frequency, nocturia, urgency and bladder pain as seen in approximately 60% of patients diagnosed with ketamine-associated uropathy in 37 studies with more than 4000 patients, says symptom severity may be associated with chronicity and dose, citing a UK survey of 3806 people and a Taiwanese series second-hand, and treats an association between ketamine use and urinary tract damage as established while calling its mechanism unclear; the Conclusion calls stopping ketamine essential. risk_of_bias.note: No study compares how often urinary problems occur in people who use ketamine and in people who do not (the review reports only two small comparisons: with patients who had another bladder disease, on severity, and with an undescribed control group, on one blood test). Review of clinical series (card sc_chan_2022, AMSTAR 2 critically low): patients selected because they had urinary problems, largely in urology services; all included studies retrospective by the authors' account; how ketamine use and other drug use were established not reported; included studies neither listed nor appraised; no heterogeneity statistics; some included series written by review authors. Case series (card sc_shahani_2007, editors' checklist, high): 9 patients from one hospital service, with no account of how they were selected; ketamine use and the absence of other drugs rest on the patients' accounts, with no testing and no amounts or duration; the course after stopping is described in words, without measures or a follow-up period; and the abstract states findings for all 9 that the Results describe for some only. Survey (card sc_winstock_2012, JBI prevalence checklist, high): self-selected readers of a dance-music website with no sampling frame or response rate; five unvalidated yes-or-no items in which respondents themselves linked their symptoms to ketamine, without duration, severity, examination or urine testing; near-universal alcohol and other drug use not adjusted for; univariate three-group tests without group rates.

inconsistency.note: Every source points the same way: urinary problems are found in people who use ketamine. The pooled shares vary widely between clinical series (bladder pain 35.3% to 82.9%), and the review reports no heterogeneity statistics; this spread concerns how often each problem is recorded among patients with different workups, not whether problems are found, so it is not counted against the claim as worded.

indirectness.note: Worded for what was measured: problems recorded in patients in published clinical series (mostly in Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong, to June 2020) and in 9 hospital patients in Toronto, and self-reported symptoms that respondents linked to ketamine in a mostly British online sample of people in the dance-music scene in 2009 and 2010; not worded as how often people who use ketamine develop bladder damage.

imprecision.note: The pooled shares among patients have wide intervals (frequency 56.9% to 92.2%), but they are reported as descriptions of selected patients, with their intervals; the survey's overall share is precise for its own sample (about 24.1% to 28.9%, editors' calculation). The size of any difference from people who do not use ketamine is unknown because nobody was compared, which is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not assessable. Series of patients with the condition may be published more readily than series that find no problems, which would not change the direction of the claim as worded.

dose_response.note: The survey reports symptoms more often with larger self-reported typical amounts and more days of use, but only in univariate three-group tests without group rates, with symptoms linked to ketamine by the respondents and without allowance for alcohol and other drugs; the review does not synthesize amount, frequency or duration of use and cites the survey and one Taiwanese series second-hand; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (clinical case series, a meta-analysis of clinical series and a cross-sectional online survey) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The newer review (Chan et al., 2022) widens the evidence from two reports to 45 articles with 4890 patients, which strengthens the replication but not the certainty: its series are uncontrolled and retrospective, their patients were selected because they had urinary problems, ketamine and other drug use were not verified as far as the review reports, and the review itself is critically low on AMSTAR 2; nothing in it would support an upgrade (with no comparison group there is no effect size, and amount and duration of use are not synthesized). Rated as worded, an association in the weakest sense: urinary-tract damage and symptoms are found in people who use ketamine, many of them young. No source can show that ketamine causes these problems, because nobody who does not use ketamine was studied and other causes (infection, alcohol, other drugs, earlier bladder problems) were not ruled out; nor how common they are among people who use ketamine, because the review's shares are among patients and the survey's sample is self-selected; nor that stopping helps, because no study compared people who stopped with people who continued. The review's statements that the association is established and that stopping is necessary for improvement, the case series authors' causal reading, and the survey authors' statements that the harms are dose related and particularly common with dependence are not adopted. Status replicated: unconnected teams in Canada, in the UK and in the clinical series pooled by the review, mostly from Asian countries or regions, report the same kind of problem; the Toronto series is among the treatment studies the review cites and is counted once. The survey's amount groups are described without their amounts, and no routes are given, so that nothing reads as guidance on amounts. The five new anchors to the review await a second reader.

statement: In England from 1999 to 2019, 283 deaths notified by coroners to the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (NPSAD; np-SAD in the 2008 letter) had ketamine, or its breakdown product norketamine, recorded in the cause of death, the coroner's verdict or the post-mortem toxicology results, as counted by researchers who run the register (Corkery et al., 2021; cases extracted on 31 January 2020; deaths in which ketamine had been given in medical care, or in which its source could not be determined, were left out; none occurred in 1997 or 1998). An earlier letter by the same team counted 23 deaths in the UK from 1993 to 2006 with ketamine mentioned in a coroner's report to the register or on a death certificate (Schifano et al., 2008); the authors say 18 of these are among the 283. Both describe deaths with ketamine recorded, whatever the recorded cause, not deaths caused by ketamine. By year of death (editors' reading of the later paper's bar chart, whose bars sum to 283), the English count was 1 or 2 a year from 1999 to 2004, 5 in 2005 and 7 in 2006, between 13 and 24 a year from 2007 to 2016, and 32, 31 and 31 from 2017 to 2019 (2019 incomplete, as inquests take on average 7 to 10 months; the authors project about 56); as a share of all deaths notified to the register from England, these deaths rose from about 0.1% in 1999 and 2000 to about 2.2% in 2017 (approximate). For 1999 to 2006, which both reports cover, the later series counts 22 deaths where the letter counted 18 (editors' sums), so counts for the same years changed with later notifications and the case definition. UK death registrations compiled by the authors, which may include deaths after medical use, mention ketamine in the cause of death of 0 to 3 deaths a year from 1997 to 2006, 7 to 21 a year from 2007 to 2017 and 33 in 2018 (editors' reading of a line chart). Of the 283, 238 (84.1%) were men, against 73.2% of all 33,186 deaths notified from England in 1999–2019; mean age was 31.2 years (range 15 to 67), against 40.2; and, where known, 79.6% had a history of drug use. Most had other substances found: on average 4.6 drugs at post-mortem (range 0 to 13), against 3.3 for all notified deaths; alcohol was found in 117 (41.3%), and the authors' Discussion gives cocaine in 41%, heroin or morphine in 31%, diazepam in 28%, MDMA in 20%, cannabis in 18% and methadone in 10%. Coroners concluded accident in 234 (82.7%), suicide in 16 (5.6%) and undetermined intent in 31 (11.0%); the recorded underlying cause was accidental poisoning in 211 (74.6%), poisoning of undetermined intent in 13, hanging in 12, intentional self-poisoning in 6, drowning in 5, a fall in 4 and a road traffic collision in 3 (editors' sums of a table whose rows account for 276 of the 283), and other cause-of-death fields record 16 drownings or immersions; 179 (63.3%, editors' arithmetic; 66.8% in the text) died at home or in another private residence and 45 (15.9%) in hospital. Deaths with ketamine alone are counted in three ways: ketamine was the only drug implicated in 32 deaths (11.3%), which the Discussion calls ketamine detected on its own, but other drugs were found at post-mortem in 17 of these and no drug in 1, so it was both the only drug implicated and the only drug found in 14; and it was the only substance mentioned in the cause-of-death fields in 13 of the 119 deaths whose fields mentioned it. The paper does not reconcile these counts and gives the causes of the 14 only within the 32, of whom 26 died by accident and 4 by suicide. In UK death registrations, ketamine was the only cause-of-death mention in 2 to 9 deaths a year from 2007 (editors' reading). In the letter's 23 deaths (19 of them men), ketamine was the only drug found in 4, all recorded as poisoning (3 accidents, 1 suicide), and other substances were found with it in the rest, most often opiates or opioids (10), alcohol (8) and benzodiazepines (7). These counts include only deaths in which ketamine was tested for, found and written down, so they are minimums, and part of the rise may reflect testing and reporting rather than more deaths: reporting to the register is voluntary (80.5% of coroners in England reported regularly), toxicology was part of 13% of post-mortem examinations in England and Wales in 2011 and 24% in 2019, and ketamine is screened for routinely only in some specialist laboratories or on request. They cannot show that ketamine caused or contributed to any death, which drug did, or the risk of death for people who use ketamine: the authors' crude rate, 7.3 deaths a year per 100,000 people with past-year use, divides 116 deaths involving ketamine registered in England and Wales in 2010–2018 (of unspecified type of use, possibly including deaths after medical use) by an average household-survey estimate of 176,444 people aged 16 to 59 with past-year use, so it is not a death rate for the deaths counted here. The authors conclude that "Ketamine on its own can kill" and that their series should dispel the view that ketamine-related deaths are rare; their own tables give 14 deaths in which ketamine was the only drug found and implicated, with no denominator. The authors analysed the register they run, which was part-funded in 2004–2019 by the Department of Health, the National Treatment Agency for Substance Misuse and Public Health England, and four of them sit on a committee of the UK's Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In England, ketamine was found or named in the records of 283 deaths from 1999 to 2019, counted by the researchers who run a national register of drug-related deaths that coroners report to. The number rose from 1 or 2 a year around 2000 to between 13 and 24 a year from 2007 to 2016, and about 30 a year from 2017. Most of the people who died were men (84 in 100), and their average age was 31. Most had other drugs found too, between 4 and 5 on average; alcohol and cocaine were each found in about 4 in 10. About 3 in 4 deaths were recorded as accidental poisonings; 16 were suicides, and others included drownings, falls and road crashes. Records linked only ketamine to 32 deaths, but other drugs were found in 17 of those, and ketamine was the only drug found in 14. An earlier count by the same team found ketamine recorded in 23 UK deaths from 1993 to 2006, with ketamine the only drug found in 4. Finding ketamine after a death does not show that it caused the death. The counts are a minimum, because only some deaths are tested for drugs and only some laboratories look for ketamine routinely, and part of the rise may come from more testing and reporting. Without a matching count of how many people used ketamine, no death rate can be given.
population: Deaths in England from 1999 to 2019 notified by coroners to the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths in which a text search found ketamine or norketamine in the cause of death, the coroner's verdict or the toxicology results (cases extracted on 31 January 2020; 2019 incomplete); and deaths in the UK from 1993 to 2006 with ketamine mentioned in a coroner's report notified to the same register (July 1997 to December 2006) or on a death certificate in General Register Office drug-poisoning statistics for England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (January 1993 to December 2006); both excluding deaths in which ketamine had been given in medical care, the later series also deaths in which the source of the ketamine could not be determined
exposure: Ketamine recorded after death: found in the toxicology results or written in the cause of death or the coroner's verdict (later series), or mentioned in a coroner's report or on a death certificate (letter); amounts, frequency and route of use not reported; the later series' post-mortem concentrations are not used here
comparator: None: no deaths without ketamine apart from descriptive figures for all 33,186 deaths notified to the register from England in 1999–2019 (which include the 283), and no count of people who used ketamine that matches the deaths counted
outcome: Number of deaths with ketamine recorded, by year; sex and age; other substances found; deaths with ketamine as the only drug implicated, the only drug found or the only cause-of-death mention; coroner's conclusion on the manner of death, recorded underlying cause, place and circumstances

evidence.locator: To the Editors, 2nd paragraph (right column)
evidence.extracted: To gather the UK ketamine misuse mortality figures for 1993–2006, two sources were combined: the np-SAD database at St George's, University of London, for July 1997 to December 2006, and the drug-poisoning mortality statistics of the General Register Offices for England and Wales and for Scotland, with data provided to np-SAD by the General Register Office for Northern Ireland, for January 1993 to December 2006. np-SAD receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK; a death is recorded if one or more psychoactive substances were directly implicated, the person had a history of dependence on or misuse of psychoactive drugs, or controlled drugs were found at post-mortem examination; the coroners' response rate has been estimated to have been as high as about 90% to 95%. A ketamine-related death was one in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report (other illegal drugs could also be written); np-SAD cases were not counted again among those from the other records; deaths with ketamine present because it had been given for medical reasons were excluded.

evidence.extracted: To the best of their knowledge, the authors say, the series is the largest available collection of ketamine misuse mortality data from the UK and elsewhere; they say the 4 deaths with ketamine alone somewhat question the high safety profile suggested elsewhere, while allowing that these may have been accidents from misjudged risk linked to ketamine's dissociative effects; they ask whether interactions between the drugs taken were the real cause of the deaths involving several drugs. evidence.extracted: The register (NPSAD, at St George's, University of London) receives information on drug-related deaths from coroners on a voluntary basis; 80.5% of coroners in England were then reporting regularly, data for England are much more complete than for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and more than 35,100 deaths had been received from English jurisdictions since July 1997 and processed by 1 February 2020. evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: reporting to the register is voluntary and varies over time and between coroners' areas; late notifications and unfinished inquests mean the numbers should be regarded as a minimum; in England and Wales the share of deaths reported to coroners that went to inquest fell from 61% in 1995 to 39% in 2019, post-mortem examinations were held in 98% and then 59% of inquests opened, and toxicology was part of 13% of post-mortem examinations in 2011 and 24% in 2019 (the authors put the share of deaths reported to coroners with toxicology in 2019 at about 9.15%); it would appear, they write, that 94% of forensic laboratories responding to a European (EMCDDA) survey could screen routinely for ketamine and 4% on request, but routine screening is typically done only in some highly specialised laboratories or on specific request; general-register deaths include some after medical use of ketamine. risk_of_bias.note: Cards sc_corkery_2021 and sc_schifano_2008 (editors' checklist, high): a death enters only if a coroner reported it to the register, which is voluntary (80.5% of coroners in England reporting regularly), and ketamine was tested for, found and written down (toxicology in 13% of post-mortem examinations in England and Wales in 2011 and 24% in 2019; ketamine screened for routinely only in some specialist laboratories or on request), so the counts are minimums and their rise may partly reflect testing and reporting; the case definition is any mention of ketamine, including toxicology alone, and what makes a drug implicated is not defined; the later paper calls all 283 deaths ones in which ketamine was implicated while its own table accounts for 200, gives three unreconciled counts of deaths with ketamine alone, and its text and tables disagree in several places (accidental manner 234 or 242; death at home 63.3% or 66.8%; underlying causes summing to 276); the letter's table lists each characteristic separately, its periods differ by source, and its text and table differ on cocaine (6 and 5).

inconsistency.note: Two reports from one register by the same team, which agree in kind (most deaths with ketamine recorded had other drugs found; few had ketamine as the only drug found); their counts for the years both cover differ (22 against 18 for 1999 to 2006) in ways that later notifications and a different case definition can explain; not rated.

indirectness.note: Worded for deaths with ketamine recorded in England from 1999 to 2019 and in the UK from 1993 to 2006, not for deaths caused by ketamine, for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland after 2006, or for later years.

imprecision.note: 283 deaths over 21 years, but annual counts of 1 to 32, small counts for the questions that matter most (14 deaths with ketamine both the only drug implicated and the only drug found, 13 with it the only cause-of-death mention, 4 of 23 in the letter; 16 suicides), no intervals, and no count of people who used ketamine that matches the deaths counted, so neither a death rate nor a trend in risk can be estimated.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive count from a national register run by the authors starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); rated down for risk of bias (voluntary reporting, incomplete testing, a case definition by mention, internal inconsistencies) and imprecision (small counts for deaths with ketamine alone, no matching denominator), it is very low. The later series (Corkery et al., 2021) covers 283 deaths in England over 21 years, beside the letter's 23 UK deaths, with counts by year, three ways of counting deaths with ketamine alone and the recorded manner and cause of death; the evidence base is larger, but it comes from the same register and team, its counts are still minimums shaped by testing and reporting, and it still has no matching denominator, so the certainty stays very low. The 283 are deaths with ketamine recorded, whatever the cause; the claim does not say how many deaths ketamine caused, and the authors' readings (that the rise means more deaths, that ketamine alone can kill and that such deaths are not rare) are reported as theirs. The year counts are the editors' readings of charts that print no numbers (the English bars sum to the paper's total); group totals of recorded causes are the editors' sums of printed tables. Post-mortem ketamine concentrations are left out, so that nothing reads as guidance on amounts. The authors' crude death rate is reported with its mismatched numerator and denominator and not adopted (METHODS §10.2). Status replicated by the same team: two reports from one register by overlapping authors, the later including, by its authors' account, 18 of the earlier deaths, so their agreement is not independent replication (METHODS §6.3). The nine new anchors to the 2021 paper await a second reader.

statement: In adults with major depression referred or already scheduled for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), a course of ketamine infusions into a vein given by clinicians (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight over 40 minutes) compared with a course of ECT (a seizure induced under brief general anaesthesia, as ELEKT-D's article describes ECT): the evidence is insufficient to say whether ketamine relieves depression as often as ECT, because the two large randomized trials, both open label, point in opposite directions in different patients. (1) In ELEKT-D (Anand et al., 2023; five US hospitals, 2017 to 2022; funded by the US Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; the authors' disclosure forms, published separately, were not read), 403 adults aged 21 to 75 with treatment-resistant major depression without psychosis (an unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials, and moderate or more severe symptoms), 359 of them outpatients, were assigned to a 3-week course of ketamine twice a week or of ECT three times a week (started with electrodes on the right side of the head only, and switched to both sides in 39% of patients, a share the article gives without a count). Self-rated response at the end of treatment was no worse with ketamine by the trial's prespecified test, and more frequent: 108 of 195 patients given ketamine (55 in 100) and 70 of 170 given ECT (41 in 100) reported that their score on a 16-item depression questionnaire (QIDS-SR-16) had fallen by half or more, a difference of 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2) against a noninferiority margin of −10 points; an analysis of all 403 randomized (200 and 203), with missing results imputed, gave 55.4% against 41.6% (difference 13.8, 3.9 to 23.8). On clinicians' ratings the difference was smaller and its interval included no difference: 99 of 195 (51 in 100) against 70 of 169 (41 in 100) responded on the MADRS (9.3 points, −0.9 to 19.4). Remission (few symptoms left) was more frequent after ketamine on both scales, 63 of 195 against 34 of 170 self-rated and 74 of 195 against 37 of 170 clinician-rated (a MADRS score of 10 or less; 16.2 points, 7.0 to 25.4), and mean scores fell by 1.8 points more self-rated (0.8 to 2.8) and 2.2 more clinician-rated (0.3 to 4.1); these secondary intervals were not adjusted for multiple testing. On a memory test given by staff (delayed recall on the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test–Revised), scores fell more after ECT by the end of treatment (change −9.7 against −0.9; difference 8.8, 5.7 to 11.9, in a metric the article leaves unclear), and patients rated their memory lower after ECT (3.2 against 4.2 on a 1-to-7 scale); in responders followed up, the test scores had returned to levels similar to the ketamine group's by 1 month, while the overall self-rating of memory stayed lower through 6 months. Quality of life rose by similar amounts (12.3 against 12.9 points; difference −0.6, −3.4 to 2.1). Moderate or severe adverse events in the 3 weeks occurred in 49 of 195 against 55 of 170; muscle pain or weakness was more frequent after ECT (9 of 170 against 1 of 195), and dissociation scores were higher with ketamine on every treatment day (values only in a supplement not read). Patients, attending physicians and research staff knew the assignments, and 31 of 203 people assigned to ECT never started it, against 4 of 200 assigned to ketamine, which the authors attribute to patient preferences and logistics. The authors state that ECT response and remission were lower than in other reports and closer to those of community and outpatient settings; that ECT has been shown to be more effective in older adults, in psychotic depression (excluded here) and in inpatient and research settings (44 of the 403 were inpatients); and that starting ECT on both sides or giving more sessions might have produced more responses, with more adverse events. (2) In KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022; six Swedish clinics, recruitment period not given; funded by the Swedish Research Council and Swedish foundations, with three authors declaring lecture fees from Lundbeck), 199 hospitalized adults aged 18 to 85 with unipolar depression (DSM-IV; a MADRS score of 20 or more) who were already scheduled for ECT were randomized, with psychotic depression included and earlier treatment failure not named as a criterion in the article (the full criteria are in a supplement not read); 186 who received at least one session were analysed, with a mean age of 55 in the ketamine group and 50 in the ECT group, psychotic symptoms in 18 of 95 and 14 of 91, and earlier ECT in 40 of 95 and 34 of 91. Both treatments were given three times a week, for up to 12 sessions until remission or what the treating psychiatrist judged the maximal effect, and stopped after 6 sessions if the MADRS score had fallen by less than 25% (ECT under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants; electrode placement in a supplement not read). Remission (a MADRS score of 10 or less held over at least 2 sessions or 5 days), rated by treating staff who knew the assignment, was less frequent after ketamine: 44 of 95 (46 in 100) against 57 of 91 after ECT (63 in 100), a difference of 16.3 percentage points (editors' arithmetic; 95% CI 2.0 to 30 as printed; P = .026), so non-inferiority against the trial's margin (a ketamine remission rate of 40% against an assumed 60% with ECT) was not shown, as the authors conclude; adding 5 randomized patients who withdrew before treatment gave 45% against 61% (1.1 to 29). MADRS scores fell by 16.1 points with ketamine against 22.4 with ECT (difference 2.9 to 9.7). Before the 2-week evaluation, 21 of 95 stopped ketamine (2 for serious adverse events and 10 for other adverse events) and 4 of 91 stopped ECT, and all stayed in the analysed groups. In post hoc subgroups, remission was 22 of 36 with ketamine against 26 of 52 with ECT in patients aged 18 to 50 (P = .39) and 22 of 59 against 31 of 39 in those aged 51 to 85 (P < .001; age-by-treatment interaction P < .001), and 9 of 18 against 11 of 14 in psychotic depression (P = .15). Among adverse events judged treatment-related, amnesia lasting more than 24 hours was recorded in 19 of 90 patients after ECT and none of 91 after ketamine (the text gives 21 with prolonged amnesia, persisting through the 12-month follow-up in 3), and dissociative symptoms in 55 of 91 after ketamine against 14 of 90 after ECT; serious adverse events occurred in 23 of 90 against 14 of 91 (P = .09). (3) A systematic review and meta-analysis (Rhee et al., 2022; searched to April 2022, before ELEKT-D was published; no funding statement, and authors with many industry relationships, two of them also ELEKT-D authors) pooled six trials (five randomized) in 340 inpatient ECT candidates, KetECT supplying 186 of them and the other five 18 to 50 each (Germany, Iran and India; one also enrolled bipolar depression): improvement in depressive symptoms by the end of the course was larger with ECT, a standardized mean difference of −0.69 (95% CI −0.89 to −0.48; I² 39%), with KetECT carrying about half the weight (editors' calculation: 49%; without KetECT −0.79, −1.08 to −0.50). It did not pool remission or response; its only remission figures are KetECT's. ELEKT-D's authors cite it (their reference 29) and KetECT as having shown remission with ketamine inferior to ECT, and list as differences from those studies their trial's exclusion of psychotic depression, its larger sample and its mostly outpatient population, without saying these explain the results. The two large trials thus disagree: on the same clinician-rated cut-off (a MADRS score of 10 or less), remission was 16.2 percentage points more frequent with ketamine in ELEKT-D and 16.3 points more frequent with ECT in KetECT, with intervals that do not overlap, and every trial estimate in the meta-analysis, all of them in inpatients, pointed towards ECT, while the one mostly outpatient trial found ketamine no worse. Because both large trials were open label and differ in setting, psychotic depression, age, schedules, ECT technique and outcome definitions, neither can show what explains the difference. There was no placebo group in any trial, and relapse after treatment was followed only in responders (ELEKT-D) or remitters (KetECT) under continuation treatment that was not randomized, so it is not used here. Certainty: low. Status: contested.
plain: Two big trials that picked people at random for ketamine drips or electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) came out opposite ways, so nobody can yet say whether ketamine works as well as ECT. In a US trial of 403 adults whose depression had not got better with at least two antidepressants, who had no psychosis and most of whom lived at home, 55 in 100 people on ketamine and 41 in 100 on ECT said their depression had dropped by half or more after 3 weeks, so ketamine did at least as well, and more people on ketamine had few symptoms left. In a Swedish trial of 186 people in hospital who were already due to have ECT, some of them with psychosis and many over 50, 63 in 100 had few symptoms left after ECT, against 46 in 100 after ketamine, so ECT did better. A review that combined six hospital trials also found that ECT eased depression more, but about half of its data came from the Swedish trial, and it did not compare how many people got well. In both big trials everyone knew which treatment they had, and the trials treated different people in different ways, so nobody knows why they disagree. Memory problems were more common after ECT; in Sweden, more people stopped ketamine early, mostly because of side effects. No trial used a dummy treatment.
population: Adults with major depression referred to or already scheduled for ECT, in randomized comparisons of ketamine and ECT. ELEKT-D (Anand et al., 2023): 403 adults aged 21 to 75 (mean age 46; 206 women; 355 White; 359 outpatients and 44 inpatients) with DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features, an unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials and a MADRS score above 20 (baseline means about 32), referred to the ECT services of five US sites (an urban community hospital, a Veterans Administration hospital and three university hospital centres), March 2017 to September 2022; 157 had attempted suicide; 365 analysed (195 ketamine, 170 ECT); existing psychiatric medicines continued in both groups. KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022): 199 hospitalized adults aged 18 to 85 with DSM-IV unipolar depression and a MADRS score of 20 or more, already scheduled for ECT at six Swedish clinics, mostly in Lund (recruitment period not given; earlier treatment failure not named as a criterion in the article; full criteria in a supplement not read); 186 analysed (95 ketamine, 91 ECT; mean age 55 and 50; women 61 of 95 and 58 of 91; psychotic symptoms 18 of 95 and 14 of 91; earlier ECT 40 of 95 and 34 of 91; baseline MADRS 33.1 and 34.5); bipolar disorder, primary psychosis, substance use disorder and coercive care were among the reasons for not being eligible, while suicidal patients and patients with other psychiatric conditions were included; medicines unrestricted. Rhee et al. (2022): six trials (five randomized) published to April 2022, 340 inpatient ECT candidates (178 ketamine, 162 ECT), KetECT supplying 186 and the others 18 to 50 each, in Germany, Iran and India, one also enrolling bipolar depression.
exposure: A course of ketamine infusions into a vein given by clinicians at the trial sites (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight over 40 minutes; racemic ketamine in KetECT). ELEKT-D: twice a week for 3 weeks, with dose changes allowed if clinically indicated and made in almost no one; 180 of 195 completed all six sessions. KetECT: three times a week, up to 12 sessions until remission or the treating psychiatrist's judgement of maximal effect, ended after 6 sessions with less than a 25% fall in MADRS (median 6 sessions, IQR 5 to 9). Meta-analysis (trial conditions): intravenous ketamine in five trials, intramuscular or oral ketamine in one.
comparator: A course of ECT, with no placebo group in any trial. ELEKT-D: three times a week for 3 weeks, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse at six times the seizure threshold, with later changes of settings and electrode placement allowed (switched to bilateral in 39% of patients; 158 of 170 completed six to nine sessions). KetECT: three times a week under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants, stimulus set by age and sex, under the same session rules as ketamine (median 8 sessions, IQR 6 to 10; electrode placement in a supplement not read, listed as right unilateral in the meta-analysis's table). Meta-analysis: right unilateral ECT in two trials, bilateral in three, bifrontal or right unilateral in one.
outcome: Depression at the end of a course. ELEKT-D: self-rated response (a fall of at least 50% in the QIDS-SR-16 score from the first treatment visit) at the end-of-treatment visit, within 3 days after the last session (primary); clinician-rated response (MADRS); remission on both scales; changes in both scores; memory tests and self-rated memory; quality of life; moderate or severe adverse events. KetECT: remission (MADRS 10 or less, held over at least 2 sessions or 5 days) after the completed series, rated by unblinded treating staff (primary); MADRS change; sessions; adverse events judged treatment-related; relapse among remitters over 12 months. Meta-analysis: end-of-course improvement in depressive symptoms as a standardized mean difference (Hedges g); remission and response not pooled.
magnitude: Anand et al. (2023), ELEKT-D, modified intention-to-treat population: QIDS-SR-16 response 108/195 (55.4%) against 70/170 (41.2%), difference 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2), Farrington–Manning statistic 4.64, P<0.001 for noninferiority (margin −10); intention-to-treat with multiple imputation 55.4% against 41.6%, 13.8 (3.9 to 23.8). Never started the assigned treatment: 4/200 against 31/203. Ekstrand et al. evidence.extracted: Prospective, open-label, randomized noninferiority trial (ELEKT-D) at five US sites: an urban community hospital (Cleveland Clinic), a Veterans Administration hospital (Baylor College of Medicine) and three university hospital centres (Yale, Johns Hopkins, Mount Sinai); a 3-week initial treatment phase, after which responders were followed for 6 months (visits at months 1, 3 and 6) under treatment prescribed by their own clinicians. From March 2017 through September 2022, outpatients or inpatients referred to an ECT service at a site were invited; eligible if aged 21 to 75 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features, an unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials (verified from the referring provider, Antidepressant Treatment History Form guidelines and interview), a MADRS score above 20 and no contraindication to ketamine or ECT. Randomized 1:1 through a secure electronic data-management system, stratified by site; patients, attending physicians and research staff were aware of the assignments. The Introduction lists advances in ECT (administration under brief general anaesthesia, unilateral electrode placement, and refined seizure-elicitation techniques such as ultrabrief pulse stimulation) that have let it be given more often as an outpatient procedure.

evidence.extracted: The authors attribute the higher withdrawal before treatment in the ECT group to patient preferences and logistic issues, and report that imputation analyses in the intention-to-treat population supported noninferiority. They state that a recent European trial (KetECT) and a meta-analysis that included it found remission with ketamine inferior to ECT, and that their trial differs in including only depression without psychosis, a larger sample and a mostly outpatient population (89%). They state that ECT response and remission were lower than in other reports and closer to those of community and outpatient settings; that ECT has been shown to be more effective in older adults, in depression with psychosis and in inpatient and research settings; that comparisons are needed in older patients, bipolar depression and emergency inpatient settings; that starting ECT bilaterally or giving more sessions might have produced more responses, though with more adverse events, while most ECT patients had six to nine sessions; and that the open-label design could have influenced response, maintenance treatment was not studied, and there was no placebo.

evidence.extracted: KetECT: randomized, parallel, open-label trial at six clinics testing whether ketamine is non-inferior to ECT. With remission assumed at 60% after ECT, the non-inferiority margin for ketamine was set at a remission rate of 40%; 97 patients per group were planned (5% significance, 80% power), and the authors state that ketamine would have needed 54% remission to show with 95% confidence that its rate was not below 40%. Registered in EudraCT (2011-001520-37) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02659085). Hospitalized patients scheduled for ECT at the participating university hospitals were screened; eligible were hospitalized patients aged 18 to 85 with DSM-IV unipolar depression and a MADRS score of 20 or more, who were told of a study comparing ECT with a new experimental treatment; none were recruited through referrals or advertisements. Allocation 1:1 by sequentially numbered sealed envelopes opened after written consent, in blocks of 6 per site, from a scheme made by a statistician not otherwise involved; the full inclusion and exclusion criteria are in supplementary Table 1 (not read). The article gives no recruitment period and does not name earlier treatment failure as a criterion. Study conditions: racemic ketamine intravenously at a fixed 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes; ECT with oxygenation, anaesthesia and muscle relaxants by clinical routine, stimulus based on age and sex (parameters in supplementary Table 2, not read); both three times a week in the morning, concomitant medicines unrestricted; up to 12 sessions until remission or maximal effect as judged by the treating psychiatrist, with a checkpoint after 6 sessions at which patients whose MADRS score had fallen by less than 25% were classified as non-responders and given no further study sessions. Primary outcome: remission after completed treatment, a MADRS score of 10 or less held over at least 2 subsequent sessions or at least 5 days; neither raters nor patients were blinded. Main analyses in all patients given at least one session, with an intention-to-treat analysis of the primary outcome; proportions compared with chi-square tests and the interval of the difference by Newcombe's method.

risk_of_bias.note: Both large trials are rated high overall on RoB 2 on their first-pass cards (sc_anand_2023, sc_ekstrand_2022), from the measurement domain: both were open label; ELEKT-D's primary outcome was self-rated by patients who knew their treatment and its MADRS was scored by staff aware of the assignment; KetECT's remission was rated by the treating staff, who knew the assignment, recorded adverse events and decided how many sessions to give, at sites experienced with ECT and new to ketamine, and its authors rejected independent raters. Withdrawal was uneven in both trials, in opposite directions: 31 of 203 assigned to ECT never started it in ELEKT-D (an intention-to-treat analysis with imputation gave the same result), and 21 of 95 stopped ketamine before the 2-week evaluation in KetECT, mostly for adverse events, and stayed in the analysed groups. Allocation was concealed in both (an electronic system stratified by site; sequentially numbered sealed envelopes). The meta-analysis rated outcome measurement at low risk in every trial, open-label ones included (card sc_rhee_2022: AMSTAR 2 critically low). Expectation could favour either treatment, and its direction cannot be known.

inconsistency.note: The two large randomized comparisons point in opposite directions. On the same clinician-rated cut-off (MADRS 10 or less), remission was 16.2 percentage points more frequent with ketamine in ELEKT-D (7.0 to 25.4; secondary, not adjusted for multiplicity) and 16.3 points more frequent with ECT in KetECT (editors' arithmetic; 2.0 to 30), intervals that do not overlap, although KetECT also required the score to hold over 2 sessions or 5 days. All six trial estimates in the meta-analysis, every one in inpatients, point towards ECT on symptom scores (without KetECT, editors' calculation −0.79, −1.08 to −0.50), so the disagreement runs between settings: the inpatient trials favour ECT and the one mostly outpatient trial finds ketamine no worse. Setting is a plausible explanation that ELEKT-D's authors also raise (ECT more effective in inpatient and research settings, in psychotic depression and in older adults), and KetECT's post hoc age interaction fits it, but no trial has tested it, and the trials also differ in ketamine schedule, ECT technique and number of sessions, primary outcome, age and country. Down one level because a plausible but untested explanation exists; a stricter reading of opposite results with non-overlapping intervals would rate down two levels, to very low.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for adults with major depression referred or scheduled for ECT, as studied (ELEKT-D: mostly outpatients with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression, ECT started on the right side of the head; KetECT: inpatients, psychotic depression included; the meta-analysis: inpatient ECT candidates), and for the end of one course of each treatment as given in these trials. It does not cover people who are not ECT candidates, bipolar depression (one small trial in the meta-analysis), maintenance treatment or other ways of giving ECT. The meta-analysis's outcome (symptom improvement as a standardized difference) is not the remission or response the question is about, and it is reported as what it measured.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: each large trial's main interval lies well away from no difference (ELEKT-D's self-rated response difference 3.9 to 24.2 against a −10 margin; KetECT's remission difference 2.0 to 30), and the meta-analysis's pooled interval excludes zero; the uncertainty that matters, which result applies to whom, is rated under inconsistency and is not counted twice. KetECT's subgroups (14 to 59 patients) are imprecise and post hoc and are not used to grade.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down: ELEKT-D (NCT03113968) and KetECT (EudraCT 2011-001520-37, NCT02659085) were registered, though neither registry record was read; the meta-analysis found no funnel-plot asymmetry (Egger P = .32, Begg and Mazumdar P = .57), tests with little power for six trials, in which two trials of 22 and 25 patients gave the largest effects.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one level for risk of bias (open label in both large trials, with outcomes rated by patients or treating staff who knew the treatment, and uneven withdrawal in opposite directions) and one for inconsistency (ELEKT-D, in mostly outpatient adults with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression, found ketamine no worse on self-rated response and remission more frequent, while KetECT, in inpatients with psychotic depression included, found remission less frequent with ketamine, with non-overlapping remission intervals; setting is a plausible, untested explanation): low. Re-graded from the sources (version 0.2.1 rated the disagreement second-hand, from ELEKT-D's Discussion): the level is unchanged, but the question now covers both trials' patients, so the relation is 'insufficient evidence' rather than 'is associated with' and the status is contested, with the debate box (METHODS §6.3, §7); each trial's own result is stated for its own patients. The meta-analysis (Rhee et al., 2022; AMSTAR 2 critically low on its first-pass card) predates ELEKT-D, has KetECT as about half its weight and is not counted as independent replication of KetECT (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence); its five smaller inpatient trials add independent but small support for ECT on symptom scores. It did not pool remission, so ELEKT-D's authors' description of it as having shown remission inferior with ketamine does not match its analyses; its only remission figures are KetECT's. Memory and adverse events are reported as measured at the end of the course (ELEKT-D) or as adverse events judged treatment-related (KetECT). Relapse in both trials concerns only responders or remitters under continuation treatment that was not randomized and is not used. Funding: ELEKT-D by PCORI (disclosure forms not read); KetECT by the Swedish Research Council and Swedish foundations, three authors with lecture fees from Lundbeck; the meta-analysis states no funding, its authors list many industry relationships, and two of them are also ELEKT-D authors.

debate.question: Is a course of ketamine infusions as good as a course of ECT for adults with depression who have been referred for ECT?
debate.evidence_yes: The largest randomized comparison, ELEKT-D (Anand et al., 2023; sc_anand_2023; 403 randomized at five US hospitals, 365 analysed; funded by PCORI), enrolled adults aged 21 to 75 with treatment-resistant major depression without psychosis, 359 of the 403 outpatients. At the end of a 3-week course, self-rated response (a halving of the QIDS-SR-16 score) was 108 of 195 with ketamine twice a week against 70 of 170 with ECT three times a week, a difference of 14.2 percentage points (3.9 to 24.2), clearly within the prespecified noninferiority margin of −10, and the intention-to-treat analysis of all 403 with imputation agreed (13.8, 3.9 to 23.8). Remission was more frequent with ketamine on both scales, including the clinician-rated MADRS (74 of 195 against 37 of 170; 16.2 points, 7.0 to 25.4; a secondary outcome, not adjusted for multiplicity). Memory test scores fell more after ECT by the end of the course, and self-rated memory stayed lower after ECT through 6 months in responders followed up. Its authors note that ECT in the United States is increasingly given to outpatients with treatment-resistant depression, the group their pragmatic trial enrolled. In KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022), patients aged 18 to 50 remitted about as often with ketamine as with ECT (22 of 36 against 26 of 52; P = .39; post hoc); its authors suggest ketamine as an option for younger patients and when ECT is unavailable, contraindicated or declined; and amnesia lasting more than 24 hours was recorded in 19 of 90 patients after ECT against none of 91 after ketamine.
debate.evidence_no: KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022; sc_ekstrand_2022; funded by the Swedish Research Council and Swedish foundations), the other large randomized comparison, treated 186 hospitalized adults aged 18 to 85 with unipolar depression who were already scheduled for ECT at six Swedish clinics, psychotic depression included. With up to 12 sessions of either treatment three times a week, remission (MADRS 10 or less, held over 2 sessions or 5 days) was 57 of 91 after ECT against 44 of 95 after ketamine, 16.3 percentage points more with ECT (editors' arithmetic; 95% CI 2.0 to 30), so the trial's non-inferiority margin was not met; depression scores fell by 22.4 against 16.1 points (difference 2.9 to 9.7), and remission came no sooner with ketamine (11% and 10% after 3 sessions, 39% and 25% after 6). Five smaller inpatient trials (18 to 50 patients each, in Germany, Iran and India) also pointed towards ECT on symptom scores, and the meta-analysis of all six (Rhee et al., 2022; sc_rhee_2022) gave a standardized difference of −0.69 (−0.89 to −0.48) in favour of ECT, and −0.79 (−1.08 to −0.50) without KetECT (editors' calculation). ELEKT-D's own authors write that its ECT response and remission were lower than in other reports, that ECT has been shown to be more effective in older adults, in psychotic depression and in inpatient and research settings, and that starting ECT on both sides of the head or giving more sessions might have produced more responses; 31 of 203 people assigned to ECT in that trial never started it.
debate.neither_can_show: Both large trials were open label, and depression was rated by patients (ELEKT-D's primary outcome; Anand et al., 2023) or by treating staff (KetECT; Ekstrand et al., 2022) who knew the treatment; no trial had a placebo or sham group. The two trials differ at once in setting (359 of 403 outpatients against all inpatients), psychotic depression (excluded against included), age (mean 46 against 50 and 55), country, ketamine schedule (twice a week for 3 weeks against three times a week for up to 12 sessions), ECT technique and number of sessions, and primary outcome (self-rated response at the end of treatment against clinician-rated remission held over at least 2 sessions or 5 days), so neither design can show which of these explains the opposite results. KetECT's age and psychotic-depression comparisons are post hoc subgroups of 14 to 59 patients; the meta-analysis (Rhee et al., 2022) tested moderators only across six trials, did not pool remission and predates ELEKT-D. Relapse after treatment was followed only in responders (ELEKT-D) or remitters (KetECT), under continuation treatment that was not randomized.
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading, at low certainty: a course of ketamine and a course of ECT have each come out ahead in one large open-label trial, and the split follows the setting. In inpatients already scheduled for ECT, including people with psychotic depression and many over 50, the evidence (KetECT, Ekstrand et al., 2022, and five smaller trials) favours ECT; in mostly outpatient adults with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression, the one large trial (Anand et al., 2023) found ketamine no worse, with more remissions. Whether setting, psychotic features, age, the schedules or the unblinded ratings explain the split is not known. The meta-analysis (Rhee et al., 2022) is about half KetECT and is not a second, independent confirmation; it pooled symptom scores, not remission, although ELEKT-D's authors describe it as having shown remission inferior with ketamine.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of ketamine and ECT with depression rated by assessors who do not know the treatment, prespecified definitions of remission and response, the same session frequency in both arms, inpatients and outpatients both included, randomization stratified by setting, age and psychotic features, and randomized continuation treatment with relapse followed in everyone; or an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of ELEKT-D (Anand et al., 2023), KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022) and the smaller trials in Rhee et al. (2022) that tests setting, age and psychotic features at the patient level.
