statement: In patients given ketamine by clinicians to treat depression in studies, the side effects reported most were short-lived effects during or soon after a dose, while harms of repeated or long-term treatment were seldom looked for. A systematic review of 60 studies published from 1999 to 2016 (Short et al., 2018; 20 randomized trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case reports or series and 3 retrospective studies; about 899 patients, about 737 of them given ketamine into a vein and about 356 given more than one dose, so most had a single dose (editors' arithmetic); most study reports had no placebo or control group) counted studies, not people, and gives no rates: dissociative or psychotomimetic effects (such as feeling detached or unreal, or changed perception) were described in 43 of the 60 studies, other psychiatric effects (most often anxiety) in 23, cardiovascular changes (most often raised blood pressure and heart rate) in 23, and other side effects (most often blurred vision and nausea) in 32; the side effects named in the most studies were headache (21 studies), dizziness (20), dissociation (18; the figure's other panel plots 17), raised blood pressure (17) and blurred vision (14) (editors' reading of a figure). Blood pressure and heart rate changes came mostly during or just after an infusion and generally settled within 90 minutes; no dissociative effects were reported to last, but most studies looked for them only within about 4 hours; and the review's authors conclude that most reported side effects followed infusion into a vein and resolved shortly after the dose. Across the studies, 12 people withdrew because of worsening mood, 6 because of anxiety, 5 because of suicidal thoughts, 2 because of dissociation and 5 because of cardiovascular effects; one study reported a suicide attempt, and whether delayed symptoms (anxiety, worsening depression or suicidal thoughts, hypomania) were linked to ketamine was unclear. Side effects were looked for within 4 hours of a dose in 55 of the 60 studies, after repeated doses in 24 and 2 weeks or more after the last dose in 12; urinary symptoms were assessed in 5 studies, liver tests were reported in 7 (abnormal after dosing in 2) and questions about dependence were asked in 2; most studies relied on side effects that patients mentioned and reported them only when they occurred. In the largest randomized trial read here (Anand et al., 2023; five US hospitals, 2017 to 2022; adults with treatment-resistant depression without psychosis), 49 of 195 patients given six ketamine infusions over 3 weeks (25 in 100) had at least one moderate or severe adverse event, against 55 of 170 given ECT (32 in 100); with ketamine these were headache in 16, stomach or gut problems in 13, severe or prolonged high blood pressure in 6, new suicidal thoughts in 4 and muscle pain or weakness in 1 (against 9 of 170 with ECT, the only difference the authors report as significant); there were no suicide attempts in the 3 weeks and no deaths in the trial, and dissociation scores were higher with ketamine than with ECT on every treatment day (values in a supplement not read). In the 6 months after treatment, of the 108 people who had responded to ketamine and were then treated as their own clinicians chose, 17 had a moderate or severe adverse event, 4 suicidal thoughts, 2 severe or prolonged high blood pressure and 1 a suicide attempt (against 10, 1, 0 and 0 of 70 ECT responders). In an early randomized crossover pilot against salt water (Berman et al., 2000; 7 people who completed both infusion days; also one of the review's 60 studies), every patient rated feeling 'high' at 50 mm or more on a visual analogue scale during the ketamine day and none rose on the salt-water day; on average the feeling was gone by 110 minutes after the infusion, and the authors say patients could readily tell the two infusions apart. The trial's article lists moderate and severe events only, so how often milder side effects occurred is not known from it; the review's statement that every kind of side effect was reported more often with ketamine than with placebo has no counts behind it; and its discussion of bladder, liver, memory and dependence harms in people treated for pain or using ketamine outside medicine draws on studies outside its search and is not used here. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When ketamine was given to treat depression in studies, the side effects reported most were headache, dizziness, feeling detached or unreal, higher blood pressure and blurred vision, and most passed soon after the dose. Blood pressure rises came during or just after the drip and mostly settled within 90 minutes. In an early small trial, every patient felt 'high' during the ketamine drip and none with salt water; on average the feeling was gone within 2 hours. In one large trial, 25 in 100 people on ketamine drips had at least one moderate or severe side effect over 3 weeks, against 32 in 100 on ECT; 4 of 195 on ketamine had new suicidal thoughts, against 2 of 170 on ECT. A review of 60 studies could not say how often each side effect happens, because it counted studies, not people, and most studies only noted what patients mentioned; most people in them had one dose. Effects of repeated treatment were seldom checked: only 12 of the 60 studies looked 2 weeks or more after the last dose, 5 checked for bladder problems and 2 asked about dependence.
population: Patients given ketamine by clinicians for depression in studies: about 899 patients with unipolar or bipolar depression in 60 studies published from 1999 to 2016 (systematic review); 195 adults with treatment-resistant depression without psychosis given six infusions over 3 weeks in one US randomized trial (2017 to 2022); and 9 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode in a crossover pilot (7 completed both days; one of the review's studies)
exposure: Ketamine given by clinicians in studies, by any route (about 737 of about 902 patient-route entries into a vein), once or repeatedly (about 356 patients given more than one dose); trial conditions in the randomized trial: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight over 40 minutes into a vein, twice a week for 3 weeks; in the pilot, one infusion under the same conditions
comparator: None in most of the review's studies (most study reports had no placebo or control group); ECT three times a week for 3 weeks in the randomized trial; an infusion of salt water (saline) on another day in the pilot
outcome: Which side effects were reported, in how many studies, when they occurred and how long they lasted; how often side effects were looked for after repeated doses and in the long term; moderate or severe adverse events per patient in the trial; self-rated 'high' in the pilot
magnitude: Short et al. (2018), counts of 60 studies (no rates): psychotomimetic or dissociative effects 43 (72%), psychiatric 23 (38%), cardiovascular 23 (38%), other 32 (53%); assessed acutely 55 (92%), cumulatively 24 (40%), long term 12 (20%); urinary symptoms assessed 5, liver tests reported 7 (abnormal 2), dependence asked 2; structured scales for other side effects 15 (25%); systematic reporting 25 (42%) psychiatric or psychotomimetic, 19 (32%) cardiovascular, 14 (23%) neurological or cognitive, 14 (23%) other; withdrawals: worsening mood 12, anxiety 6, suicidal ideation 5, panic attack 2, irritability 1, dissociation 2, cardiovascular 5; one suicide attempt in one study; Figure 5 (editors' reading): headache 21 studies (11 randomized), dizziness 20 (11), dissociation 18 (8) (Figure 5A plots 28%, 17 of 60), raised blood pressure 17 (9), blurred vision 14 (9). Anand et al. (2023), moderate or severe adverse events in the 3 weeks, ketamine against ECT: any 49/195 (25.1%) against 55/170 (32.4%); headache 16/195 (8.2%) against 12/170 (7.1%); gastrointestinal 13/195 (6.7%) against 9/170 (5.3%); severe or prolonged hypertension 6/195 (3.1%) against 4/170 (2.4%); suicidal ideation 4/195 (2.1%) against 2/170 (1.2%); muscle pain or weakness 1/195 (0.5%) against 9/170 (5.3%), P = 0.01; P>0.05 for all others; suicide attempts 0 and 0; no deaths; follow-up of responders: any 17/108 (15.7%) against 10/70 (14.3%), suicidal ideation 4/108 against 1/70, suicide attempt 1/108 against 0/70, severe or prolonged hypertension 2/108 (1.9%) against 0/70. Berman et al. (2000), 7 completers: VAS-high condition × time F = 16.9, p = .0001; every patient's maximum at least 50 mm on the ketamine day, no rise on the saline day; back to baseline by 110 minutes after the infusion; BPRS positive symptoms condition × time p = .068 (not significant).

evidence.extracted: Systematic review of the reporting of side-effects in studies of adults with a validated diagnosis of unipolar or bipolar depression given at least one dose of ketamine by any route, with change in depression as a primary outcome; MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Database searched for articles published from 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, without language restriction; many types of study design were included because randomized trials are unlikely to detect rare serious adverse events or long-term adverse effects. 568 records from databases and 23 from other sources, 591 screened; 60 studies included (20 randomized controlled trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case series or reports, 3 retrospective studies). A side-effect counted as having occurred if a report listed it in at least one patient; the review recorded whether side-effects were sought actively or monitored passively (spontaneous reports), reported systematically (presence and absence) or ad hoc (only if they occurred), and over which time frame: immediately after a single dose (acute), after repeated doses (cumulative) or at least 2 weeks after the last dose (long term). The summary's 288 articles identified are not printed in the flow diagram (288 equals the 591 screened minus the 303 that met exclusion criteria; editors' calculation).

evidence.extracted: A planned meta-analysis was judged inappropriate after data extraction because of clinical diversity, different routes, doses and comparators, differing reporting methods and reporting bias. The authors' ten main findings include that acute side-effects are common after ketamine; that active assessment and reporting of side-effects in depression trials are inadequate; that most reported side-effects followed intravenous dosing and resolved shortly after the dose; that the most common were headache, dizziness, dissociation, elevated blood pressure and blurred vision; and that conclusions could be drawn only for single dosing and acute side-effects. The Conclusion states that the safety of long-term repeated dosing is uncertain, and that urological, hepatic, craving or dependence and cognitive harms reported with high doses and repeated use in people treated for chronic pain and in people who use ketamine recreationally have not been adequately assessed in depression studies.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement: in most of the review's studies side effects were found by passive monitoring and reported only when they occurred (systematic reporting in 14 to 25 of 60 studies, by category), so the study counts reflect what was looked for; the review counts studies, not people, its summary's 288 articles do not match its flow diagram, and its confidence is critically low by AMSTAR 2 (card sc_short_2018: no protocol, no list of excluded studies). The trial's article lists moderate and severe events only, in an open-label design (card sc_anand_2023, RoB 2 high). The pilot had 7 completers and an inert placebo that patients could tell apart (card sc_berman_2000, RoB 2 high).

inconsistency.note: The same short-lived effects (dissociation, raised blood pressure, headache, dizziness) appear across designs and teams in the review, and the trial's moderate and severe events are of the same kinds.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for patients given ketamine for depression in studies, most of them once and into a vein, and it says that repeated and long-term treatment was seldom examined; the review's statements about harms in people treated for pain or using ketamine outside medicine are not used.

imprecision.note: The review gives no rates and none are claimed from it; the trial's shares rest on 195 and 170 patients and are given as counts; single events (1 to 6 patients) are given as counts, and rare harms are not claimed to be absent.

publication_bias.note: Selective reporting of harms within studies is the review's own finding and is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the patients studied (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one level for risk of bias (measurement: passive monitoring and ad hoc reporting in most studies, study counts rather than people, moderate and severe events only in the trial's article): very low, the floor; never upgraded. The review is used for which side effects were reported and how often harms were looked for; its sentence that side effects were more common with ketamine than with placebo has no counts behind it and is not used, and its discussion of bladder, liver, memory and dependence harms in other populations comes from outside its systematic search and is not used. The trial's comparison with ECT is randomized, but here it only describes how often moderate or severe events occurred in each group; muscle pain or weakness is the only difference the authors report as significant, and the dissociation values are in a supplement not read. Status replicated: the kinds of short-lived side effects are reported across many independent studies in the review and again in the later trial; it concerns which side effects occur, not how often. Overlap: the pilot (Berman et al., 2000) is one of the review's 60 studies and is not counted separately. No route comparison is used (the review's intravenous against other-route figures are probably misprinted, card sc_short_2018).

statement: In adults with major depression, most of them with depression that had not responded to earlier antidepressants and, in the three trials read, taken off their psychiatric medicines, one 40-minute infusion of racemic ketamine into a vein, given by clinicians in randomized trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight), compared with an infusion of salt water (saline) or of midazolam, a sedative chosen as an active placebo so that people could less easily tell which infusion they had, is associated with lower clinician-rated depression scores within hours, largest at about one day, with most responses fading within weeks. In the first small trial (Berman et al., 2000; Connecticut, USA; 9 people, 7 of whom had both infusion days of a crossover), depression scores (25-item Hamilton scale) fell by 14 points (SD 10) within 72 hours after ketamine and by 0 (SD 12) after saline; 4 of 8 people had their score fall by half or more within 3 days after ketamine, against 1 of 8 after saline, a difference that was not statistically significant; by the authors' account mood was back near its starting level 1 to 2 weeks after the infusion, an observation outside the trial's rating schedule, and patients could readily tell the two infusions apart, which, the authors write, may have biased their reporting. In a crossover trial at the US National Institute of Mental Health (Zarate et al., 2006; November 2004 to September 2005; 18 inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, 5.7 lifetime trials on average; 17 given ketamine and 14 saline, 13 both; funded by the Institute's intramural programme, with no conflict statement printed), Hamilton scores were lower after ketamine than after saline from 110 minutes to day 7 in the analysis of the 13 who had both infusions (standardized difference 1.46, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.01, at 24 hours and 0.68, 0.13 to 1.23, at 1 week) and from 80 minutes to day 7 in an analysis of the first infusion only (18 people compared between groups). Counting everyone with data, 12 of 17 (71 in 100) had their score fall by half or more the day after ketamine, against 0 of 14 after saline; 5 of 17 reached remission (a score of 7 or less) against none; and 6 of 17 (35 in 100) kept the response for at least a week, 2 of them for at least 2 weeks; about half of those given ketamine had responded by 110 minutes (editors' reading of a figure). After correction for repeated testing only the day-1 difference in responders stayed significant, and remission did not differ significantly at any time; the trial stopped at 18 of a planned 22 after an interim analysis, and people given ketamine first began their saline week less depressed (Hamilton 17.2 against 24.9), a carry-over; its authors write that ketamine's short-lived perceptual effects could have affected the blind and biased patients' reporting. In a two-site trial with parallel groups (Murrough et al., 2013; Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, New York, November 2010 to August 2012; 73 medication-free adults who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, randomized 2 to 1, 72 analysed: 47 given ketamine and 25 midazolam; raters kept away from the infusion day), depression scores 24 hours after the infusion, the primary outcome, were 7.95 points lower after ketamine on the 0-to-60 MADRS (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71; means 14.77 against 22.72), and 30 of 47 (64 in 100) against 7 of 25 (28 in 100) had their score fall by half or more, a difference of 36 percentage points (95% CI 12 to 54, editors' calculation; the printed odds ratio of 2.18 is smaller than these counts give, 4.5). Over days 1 to 7 ketamine scores stayed lower on average (16.93 against 23.19), but at day 7 depression scores and response rates no longer differed significantly in the authors' analysis adjusted for site and baseline. At day 7, 21 people given ketamine and 4 given midazolam still met the response criterion and chose to continue in the study: 21 of 47 (45 in 100) against 4 of 25 (16 in 100), counting everyone analysed and treating anyone not rated that day as not responding (editors' arithmetic, used here because the article prints these group sizes and no day-7 denominators); the article's bars (about 46% and 18%) fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22, the people rated that day. Among those 21 ketamine responders, followed for up to 4 more weeks, the share still without relapse fell to about 4 in 10 by about the 17th day of follow-up (editors' reading of a figure; no numbers are printed). Dissociation (feeling outside one's body, time running slower or faster) was significant in 8 of 47 after ketamine and resolved within 2 hours, and blurred vision on the infusion day was reported by 20 of 47 against 2 of 25; the authors say no control for ketamine is perfect and that dissociation was more frequent with ketamine, and none of the three trials reports asking patients or raters which infusion they thought they had. The 2013 trial was funded by the US National Institutes of Health, the Department of Veterans Affairs, a NARSAD award and the Brown Foundation; one author and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai were named on a use-patent application of ketamine for depression, another author was named as an inventor on a pending use patent and had given up any royalties, and several authors reported research support or fees from drug companies. A meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials (3299 participants) of racemic ketamine or esketamine against control conditions, searched to April 2023 (Nikolin et al., 2023; no funding; one author, the first author of the 2006 trial, is co-inventor on patents for ketamine in depression, with rights assigned to the US government and a share of royalties), gives no estimate for the intravenous route alone: its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose judged equivalent by another route) includes 25 trials with a racemic arm into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more, among them the three above (editors' count from its table: 14 with saline, 10 with midazolam and 1 with remifentanil as control; each with fewer than 100 participants, median 30), and some arms given by other routes. For this category, from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose, the standardized difference in depression scores against control was −0.73 (95% CI −0.91 to −0.56), which the authors call large, the odds ratio for response 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22) and for remission 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), with substantial heterogeneity in the model for scores (I² 60.5% across all categories); its pooled estimates for this category plotted by time are about −0.6 at 4 hours, −0.9 at day 1 and −0.6 at day 3 (editors' reading of a figure), and the authors read their model's curved time term as a fall in depression scores that peaks about one day after the dose and then returns towards baseline. The review pooled no data from single doses beyond 3 days, its later windows concerning repeated courses. Its funnel-plot analysis suggested missing null results at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, which would make the early effect look larger, an asymmetry the authors say may instead reflect a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to larger trials with better-blinded controls; they also name compromised blinding in crossover trials as a limitation. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In trials, doctors gave people with depression that had not got better with other medicines one ketamine drip into a vein, or a dummy: salt water, or midazolam, a sedative picked so people could less easily tell which drip they had. In the first small trial (2000), in 7 people who had both drips, depression scores fell over the next 3 days after ketamine but not after salt water, and mood was back near where it started 1 to 2 weeks later; patients could easily tell the two drips apart. In a 2006 trial of 18 hospital patients, scores were lower than after salt water from about 2 hours to a week after the drip; the next day, 12 of 17 were much better (their score had halved), against none of 14 after salt water, and 6 of 17 were still much better a week later. In a 2013 trial of 72 people, 64 in 100 were much better a day after ketamine, against 28 in 100 after the sedative; after a week, 45 in 100 against 16 in 100 still were, a gap the authors' test no longer found clear, and of those still much better, about 6 in 10 relapsed within the next 3 weeks. A 2023 review of 49 trials found the gap biggest about a day after a dose and smaller by day 3; it gave no figure for drips alone, and it found signs that trials that found nothing may be missing. People can often tell ketamine from a dummy, which may make the lift look bigger. Authors of the 2013 trial and of the review were named on patents or patent applications for ketamine in depression.
population: Adults with major depression in randomized trials, mostly treatment-resistant: 9 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode (8 unipolar, 1 bipolar) in Connecticut, USA, 7 of whom had both infusion days (Berman et al., 2000); 18 medication-free inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, at the US National Institute of Mental Health, 2004 to 2005 (Zarate et al., 2006); 73 medication-free adults aged 21 to 80 who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, at Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, 2010 to 2012, 72 analysed (Murrough et al., 2013); and the participants of 49 randomized trials of racemic ketamine or esketamine to April 2023 (3299 participants; 33 trials in treatment-resistant samples; including trials in bipolar depression, adolescents and suicidal ideation), 25 of which had an arm of racemic ketamine into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more (Nikolin et al., 2023)
exposure: One 40-minute intravenous infusion of racemic ketamine given by clinicians in trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight; given by an anaesthesiologist in the 2006 trial); in the review, its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose it judged equivalent by another route), from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose
comparator: An infusion of salt water (saline) on another day, in random order (crossover: Berman et al., 2000; Zarate et al., 2006); an infusion of midazolam, a short-acting sedative chosen as an active placebo to mimic ketamine's sedation and disorientation so that people could less easily tell which they had (parallel groups, randomized 2 to 1: Murrough et al., 2013; trial conditions 0.045 mg per kg over 40 minutes); in the review, the trials' control arms (in the 25 trials with an intravenous high-dose racemic arm, saline in 14, midazolam in 10 and remifentanil in 1; editors' count)

Eligible: aged 21 to 80, primary major depressive disorder, inadequate response to at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials; excluded: lifetime psychotic illness or bipolar disorder, alcohol or substance abuse in the previous 2 years, serious and imminent suicide risk. Patients were free of antidepressants and other psychotropic medicines for the study (a stable non-benzodiazepine hypnotic allowed), drug-free for at least 1 week before (4 weeks for fluoxetine); infusion after an overnight fast in a clinical research unit with monitoring; discharged at 24 hours; outpatient ratings at 48 hours, 72 hours and 7 days; non-responders (less than 50% MADRS improvement) were not followed after day 7, and responders were followed biweekly until relapse or for 4 more weeks. Primary outcome: the clinician-administered MADRS 24 hours after the infusion, rated by trained raters not involved in infusion-day procedures and unaware of group and of infusion-related side effects; the 24-hour point was chosen to avoid overlap with the transient psychoactive effects. Secondary: response (a fall of 50% or more), QIDS-SR16, CGI and durability up to 7 days.

evidence.extracted: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of ketamine for depression (any language, searched to 13 April 2023; PROSPERO CRD42021221157): 49 trials, 3299 participants, 52 control and 72 ketamine arms; 13 crossover trials, for which data from before the crossover were prioritised; 27 single-dose and 22 repeated-dose trials; 39 racemic ketamine and 10 esketamine; 33 in treatment-resistant samples; ketamine arms intravenous 48, intranasal 17, subcutaneous 4, oral 2, intramuscular 1. Doses were converted to an intravenous racemic equivalent and classed 'High' at 0.5 mg/kg or more (or titration up to it), intranasal when dosing was predominantly at 84 mg or more (details in an appendix not read). Outcomes: change in depression severity against control as a standardized mean difference (negative favours ketamine), response (a fall of 50% or more) and remission as odds ratios, in three windows: from 4 hours after the first dose to 3 days or the second treatment, whichever came first; during repeated treatment; and up to 28 days after the last treatment of a course. One multivariable mixed-effects model per outcome and window, with linear and quadratic time, formulation, dose and their interaction as fixed effects and study as a random effect (in the after-course window dose was left out, as only one arm there used a low dose). Editors' count from Table 1: 25 of the 39 racemic trials had an arm given a single listed intravenous dose of racemic ketamine of 0.5 mg/kg or more and analysed on its own (19 single-dose and 6 repeated; controls saline in 14, midazolam in 10 and remifentanil in 1), among them Berman et al. (2000), Zarate et al. (2006) and Murrough et al. (2013); each lists fewer than 100 participants in Table 1's sample columns (median 30, largest 99 in Fava et al., 2018; the 20 given lanicemine in Downey et al., 2016, left out). Three more gave such doses in other forms: Sos et al. (2013) 0.27 mg/kg loading plus 0.27 mg/kg maintenance; Cao et al. (2018) 0.2 and 0.5 mg/kg arms with results presented combined; Loo et al. (2016) 0.5 mg/kg by intravenous, intramuscular and subcutaneous routes in a crossover, first dose analysed. The other 11 gave lower intravenous doses only (4) or other routes (intranasal 3, subcutaneous 2, oral 2).

evidence.extracted: Most trials had low or unclear risk of bias on the Cochrane tool (details in the appendix, not read); contour-enhanced funnel plots showed possible publication bias, and trim-and-fill suggested missing null findings at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, that is, possible bias towards larger early effects favouring ketamine. Single-dose trials enter only the first window, up to day 3 (editors' reading of the Methods); after the last dose of a course, data came from only 7 studies and 8 arms. Effect modifiers, including route of administration and control type, are reported only in the appendix (pp 49–58, not read), so the article gives no estimate for the intravenous route alone. Limitations stated by the authors: possible publication or small-study bias, which may instead reflect a shift from small early pilot trials with saline controls and samples without treatment resistance to large trials with better-blinded controls (midazolam, or saline with a bittering agent) in treatment-resistant samples, with more modest effects; dose categories rest on estimated bioavailability; crossover trials risk compromised blinding from ketamine's unique subjective effects, and carry-over; trial features were often confounded (formulation with route). Funding: none. Interests: one author (C. Zarate, first author of the 2006 trial) is listed as co-inventor on a patent for the use of ketamine in major depression and suicidal ideation, on a patent for ketamine metabolites such as (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine in depression and neuropathic pain, and on a patent application for hydroxynorketamine in depression and other conditions; he has assigned his patent rights to the US government but will share a percentage of any royalties it may receive; another (C. Loo) has served on an advisory board for Janssen Cilag; another (G. Vazquez) has been a speaker or advisory board member for companies including Janssen; the review used data obtained from the Yale University Open Data Access Project, which has an agreement with Janssen Research & Development (the article does not say which trials these data came from).

risk_of_bias.note: Cards: RoB 2 overall high for Berman et al. (2000) and Zarate et al. (2006), some concerns for Murrough et al. (2013). The ratings are clinician interviews and questionnaires that rest on what patients report, and ketamine's effects are easy to notice: Berman et al. state that patients readily told ketamine from saline; Zarate et al. say its perceptual effects could have affected the blind; midazolam matched sedation but not dissociation (significant in 8 of 47; blurred vision 20 of 47 against 2 of 25); none of the three trials reports asking patients or raters what they guessed. The two crossover trials add carry-over (the saline phase began lower after ketamine: Hamilton 17.2 against 24.9 in Zarate et al., 10.3 points lower in Berman et al.), Zarate et al. stopped early after an interim analysis, and Berman et al. analysed completers only. The review rated most trials at low or unclear risk with the Cochrane tool, which does not capture unblinding through the drug's own effects; its authors name compromised blinding in crossover trials as a limitation. One level, not two: the trial with an active placebo and raters kept away from the infusion day also found a large 24-hour difference.

inconsistency.note: Every pooled early estimate favours ketamine (all four formulation-dose categories), and the three trials agree in direction for the first day; heterogeneity in the early-window model is substantial for scores (I² 60.5%) but low to moderate for response (44.0%) and low for remission (9.9%). The two trials that rated day 7 differ (a significant difference against saline in 13 completers, none against midazolam in 72), which the statement reports; this fits an effect that shrinks over days rather than a contradiction, and it is not rated down.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (adults with mostly treatment-resistant major depression, taken off other psychiatric medicines in the three trials read) and for one infusion under trial conditions. The review's high-dose racemic figure is not for the intravenous route alone (25 of its trials had such an arm; other routes join by dose equivalence; route is analysed only in the appendix, not read), and the review also includes trials in bipolar depression, adolescents and suicidal ideation (card sc_nikolin_2023); the statement says so, so it is not rated down.

imprecision.note: Not rated down for the first-day difference: the pooled interval (−0.91 to −0.56) and the 2013 trial's intervals (3.20 to 12.71 points; response difference 12 to 54 percentage points, editors' calculation) exclude no effect. The duration figures rest on small groups (13 completers in 2006; 21 day-7 responders in 2013) and are given as counts and as the authors' non-significant day-7 test, not as precise estimates.

publication_bias.note: The review's contour-enhanced funnel plots and trim-and-fill suggested missing null results at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, the window of this claim, so the pooled early effect may be too large. The authors offer an alternative (a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to larger, better-blinded trials in treatment-resistant samples). Counted separately from risk of bias because it concerns results that may be missing from the pooled set rather than how the included trials rated their outcomes; if the asymmetry came only from unblinded small trials, the two levels would overlap (flagged for the senior author's review).

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high: three randomized trials read in full and a meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials that includes all three. Down one level for risk of bias (outcomes that rest on what patients report, with a drug whose effects patients notice, no check of what anyone guessed, and carry-over and early stopping in the crossover trials) and one for publication bias (the review's own analysis suggests missing null results in exactly the 4-hour to 3-day window): low. Rated as worded: lower depression scores within hours, largest at about a day, after one 40-minute infusion under trial conditions against saline or midazolam, with the fading given as each trial reports it; the claim does not say how large the effect is apart from expectation, how long it lasts beyond these trials' follow-up, or that ketamine works better than other treatments. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1), although the comparisons are randomized. Status replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.4): the three trials read share an author (Dennis S. Charney is an author of all three), and the review, which pools 25 trials with an intravenous arm of this kind from many groups, prints only pooled estimates, not each trial's direction (its forest plots are in an appendix not read), so independent replication is not counted from it; the review contains the three trials and its authors include the first author of the 2006 trial, so it is one body of evidence with them, not a separate confirmation. Day 7 in the 2013 trial: the counts 21 and 4 are printed without day-7 denominators; 21 of 47 against 4 of 25 (the groups as analysed, anyone not rated that day counted as not responding) is used in the plain lines because it rests only on printed numbers, while the bars fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22 (the people rated that day), and both are given. Editors' calculations, for the second reader: the 2013 risk difference (Newcombe) and crude odds ratio, the day-7 shares, the 2000 trial's two-sided Fisher p, the count of intravenous trials in the review's table, and the readings of Figure 3A (2006), Figures 2 and 3 (2013) and Fig. 2 (review). Not used: the review's estimates for repeated courses and after a course (which include racemic ketamine given under the skin, by nose and by mouth), its dose and formulation comparisons, its esketamine estimates and its conclusion that higher doses work better, which its own estimates do not bear out (card sc_nikolin_2023); side effects are covered by another answer on the page. Funding as printed: the 2000 trial by foundation, Veterans Affairs and state grants; the 2006 trial by the NIMH intramural programme; the 2013 trial by the NIH, Veterans Affairs and foundations, with patent filings for ketamine in depression and industry ties among its authors; the review unfunded, with one author a co-inventor on ketamine patents and two with Janssen ties. The review's study card is still in data/study-cards/_incoming/ketamine/, so the claim cannot be merged until the card is.

statement: In about 15,000 written reports of drug experiences on the Erowid website, covering 165 substances (reports of combinations left out; all reports for each substance merged into one document; drug names, slang and words for routes deleted), compared with 625 written accounts of near-death experiences that people gave voluntarily to research groups in the USA and Belgium (also merged into one document), reports about ketamine, compared with the reports about each of the other 164 substances, are associated with the pattern of word use most similar to the near-death accounts, as scored by a text-mining method (latent semantic analysis) that gives one similarity number per substance, with no measure of uncertainty and no check against questionnaires about experiences (Martial et al., 2019). Nobody was given a drug or interviewed for this study. With the main settings (20 dimensions), ketamine scored about 0.90 on a 0-to-1 scale, against about 0.84 for Salvia divinorum and about 0.83 for peyote and for LSD (values the editors read from a figure); averaged over all the settings tried (5 to 145 dimensions), ketamine led narrowly, about 0.64 against about 0.61 for LSD and about 0.60 for psilocybin mushrooms, and it came first with about 4 in 5 of the settings (read from a pie chart), LSD with most of the rest. Rankings made with very different settings agreed poorly below the top: peyote, third with the main settings, was about 18th on the average. When the near-death accounts were split by cause, closeness to death or how pleasant they were, ketamine stayed first in almost every subset; after cardiac arrest, LSD ranked comparably. As classes, dissociative drugs ranked first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics, with sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics or antidepressants lowest. Similar word patterns are not shown to be similar experiences: the score counts how words occur together (a word such as fear counts whether it was felt or denied, as the authors note); the near-death accounts were written on average about two decades after the event, and 30% were attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (cause missing for 228 of 625; the base of the percentage is not stated); the Erowid writers, their doses and settings are unknown and the substances were not tested; and the authors state that their analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical explanations of near-death experiences, such as the idea that the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death, although their abstract says the results support that speculation and suggests ketamine could be a safe and reversible experimental model of near-death experiences, which was not studied. Funded by public research bodies and private foundations; two of the 12 authors are at the Erowid Center, which curates the reports; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Researchers compared the words in about 15,000 reports people had posted online about 165 different drugs with 625 written accounts of near-death experiences. Ketamine reports used words most like the near-death accounts: with the main settings ketamine scored about 0.90 out of 1, against 0.84 for Salvia and 0.83 for LSD; averaged over all the settings tried, ketamine led LSD only narrowly (about 0.64 against 0.61), and the order of other drugs changed with the settings. Nobody was given a drug or asked questions for this study, which compared words, not experiences. The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, nobody checked what the online writers had taken, and the authors say the study cannot show whether a ketamine-like chemical in the brain causes near-death experiences.
population: Two existing collections of written reports, merged by substance: (1) about 15,000 reports from the Erowid Experience Vaults, a curated website holding more than 20,000 reports written by people who chose to submit them, on 165 substances with more than 10 single-substance reports each (demographic information on the writers not commonly available; the authors call the population relatively homogeneous culturally; doses and settings unknown); (2) 625 retrospective narratives (623,926 words) of near-death experiences given in an anonymous voluntary questionnaire to the Division of Perceptual Studies, University of Virginia Health System (USA), and the Coma Science Group, University and University Hospital of Liège (Belgium), all scoring 7 or more on the NDE Scale except 182 collected before the scale existed; 68% women; mean age 31 (SD 15) at the experience and 52 (SD 13) when the account was collected; cause attributed to head injury 13%, anaesthesia or drug use 30%, cardiac arrest 10% (228 missing)
exposure: Reports about ketamine, as named by their writers (substance, dose and route not verified; route words deleted from the texts)
comparator: Reports about each of the other 164 substances, ranked against one another; no collection of other kinds of experience was compared
outcome: Similarity of word use between each substance's merged reports and the merged near-death accounts: the correlation of reduced term-document columns after tf-idf weighting and latent semantic analysis (20 singular values in the main analysis, 5 to 145 in robustness checks); the resulting ranking of substances and of drug classes
magnitude: Martial et al. (2019) print no values, intervals or tests for the ranking itself. Main analysis (20 singular values; Fig. 3, editors' measurement of dot centres at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.90, Salvia divinorum 0.84, Lophophora williamsii (peyote) 0.83, LSD 0.83, 5-MeO-DMT 0.83, psilocybin mushrooms 0.82, DMT 0.82; Datura species (21st in the zoomed panel) 0.72; betel nut (lowest) about 0.08. Mean over 5 to 145 singular values (Fig. 7C, editors' measurement of bar tops at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.64, LSD 0.61, psilocybin mushrooms 0.60, S. divinorum 0.59, cannabis 0.59; L. williamsii 18th. Ketamine first in about 79% of the settings, LSD about 13%, ibogaine about 6%, L. williamsii about 1% and PCP under 1% (Fig. 7D; editors' measurement of the slice angles, approximate; no shares printed). After deleting the 500 most relevant terms of each of two context topics (20 singular values): top ten ketamine, ayahuasca, S. divinorum, L. williamsii, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, cannabis, psilocybin mushrooms, iboga, nitrous oxide. By class (Fig. 4): dissociatives first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics; dissociatives differed from every class except deliriants (pairwise tests at p < 0.05, 12 of 21 pairs marked significant, editors' count; no correction reported). NDE subsets: ketamine first in almost all; LSD comparable after cardiac arrest.

evidence.extracted: What was compared: semantic similarity between about 15,000 reports (printed as ≈15,000 in the abstract and > 15,000 in the Introduction) linked to 165 psychoactive substances and 625 narratives of near-death experiences (NDEs). NDE accounts: experiencers recruited through the Division of Perceptual Studies (University of Virginia Health System, USA) and the Coma Science Group (University and University Hospital of Liège, Belgium), anonymous questionnaire completed voluntarily; 625 retrospective narratives, 623,926 words (printed 623.926); all scored 7 or more on the NDE Scale (mean 15.2, SD 7) except 182 collected before the scale existed; 68% women; age 31 (SD 15) at the experience and 52 (SD 13) when the account was collected; loss of consciousness attributed to head injury in 13%, anaesthesia or drug use in 30% and cardiac arrest in 10% (228 missing; the base of these percentages is not stated); closeness to death rated retrospectively as not serious 27%, serious 37%, loss of vital signs 35% (209 missing); pleasant 82%, neutral 8%, unpleasant 9% (279 missing). Drug reports: downloaded from the Erowid Experience Vaults, which hold more than 20,000 curated reports; reports of combinations and duplicates discarded and only substances with more than 10 reports kept, giving 165 substances classified by hand as serotonergic psychedelics, dissociatives, entactogens, deliriants, depressants or sedatives, stimulants, antipsychotics or antidepressants, oneirogens and others. Nobody was given a drug or examined for this study.

evidence.locator: 2.3 Corpora preprocessing (p. 55); 2.4 Latent semantic analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 55, continuing on p. 56), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs and footnote 2 (p. 56); 3.1 Similarity between NDE and drug-induced experiences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 56)
evidence.extracted: How similarity was scored: words lemmatized and lowercased, words under three letters dropped, and a hand-made list of substance names, slang and route words (for example smoke, snort, inject) deleted from both collections. The authors use semantic similarity of narratives as a proxy for similarity of the experiences, on the stated assumption that two narratives mentioning the same core concepts with similar frequencies likely reflect similar experiences. Each document is all the reports of one substance, or all the NDE narratives; tf-idf weighting kept terms found in more than 5% and less than 95% of documents; singular value decomposition (latent semantic analysis) kept the first 20 singular values, a choice based on the number of drug categories and on earlier work with the same data; similarity is the correlation between the reduced columns. Footnote 2: similarity is measured from word co-occurrences, not from the frequency of single words; a word such as fear can be frequent both in a frightening report and in one stressing the absence of fear, and the authors state that its different co-occurrences with other words increase the semantic distance between such reports.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 52); 4. Discussion, 12th and 13th paragraphs (p. 65); 5. Conclusion (p. 66)
evidence.extracted: The Discussion states that the analyses neither validate nor refute neurochemical models of NDEs, because they rest on retrospective reports and nobody was examined at the time of the NDE, and that unless direct empirical evidence is obtained the authors can only affirm that the reported phenomenology of certain drugs is similar to that of NDEs and that those drugs could be effective tools for the safe and temporary induction of NDE-like states in controlled laboratory settings; such laboratory-induced states may be a mere reflection of authentic NDEs, and some effects of subanaesthetic ketamine are not among the features of NDEs. The abstract says ketamine consistently produced the reports most similar to NDEs, suggests that ketamine could be a safe and reversible experimental model of NDE phenomenology and says the results support the speculation that endogenous NMDA antagonists may be released near death; the Conclusion says ketamine can produce an altered state resembling near-death, while stating that the release of an endogenous ketamine-like agent can be neither corroborated nor refuted. Safety was not studied.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_martial_2019 (ROBINS-E, checked and adjudicated): overall high, with high judgments for confounding, measurement of the exposure, selection and measurement of the outcome. The reports are self-selected (volunteers to NDE research groups; people who chose to write for Erowid, which curates the collection), unverified (substance and dose as named by the writer) and merged by substance, with writers, doses, settings and expectations unknown and not adjusted for, in a culture that has long compared ketamine with dying (Introduction, p. 53); the outcome, correlated word use, has not been validated as a measure of experience (p. 63), and hand-made word lists and drug classes shape it (p. 55). These biases could plausibly change a ranking in which ketamine's lead is small: rated down two levels.

inconsistency.note: One study. The earlier comparison of 36 cardiac-arrest NDE accounts with 36 people's ketamine experiences (Corazza and Schifano, 2010) and the placebo-controlled DMT study in 13 volunteers (Timmermann et al., 2018) are known only as this paper summarizes them (pp. 53–54) and are not used.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for what was measured, the word use of written reports merged by substance, and states that this does not show the experiences to be alike. Whether a ketamine experience is like a near-death experience is a different question that this design cannot answer, and the claim does not answer it.

imprecision.note: The ranking carries no measure of uncertainty; averaged over settings, ketamine's lead over LSD was about 0.02 on a 0-to-1 scale (editors' reading of Fig. 7C), LSD ranked comparably for NDEs after cardiac arrest, and rankings computed with very different settings compared poorly (p. 59).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one exploratory analysis; no protocol or registration is mentioned.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional text analysis of two existing collections of written reports) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one for imprecision, it is very low, the floor. Rated as worded: an association between the substance a report names and how closely its pooled word use resembles pooled near-death accounts, in these two self-selected collections. The claim does not say that ketamine produces an experience like a near-death experience, that near-death experiences have a ketamine-like chemical cause, or that ketamine is a safe experimental model: the abstract's and conclusion's statements to that effect are not adopted, because safety was not studied and the discussion itself says the analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical models (p. 65). What the design cannot show is said in the statement: word co-occurrence is not experience, the near-death accounts were written about two decades after the events and some followed anaesthesia or drug use, and nothing about the Erowid writers or their doses is known. 'Is associated with' because the design is observational and the certainty very low (METHODS §6.1). Values are the editors' readings of figures that print none, labelled as approximate. Status single study.

statement: In adults aged 18 to 64 with moderate to severe major depression without psychosis whose current episode had not improved with at least two antidepressants, one of them watched in the trial for at least 4 weeks (people with recent moderate or severe substance use disorder, bipolar or psychotic disorders or suicidal intent were excluded), studied in two phase 3 trials run by the company that applied for its licence, Janssen, at outpatient centres in Europe and the Americas in 2015 to 2018, esketamine (the S-form of ketamine) nasal spray, which participants gave themselves in the clinic under supervision twice a week for 4 weeks together with a newly started oral antidepressant (trial conditions: 56 or 84 mg per session), compared with a placebo spray with a bitter taste added, together with a newly started oral antidepressant, is associated with clinician-rated depression scores (MADRS, 0 to 60; about 37 at the start) that fell about 3 to 4 points more by day 28, with intervals running from no difference or almost none to about 7 points: −4.0 (95% CI −7.31 to −0.64; 114 and 109 analysed; effect size 0.30) in TRANSFORM-2, where the dose could be raised from 56 to 84 mg, which met its primary endpoint (Popova et al., 2019), and −3.2 (−6.88 to 0.45; p = 0.088) with 84 mg in TRANSFORM-1 (115, 114 and 113 analysed), which did not, so that its 56 mg result (−4.1, −7.67 to −0.49) is exploratory by the trial's own rules (Fedgchin et al., 2019). TRANSFORM-2's authors report that a third short trial, in people aged 65 or older, found −3.6, also not statistically significant (cited as a conference abstract; not read). A fast start was not shown: in TRANSFORM-2 the prespecified test, a halving of scores by day 2 that lasted to day 28, was met by 9 of 114 (8 in 100) on esketamine and 5 of 109 (5 in 100) on the comparator (p = 0.321), and the day-15 difference was −2.0 (−4.78 to 0.82); in TRANSFORM-1 the same test (12 of 115 and 10 of 114 against 2 of 113) could not be formally made. Among those rated at day 28 in TRANSFORM-2, 70 of 101 (69 in 100) against 52 of 100 (52 in 100) had a halving of scores and 53 of 101 (52 in 100) against 31 of 100 (31 in 100) had few symptoms left (remission), in analyses added after the fact. In TRANSFORM-1 the 84 mg difference was 0.0 (SE 3.08) in the 121 people enrolled before an interim analysis and −5.6 (SE 2.31) in the 221 enrolled after it; the authors say that changes made while the trial was running (audio-recording of interviews, new experienced sites, more training and an open-label long-term esketamine study) affected the people enrolled later; 19 of 116 (16 in 100) left the 84 mg arm early, 11 after the first dose, against 6 of 117 and 6 of 113. In an earlier phase 2 trial of 67 adults who kept taking their own antidepressant, scores after 1 week fell 5.0, 7.6 and 10.5 points more with 28, 56 and 84 mg than with placebo spray (11, 11, 12 and 33 people), and 5 of 12 on 84 mg against 2 of 33 on placebo spray had a halving of scores; its printed P values correspond to one-sided tests (editors' calculation) (Daly et al., 2018). In a relapse-prevention trial, SUSTAIN-1, 297 of 705 people enrolled were randomized after 16 weeks on esketamine because they were in stable remission or stable response, some of them having entered after responding in the two short trials (115 by the footnotes of the paper's Table 1, whose sub-rows give other counts); among the 176 in stable remission, 24 of 90 (27 in 100) who continued esketamine relapsed against 39 of 86 (45 in 100) switched to placebo spray (hazard ratio 0.49, 0.29 to 0.84), and among the 121 with stable response, 16 of 62 (26 in 100) against 34 of 59 (58 in 100) (0.30, 0.16 to 0.55); 19 of the 39 relapses after switching came within 4 weeks, 6 of them within 2; the design cannot tell a return of depression from an effect of stopping the drug, and whether people noticed the switch was not checked (Daly et al., 2019). Dissociation (feeling detached or unreal) was reported by 26 to 28 in 100 on esketamine against about 4 in 100 on placebo spray in the short trials (30 of 115 against 4 of 109; 30 of 115 and 32 of 116 against 4 of 113), and by 35 of 152 who continued esketamine against none of 145 switched to placebo spray in SUSTAIN-1; no trial asked participants which spray they thought they had, and TRANSFORM-2's authors took a rise in dissociation scores after the placebo spray as evidence that the blinding was adequate. All four trials were funded by Janssen, whose employees were 10 of 16 (TRANSFORM-2), 10 of 18 (TRANSFORM-1), 8 of 11 (phase 2) and 12 of 23 (SUSTAIN-1) of the authors. A meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials of ketamine or esketamine, 10 of them of esketamine including three of these (no funding), found esketamine's effect on depression scores clear in the first days after a first dose (standardized differences −0.55 and −0.48 for its lower and higher dose categories) but not clearly different from control during repeated dosing (−0.15, −0.49 to 0.19; −0.22, −0.54 to 0.10) or after the last dose (−0.33, −0.96 to 0.31), while response and remission during repeated dosing were more frequent in the higher dose category (odds ratios 1.42, 1.07 to 1.90, and 1.52, 1.27 to 1.82) (Nikolin et al., 2023). Two published critiques argue that the evidence behind its approval is weak: a former reviewer at the US Food and Drug Administration argued from the regulator's advisory-committee documents that two of the three short phase 3 trials failed, that the relapse trial was enriched with people who had done well on esketamine and its result depended on one site in Poland, and that the effect was no larger than that of cheaper treatments (Turner, 2019); two psychiatrists, one a co-chair of the Critical Psychiatry Network, argued that the 4-point difference is of doubtful clinical relevance, that participants were likely unblinded by the drug's effects, and that relapse after switching could be withdrawal (Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021). A single-author commentary published with TRANSFORM-2 in the same journal issue, by a psychiatrist who declares grant support from Janssen and consulting for it among many companies, questioned whether efficacy had been clearly shown and called its strength apparently mild, asked whether, with every participant also starting an antidepressant, the trials show any need to continue esketamine beyond its first uses, called the use of the relapse-prevention study as a second positive trial unusual, and still judged that esketamine could help many people with hard-to-treat depression (Schatzberg, 2019); it enters as what it argues, and none of its figures, all second-hand and none given in full, is used. Certainty: low. Status: contested.
plain: In two 4-week trials paid for by the company that applied for its licence, adults whose depression had not lifted with at least two antidepressants were picked at random for esketamine nasal spray (a form of ketamine) or a dummy spray with a bitter taste, each with a newly started antidepressant, taken in the clinic. Depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine; one trial passed its main test and the other did not, and a fast start was not shown. In a third trial, people whose depression had lifted on esketamine relapsed less often if they kept taking it (27 in 100) than if they were switched to a dummy spray (45 in 100), but that trial cannot tell a return of depression from effects of stopping the drug. About 1 in 4 people felt detached or unreal on esketamine, against about 4 in 100 on the dummy spray, and nobody checked whether people could tell which spray they had. Pooling trials, a review found a clear effect in the first days after a first dose but not a clear difference in depression scores during weeks of treatment. Critics argue the evidence behind its approval is weak, among them a psychiatrist who has consulted for the company, writing in the journal issue that published one of the trials.
population: Adults with treatment-resistant major depression without psychotic features in trials funded by Janssen: TRANSFORM-2 (Popova et al., 2019): 227 randomized and counted, 223 analysed (114 and 109), aged 18 to 64, at 39 outpatient referral centres in the Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, Spain and the USA, August 2015 to November 2017, mean baseline MADRS 37.0 and 37.3, 93% White; TRANSFORM-1 (Fedgchin et al., 2019): 346 randomized, 342 analysed (115, 114 and 113), aged 18 to 64, outpatient centres in Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Estonia, France, Hungary, Mexico, Slovakia and the USA, September 2015 to February 2018, mean baseline MADRS 37.4 to 37.8; both requiring non-response to at least two antidepressants in the current episode, one observed prospectively for at least 4 weeks (6 weeks of treatment in all); phase 2 (Daly et al., 2018): 67 adults aged 20 to 64 with inadequate response to two or more antidepressants, at least one in the current episode, 14 sites in the USA and Belgium, 2014 to 2015; SUSTAIN-1 (Daly et al., 2019): 705 enrolled and 297 randomized after 16 weeks of esketamine in stable remission (176) or stable response (121), 115 of them transferred from TRANSFORM-1 or TRANSFORM-2 by the footnotes of Table 1 (its dose sub-rows give 228 transferred, and the paper does not say which count is right), 99 sites in the USA, Canada, Europe, Brazil and Mexico, October 2015 to February 2018. All excluded psychotic and bipolar disorders, recent moderate or severe substance use disorder (any substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year in phase 2) and suicidal intent.
exposure: Esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine) nasal spray self-administered at the clinic under supervision, three devices per session (28 mg of esketamine per active device; placebo devices to make up the number), twice weekly for 4 weeks (trial conditions: TRANSFORM-2 flexible, starting at 56 mg and raised to 84 mg at the investigator's judgment, 66.7% on 84 mg at the end; TRANSFORM-1 fixed 56 mg, or 84 mg after 56 mg on day 1), each with a newly started open-label oral antidepressant (duloxetine, escitalopram, sertraline or extended-release venlafaxine); phase 2: 28, 56 or 84 mg on days 1 and 4 added to the participant's ongoing antidepressant; SUSTAIN-1: continued at 56 or 84 mg weekly or every 2 weeks with the oral antidepressant after 16 weeks of open-label or double-blind treatment
comparator: A placebo nasal spray with a bittering agent added to mimic the taste, in identical devices on the same schedule, with the same newly started oral antidepressant (phase 2: with the ongoing antidepressant; SUSTAIN-1: switching from esketamine to the placebo spray while the oral antidepressant continued, the devices not described as identical); no active placebo mimicking esketamine's acute effects, and no comparison with other treatments
outcome: Change in clinician-rated MADRS (0 to 60; in the phase 3 trials by remote telephone raters blind to visit, clinical status and side effects) from baseline to day 28 (TRANSFORM-1 and TRANSFORM-2, primary) or day 8 (phase 2, primary); prespecified onset of response by day 2 kept to day 28; response (a fall of at least 50%) and remission (MADRS 12 or less, post hoc in TRANSFORM-2); time to relapse (MADRS 22 or more on two assessments 5 to 15 days apart, or hospitalization or other events) in SUSTAIN-1; adverse events, dissociation and stopping for adverse events
magnitude: TRANSFORM-2: least-squares mean difference at day 28 −4.0 (SE 1.69; 95% CI −7.31 to −0.64; p = 0.020; effect size 0.30); day 2 −3.3 (−5.75 to −0.85), day 8 −2.9 (−5.17 to −0.59), day 15 −2.0 (−4.78 to 0.82), day 22 −3.8 (−6.87 to −0.65); onset of response by day 2 kept to day 28 9/114 (7.9%) against 5/109 (4.6%), p = 0.321; post hoc response 70/101 (69.3%) against 52/100 (52.0%), odds ratio 2.4 (95% credible interval 1.30 to 4.54); remission 53/101 (52.5%) against 31/100 (31.0%); dissociation 30/115 (26.1%) against 4/109 (3.7%); spray stopped for adverse events 8/115 (7.0%) against 1/109 (0.9%). TRANSFORM-1 (weighted median unbiased estimates, two-sided flexible 95% CIs): 84 mg −3.2 (−6.88 to 0.45; p = 0.088); 56 mg −4.1 (−7.67 to −0.49; nominal p = 0.027); stage 1 (n = 121) 84 mg 0.0 (SE 3.08), 56 mg −3.6 (SE 3.13); stage 2 (n = 221) −5.6 (SE 2.31) and −4.5 (SE 2.21); onset of response 12/115 (10.4%), 10/114 (8.8%) against 2/113 (1.8%), not testable; response 54.1%, 53.1% and 38.9%, remission 36.0%, 38.8% and 30.6% (denominators not printed); withdrawals 6/117, 19/116 and 6/113; dissociation 30/115 (26.1%), 32/116 (27.6%) and 4/113 (3.5%). Phase 2 (period 1, day 8): −5.0 (SE 2.99), −7.6 (2.91) and −10.5 (2.79) for 28, 56 and 84 mg; periods combined −4.2 (90% CI −7.67 to −0.79), −6.3 (−9.71 to −2.88) and −9.0 (−12.53 to −5.52), P = .02, .001 and < .001, one-sided (editors' calculation; 95% CIs −8.3 to −0.1, −10.4 to −2.2 and −13.2 to −4.8); day-8 responders 2/33, 1/11, 2/11 and 5/12. SUSTAIN-1: stable remission 24/90 (26.7%) against 39/86 (45.3%), hazard ratio 0.49 (0.29 to 0.84), P = .003; stable response 16/62 (25.8%) against 34/59 (57.6%), 0.30 (0.16 to 0.55), P < .001; editors' calculation: absolute differences 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 4.7 to 32.6) and 31.8 (15.2 to 48.5), over event-driven follow-up of varying length; 19 of 39 relapses after switching within 4 weeks (6 by week 2); maintenance dissociation 35/152 (23.0%) against 0/145. Meta-analysis (Nikolin et al., 2023; 10 esketamine trials among 49): standardized mean differences after a first dose −0.55 (−0.87 to −0.24) low and −0.48 (−0.75 to −0.20) high dose category; during repeated dosing −0.15 (−0.49 to 0.19) and −0.22 (−0.54 to 0.10); after the last dose −0.33 (−0.96 to 0.31); response during repeated dosing odds ratio 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90) high and 1.37 (0.91 to 2.05) low; remission 1.52 (1.27 to 1.82) high; remission after the last dose 1.80 (1.14 to 2.82).

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Study Design, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs, and Study Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 2–3); Randomization and Blinding; Intranasal Study Drug and Administration, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Newly Initiated Oral Antidepressant, 1st paragraph; Efficacy Assessments, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial (the trial the answer calls TRANSFORM-2; that name is not printed in this paper) at 39 outpatient referral centres: 6 in the Czech Republic, 9 in Germany, 7 in Poland, 7 in Spain and 10 in the USA, August 2015 to November 2017. Adults aged 18 to 64 with single-episode (2 years or more) or recurrent DSM-5 major depression without psychotic features, IDS-C 34 or more, and non-response to adequate trials of at least two antidepressants in the current episode, one observed prospectively: entrants had documented non-response (25% improvement or less) to one to five antidepressants and were taking a different one, continued for 4 more weeks (at least 6 weeks in all); those with 25% or less MADRS improvement from week 1 to week 4 and a MADRS of 28 or more at weeks 2 and 4 stopped all antidepressants and were randomized 1:1 (computer-generated schedule, permuted blocks, stratified by country and antidepressant class). Key exclusions: suicidal ideation with intent in the past 6 months or suicidal behaviour in the past year; psychotic, bipolar and several personality disorders; uncontrolled hypertension; moderate or severe substance use disorder in the past 6 months or lifetime ketamine use disorder; positive urine tests for specified drugs (no ketamine test was available); earlier non-response to esketamine, ketamine or ECT. Trial conditions: identical devices, each giving two sprays (28 mg of esketamine, or placebo with a bittering agent to mimic its taste), three devices at every session in both arms; esketamine started at 56 mg on day 1 and could be raised to 84 mg on day 4, 8, 11 or 15 at the investigator's judgment; self-administered at the clinic under the investigator's direct supervision twice weekly for 4 weeks, each arm with a newly started open-label oral antidepressant (escitalopram, sertraline, duloxetine or extended-release venlafaxine) chosen by the investigator. Because esketamine's dissociative effects are difficult to blind, all MADRS ratings were done by independent remote raters by telephone, blind to protocol details, study visit, clinical status and side effects; patients, investigators, site staff, assessors and analysts are described as blind.
