risk_of_bias.note: Cards (RoB 2, checked and adjudicated): sc_popova_2019 and sc_fedgchin_2019 some concerns; sc_daly_2018 high; sc_daly_2019 high (measurement of the outcome). Esketamine's acute effects (dissociation in 26 to 28 in 100 against about 4 in 100; sedation; blood-pressure rises) could have told participants and the staff supervising dosing which spray was given; the outcome rests on what participants told telephone raters; no trial checked blinding, and the inert comparator could not mimic the drug's effects. With differences of 3 to 4 points whose intervals reach almost zero, a modest expectation bias could account for much of the effect, and its direction (favouring esketamine) is known. In SUSTAIN-1, people switched to placebo after 16 weeks could notice the loss of familiar effects, and relapse cannot be separated from effects of stopping. Rated down one level, not two, because randomization, identical devices, remote raters and prespecified analyses are sound and losses were small except in TRANSFORM-1's 84 mg arm (19 of 116).

inconsistency.note: Not rated down: the short trials' point estimates agree (−3.2 to −4.1 against a newly started antidepressant with placebo spray; −3.6 in people aged 65 or older as reported second-hand) and differ in statistical significance because of imprecision, rated there. The stage-to-stage difference within TRANSFORM-1 (0.0 against −5.6) coincided with changes in how the trial was run and is not inconsistency between studies. The meta-analysis's repeated-dosing estimates pool largely the same trials and are counted with imprecision.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for the trials' population (adults up to 64 with treatment-resistant depression, with many exclusions), for esketamine added to a newly started or ongoing oral antidepressant under supervision, against a placebo spray with an antidepressant (not against other treatments), for 4 weeks (short trials) or for people who had already responded (relapse trial). It says nothing about other groups, esketamine alone or comparisons with other treatments, none of which were tested.

imprecision.note: The 95% intervals for the 4-week differences reach from −0.64 (TRANSFORM-2) or past zero (TRANSFORM-1, 84 mg, up to +0.45) to about −7 points, so they include both a trivial and a moderate effect; TRANSFORM-2 was sized for 6.5 points and found 4.0; the pooled esketamine estimates during repeated dosing include no difference (Nikolin et al., 2023). SUSTAIN-1 stopped at 63 relapses among remitters, fewer than the 84 first planned, and its absolute difference (editors' calculation) is 18.7 points with an interval from 4.7 to 32.6.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down: the failed TRANSFORM-1 was published, and the trial in older adults, unpublished when TRANSFORM-2 and Turner (2019) were written, is pooled in the 2023 meta-analysis; that every trial was run by the manufacturer is recorded under risk of bias and in the debate box.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; rated down one level for risk of bias (unchecked blinding against a drug with noticeable effects, on a participant-reported outcome) and one for imprecision (intervals from almost no effect to a moderate one; one of two phase 3 short trials failed its primary test): low. Rated as worded: a short-term difference of about 3 to 4 MADRS points against a newly started antidepressant with placebo spray in adults with treatment-resistant depression, and, in people who had already responded, fewer relapses when esketamine was continued than when it was switched to placebo spray; the claim does not say that esketamine works fast, that it is better than other treatments, or that the relapse result shows prevention rather than effects of stopping. The phase 2 dose ordering is not used to rate up, because randomized evidence is not upgraded (METHODS §6.3) and its P values are one-sided. Overlap: the four trials share the sponsor and several authors (Daly, Lim, Manji, Drevets and Singh are on all four), some of SUSTAIN-1's 297 randomized patients came from the two short trials (115 by the footnotes of its Table 1, whose sub-rows give other counts), and the meta-analysis contains three of the trials, so agreement among them is not independent replication. Status contested (METHODS §6.4, §7): two credible published critiques, one by a former FDA medical officer working from the regulator's own documents, change how the approval evidence is read (failed trials, enrichment, a single-site result, unblinding, withdrawal), and the pooled estimates during repeated dosing do not clearly separate esketamine from control, so the six-part debate box applies. The critiques enter as what they argue, not as data, and so does a commentary published with TRANSFORM-2 by a psychiatrist who declares grant support from and consulting for Janssen, which raises overlapping doubts (Schatzberg, 2019); none of its figures, all second-hand and none given in full, is used. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). The journal's correction to TRANSFORM-2 (Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(8):669), now read, changes only one Table 1 percentage, which this answer does not use; the numbers used are from the advance version. TRANSFORM-3 (older adults) is reported only as TRANSFORM-2's authors cite it and is not used as data. Stays draft until the new anchor to Schatzberg (2019) is checked.

debate.question: Does esketamine nasal spray, added to an oral antidepressant, lift hard-to-treat depression more than an antidepressant with a dummy spray, and does continuing it prevent relapse, as the manufacturer's trials report (Daly et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019), or are the differences too small, too uncertain and too exposed to unblinding and to the effects of stopping to show that it works, as published critiques argue (Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021; Turner, 2019)?
debate.evidence_yes: In TRANSFORM-2, 223 adults with treatment-resistant depression were randomized to esketamine spray or a bitter placebo spray, each with a newly started antidepressant; by day 28, scores on a 0-to-60 depression scale had fallen 4.0 points more with esketamine (95% CI −7.31 to −0.64), the prespecified primary result, rated by telephone raters blind to visit, clinical status and side effects (Popova et al., 2019). The 4-week differences in TRANSFORM-1 were of similar size (−3.2 with 84 mg, −4.1 with 56 mg), and −5.6 and −4.5 among the 221 people enrolled after its interim analysis (Fedgchin et al., 2019). In the phase 2 trial the 1-week differences rose with dose (−5.0, −7.6 and −10.5 points with 28, 56 and 84 mg) (Daly et al., 2018). Among people who had responded, those who continued esketamine relapsed less often than those switched to placebo spray (24 of 90 against 39 of 86 in stable remission, hazard ratio 0.49; 16 of 62 against 34 of 59 in stable response, 0.30), with similar hazard ratios for patients who entered directly (0.49) and those transferred from the short trials (0.45), when each site was left out in turn (0.42 to 0.57; no intervals printed), and when 3 relapsing patients whose dissociation scores changed around randomization were censored (0.50) (Daly et al., 2019). Among those rated at day 28, 53 of 101 on esketamine against 31 of 100 on the comparator were in remission (Popova et al., 2019). Pooling 10 randomized esketamine trials, depression scores in the first days after a first dose were lower than with control (standardized differences −0.48 and −0.55), and response and remission during repeated dosing were more frequent in the higher dose category (odds ratios 1.42 and 1.52), as was remission after the last dose (1.80) (Nikolin et al., 2023). The trial authors note that the comparator was itself a newly started antidepressant, not a placebo alone, and argue that differences of this size exceed thresholds considered clinically meaningful for approved antidepressants (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019).
debate.evidence_no: Of the two phase 3 short trials read, the fixed-dose one failed its primary test (84 mg −3.2, 95% CI −6.88 to 0.45), so its 56 mg result is exploratory; its 84 mg difference was 0.0 in the 121 people enrolled before changes were made to how the trial was run, and 19 of 116 left that arm early (Fedgchin et al., 2019); the authors of the positive trial report that the third short trial, in people aged 65 or older, also missed significance (−3.6) (Popova et al., 2019). The positive trial found 4.0 points, less than the 6.5 it was designed to detect, with an interval reaching −0.64; its prespecified test of a fast start failed (9 of 114 against 5 of 109), and its day-15 interval included no difference (Popova et al., 2019). Dissociation affected 26 to 28 in 100 on esketamine against about 4 in 100 on placebo spray, yet no trial asked participants what they thought they had received, and the outcome rested on what they told telephone raters (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019); the phase 2 trial's P values were one-sided and its authors name the difficulty of blinding esketamine as a limitation (Daly et al., 2018). In the relapse trial only 297 of 705 enrolled people, those who had done well on esketamine for 16 weeks, were randomized; half of the relapses after switching came within 4 weeks; and people switched to placebo spray stopped having effects they had felt for months (dissociation in 0 of 145 against 35 of 152) (Daly et al., 2019). Pooling 10 trials, esketamine's effect on depression scores was not clearly different from control during repeated dosing (standardized differences −0.22, 95% CI −0.54 to 0.10, and −0.15, −0.49 to 0.19) or after the last dose (−0.33, −0.96 to 0.31) (Nikolin et al., 2023). A former FDA medical officer argued that the relapse result depended on one site in Poland and that the effect was no larger than that of cheaper treatments (Turner, 2019), and two psychiatrists argued that relapse after switching could reflect withdrawal and that a 4-point difference is of doubtful clinical relevance (Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021). A commentary published with TRANSFORM-2, by a psychiatrist who declares grant support from and consulting for Janssen, questioned whether efficacy had been clearly shown and whether, with every participant also starting an antidepressant, the trials show any need to continue esketamine beyond its first uses (Schatzberg, 2019).
debate.neither_can_show: No trial checked whether participants could tell which spray they had, so neither side can say how much of the 3- to 4-point differences reflects expectation rather than the drug (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019); an inert spray with a bitter taste cannot mimic dissociation (Daly et al., 2018). The relapse trial's design cannot separate a return of depression from an effect of stopping the drug, and it had no tapering arm; the withdrawal explanation is an argument, not a measurement, and so is the trial authors' contrary reasoning from esketamine's short half-life (Daly et al., 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021). The short trials lasted 4 weeks and compared esketamine with a placebo spray, not with other treatments for hard-to-treat depression, so the comparisons with other drugs that trial authors and critics make across different trials cannot settle which works better (Popova et al., 2019; Turner, 2019). All four trials were run by the manufacturer in adults up to 64 years old without psychosis, recent substance use disorder or suicidal intent (Daly et al., 2018; Daly et al., 2019; Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019), and the meta-analysis pools largely the same trials, so its agreement with them is not independent replication (Nikolin et al., 2023).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: low). In adults with treatment-resistant depression, esketamine spray added to a newly started oral antidepressant was followed by depression scores about 3 to 4 points lower on a 0-to-60 scale after 4 weeks than a placebo spray with an antidepressant, in two manufacturer-run trials, one meeting its primary test and one not (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019); the intervals run from almost no effect to a moderate one, a fast start was not shown in the trial that tested it, and how large the difference is once expectation is removed is unknown, because blinding was never checked. In people who had already done well on it for 16 weeks, those switched to a placebo spray relapsed more often and sooner than those who continued (Daly et al., 2019), which fits a benefit of continuing, an effect of stopping a drug with noticeable effects, or both; the evidence read cannot tell these apart. Pooled trials agree on a short-term difference after a first dose but not clearly on a sustained one during treatment (Nikolin et al., 2023). The critiques' re-analyses of summary data and a commentary's doubts, like the trial authors' comparisons with other drugs, are arguments rather than findings and are not used as data (Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021; Schatzberg, 2019; Turner, 2019). The editors' answer: a small short-term difference that may be real but whose size is uncertain, and a relapse result in responders that cannot be separated from the effects of stopping.
debate.what_would_settle_it: An independent trial, not run by the manufacturer, in people with hard-to-treat depression, comparing esketamine spray with an active placebo that has noticeable effects of its own, asking participants, raters and staff to guess the allocation, and following remission, daily functioning and harms for 6 to 12 months, which the short trials did not do (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019); a relapse-prevention trial with a gradual-taper arm and a blinding check, to separate relapse from effects of stopping, the alternative that the critics raise and the trial could not exclude (Daly et al., 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021); and large head-to-head trials of esketamine against racemic ketamine and other treatments for hard-to-treat depression, which the meta-analysis authors call for (Nikolin et al., 2023).
